THE BELLS OF TRINITY. The bells of Trinity ring out, And far and wide their music ring; Above the noise and tramp and shout, Between the earth and heavens they ring. A moment stay Upon your way, And hear them say: "Chime, happy bells, all strife above— Chime, chime, The Bread of Life is Lore.'" The bells of Trinity ring out Like tongues of angels, glad and stron, • The hammer's beat, the workman'sohout, Their wondrous harmonies prolong. A moment stay Upon your way, And hear them say: "Brave hearts, true hearts, no duty shirk; Labour: The Salr of Life is Work.'" The bells of Trinity ring glad, Ring happily o'er ioy and grief, And hearts with dark despairing sad Find in their chime some sweet relief. "Hope on," they say; "The dalining day Drives clouds away. If faint and thirsty In the serife, Then Hope, for Hope's the Stream of Life." The bells of Trinity ring clear , Above the sounds of trade and gain ; And weak souls, halting in their fear, Perchance may hear this bolder strain: "Flee not from grief ; Time brings relief— The watch is brief. Hold on ; be patient iu the strife, For Patience is the Strength of Life." The bells of Trinity ring sweet. Ah ! gentle soul, if you draw near, Perchance may drop into the street Some tones so musical and clear That day by day Upon your way, Your soul shall say, "I know, though I be true and strong, The Sweetness of my Life is Song." The bells of 'Trinity ring high, Ring far and wide, ring east and west. 0 toiling men that fear and sigh, Hear what they say and be at root: " True hearts, good cheer! There is no fear, For God is near. However hard and dark the strife, Trust Rim: Faith is the Light of Life." —Harper's Weekly.

• THE SELFISH OYSTER. There once was a selfish old Oyster Who lived like a snook in a moister. Safely housed in his shell. Like the monk in his cell, Though the bivalve's apartment was moister. Anchored tight in the mad of the bay This lazy old party did stay , Nor cared he to roam Very far from his horn.. For exertion, he thought, did not pay. And you will be wondering, I think, What he did tar his victuals and drink. Well, the OyC'er was sly. And when young crabs came by. He would catch them as quick as a *Elk. Then in him the poor crabs had to stay. Till in time they had melted away. So the Oyster got fatter, And the crahs —but no matter— For crabs have no souls, poople say. " And. Oho!" said the Oyster, said be: "What a lucky old party I be! Like a king in his pride I wait here, and the tide Every day brings my living to me." But there came a grim Starfish, who spied, Our friend lying flat on his side. For the greedy 91,1 sinner Had just bad his dinner, And now could not run had be tried. With a spring to the Oyster became, And he threw his five ar/IS round the etMe ; He shut off his breAt'i. And be equees?.l him to death Toon he ate him, nor felt any shame. The point of this story, my dears. 'Just • as plain as a pikestaff" appears. But p'ecune give attrnsion. While briefly I mention The mere( again, for your ears : .Don't be greedy and live but to eat. Caring only for bread and for meat ; Nor selfishly dwell . All alone in your shell.— Don't be oysters. In short. I repeat. But, you'd find it much better for you To be kind, and unselfish. ard true Then you'll not lack a friend Your cause to defend, Wlaen a Starfish rolls Into7your view.

Two menageries arrived in a town, one of which was under the management of Signor B—, and the other that of his wife, travelling respectively on their own account. Here they decided to join their forces, and the fact was nonnced on the bills as follows:—" Owing to the arrival of my wife, my collection of living animals is considerably augmented.—B—." An actor bought a gallon of gin to take home and, by way of label, wrote his name upon a Card, which happened to be the seven of clubs and tied it to the handle. Sheri- dan coming along, and Observing the jag, quietly' remarkei, "That's an awful careless way to leave that 'liquor!" "Why?" asked a friend. "Because some one might come along with the eight of clubs and take it." "Mr. Smith. do you know the character of Mr. Jones?" Wall, I rather guess I do, Jedge." "Well, what do you sty about it ?" "Wall, he ain't so bad a man after all." Well, Mr. Smith, what we want to know is—ls Mr. Jones of a quarrelsome :led dangerous disposition ?" "Wall, Jedge, I should say that Tom Jones is very vivid in verbal exercise, but when it comes to personal adjustment he hain't eager for the contest." One evening a certain Midi saw in his book that "Every- body who has a small head and a large beard is a fool." The Kddi had a small head and a very large beard. He said to himself, "To make my head large is not in my power, but I'll make my heard small." He looked for the scissors—didn't find them. Helpless, he:grasped half his beard with his hand, and held the middle of it to a lamp; but the fire spread and burned the whole of his beard away. The Kith was much abashed to find that what the book said turned out to be so true.—Aunt Judy's Magazine. Once at a little dinner party one oithe guests, the younger " brother of an English nobleman, expressed with commend- able freedom his opinion of America and its people. "I do not altogether like the country," said the young gentleman. "for one reason; because you have no gentry here." that do you mean by gentry ?" asked another of the MD* y. Well, you know," replied the Englishman, "well— oh, gentry are those who never do any work themselves, and whose fathers before them never did any:' "Ah !" ex- claimed his interlocutor, " then we have plenty of gentry in America. But we don't call them gentry; we call them tramps !" A laugh went round the table, and the young Englishman turned his conversation into another channel." SCENES IN THE ROMAN SENATE.—We complain' and justly, of obstruction in the English Parliament, but it must be admitted that the following scenes in the Roman • Senate when it was proposed to restore to Cicero the site of his house destroyed at the time of his exile, for services to the State, exceeded anything as yet common in our High Court of Parliament mot' m was made that the site should be restored. Clodius opposed it, talking for three hours, till the anger of his amlience compelled him to bring his speech to an end. One of the tribunes in his interest put his veto on the motion, but was frightened into with- drawing it. But Clodins was not at the end of his resources. A set of armed ruffians under his command drove out the workmen who were rebuilding the house. A few days after- wards he made an attack on Cicero himself. He was wounded in the struggle which followed, and might, says Cicero, have been killed, "But," he adds, "I am tired of surgery." Pompey was another object of his hatred, for he knew perfectly well that without his consent his great enemy would not have been restored. Cicero gives a lively picture of a scene in the Senate, in wtdch this hatred was ' vigorously expressed. "Pompey spoke' or rather wished to speak; for.as soon as he rose,Clodius's hired ruffians shouted at him. ill through his speech it was the same; he was hi- tented not only by shouts, but by abuse and curses. When he came to an end—and it must be allowed that he showed courage; nothing frightened him; he said his say and sometimes even obtained silence—then Clodius rose. He was met with such an uproar from our side (for we had deter- mined to give him back as good as he had given) that he could not collect his thoughts, control his speech, or command his countenance. This went on from three o'clock, when Pom- pey had only just finished his speech, till five. Meanwhile every kind of abase, even to ribald verses, were shouted out against Clodias and his sister. Pale with fury he turned to his followersaind in the midst of the uproar aAked them, Who is it that is killinc the people with hunger?' Pom- pey,' they answered. Who wants to go to Alexandria?' , 'Pompey,' they answered again. ' And whom do you want to go?' 'Crassus,' they said. About six o clock the party of Clodius began, at some given signal, it seemed, to spit at "- our side. Our rage now burst out. They tried to drive no from our place, and we made a charge. The partisans of Cledias fled. He was thrust down from the hustings. I then made my escape, lest anything worse phonic! happen." —"Roman Life in the Days of Cicero." Professor T. G. Bonney some time ago announced the discovery at Anglesea of a boulder of picrite which he re- gards as unique, and as evidencing a very extended trans- port, since picrite4o far as he knows, is not found in situ in Britain. Mr. John Plant, the curator of the Salford Royal Museum, writes to the Geological I.lageLs-ine to say that he had known the boulder at Pen-y-Carnisiog for some years before its removal to London, and that in the prepara- tion of the monograph on the south-west coast of.Anglesea, which has occupied his holidays for several summZrs, he has constructed a map which will show more than one locality where the mineral picrite is bedded in. situ. M. Melsens, of the Belgian Academy of Sciences, has re- cently been performing experiments to show that water in boilers may be prevented from entering into the speroidal state in consequence of over-heating (an alleged frequent cause of explosions), by covering the surface of the metal with small conical protuberances. Two metal compart- ments, one with a smooth interior, and the other with the interior raised into minute points as described, were heated to a very high temperature, and water was then poured into both. The water on the pointed surface immediately en- tered into ebullition, and gave off vapours, while that on the smooth surface of course assumed the speroidal state. TRH NEW COMET.—As seen by M. Fronnelot at Mar- seilles the Pons-Brooks comet (believed to be that of 1812) has a pear shape, the head enclosing a nucleus several de- grees brighter than the hair or corona around it. The dia- meter of the hair was about 10min., and -the length of the tail 25min. from the nucleus. The brightness of the nucleus is that of a star of the sixth magnitude, and it is almost spherical in shape, an elongation in the direction of the tail being noticeable. Notes to the French Academy of Sciences by MM. Thollon and Trepeid state that the head displays the three-band spectrum of hydrocarbon compounds ; and M. Trepeid has also observed a faint continuous spectrum from the nucleus which he considers lobe that of reflected sunlight. Mr. C. J. Seddon, of New Ferry, writes under date Jan. 16: —"lt is'very curious"that, so far as I have seen, there have not been any csmtnunications to the papers about a comet that is now visible or leading the public to expect one about this time, and only a very few have seen it; but I, along with others, most distinctly saw one last evening at seven o'clock. It was a beautiful object in the west, at an altitude of 35 degrees. The sky after sunset became very clear, brighter than it had been for a long time past, and remained so for about half an hour, and 1 think it possible that it is because of the thick weather we have had lately that the comet has not been observed before." NEW MATERIAL FOR MAKING PAPER.—Consul Gade, of Christiania, has submitted to the United States Govern- ment a report relative to a new industry, or, rather, the use of a raw material for the manufacture of paper which will soon be in use in Norway and Sweden. Among the raw materials already employed in the manufacture of paper are rags, esparto, straw, and wool, but all these are expen- sive, and this new and cheaper one, which consists of white moss, will now be added to the list. The moss is found in immense quantities in Norway and Sweden but it is not the living plant which grows in the fields which is used for making paper, but the remains of this kind of moss which has gradually accumulated in the woods. The mouldering which the moss has gradually undergone constitutes a pre- paration for the paper manufacture made by nature herself. A factory is now building for the manufacture in Sweden, and examination has shown that near this place many millions of pounds of this raw material are to be found; in fact, a quantity sufficient to support a large manufactory for many years. Paper of different thicknesses and paste- board made of the white moss have already been shows, the latter even in sheets three-quarters of an inch thick. It is as hard as wood, and can easily be painted and polished. This manufacture is said to be very well gaited for taking the place of wood for many purposes. It has all the good qualities, bat none of the defects of wood, as it neither cracks nor warps. The pasteboard can consequently be used for door and window frames, and for architectural ornaments and all kinds of furniture. It remains to be seen what effect this new discovery will have upon the paper

STORING SEED POTATOES.—There is great fuss and con- fusion in some gardens about storing seed potatoes. Some people spread them out on the floor of a lot t, where they are always in the way to prevent free locomotion, and some- times have to be gathered up and put away, and then brought out again, because of some small business; others put them in boxes and baskets, and then know not what next to do, and so the boxes and baskets become the plagues of their life. I think my plan as good as any. Long nar- row baskets, of the cheapest description, and a sufficient amount of stout tarred cord or rope, make an end of the matter. Pack them close, nose end upwards, and suspend the baskets to the rafters, leaving room to move about under them without getting a knock on the head, and there you are. They get quite enough light in any ordinary loft or shed when stored in this way, and make short, stout sprouts, and being in bulk keep one another just moist enough.— Ifibberd's Garden Oracle. A PROPOSED "BLACK LIST."—The Mark-lane Express I says:—" We shall he greatly obliged to any reader who will I send us a copy of any agreement which a tenant ie expected to sign in order to bar the compensation provisions of the Agricultural Holdings Act. To be of much value the I agreement should be accompanied with the name of the landlord who is responsible foe it, and the name and locality of the estate to which it is to be applied. The strictest privacy as to the name of any sender may be relied on. No notice, however, will be taken of any communication not accompanied with the name and address of the sender, which will be necessary as a guarantee of good faith, and possibly to enable us to make inquiries into details not suffi- ciently supplied in the first instance. We trust we may rely upon everyone to make sure of the exact truth of any state- ment he may send us, as we shall be responsible if we pub- lish what is untrue. We propose to give descriptions .of the agreements as they come in, and to publish the names of the landlords who are repeonsible for them. It may then be possible to make a kind of " Black List" of flagrant attempts to evade the intentions of the Act." Ashforth, Sheffield. Gentlemen wishing to join the earn, eion should communicate with Mr. H. M. Jenkins, 12, Han- over-square, London, W. ENSILAGE AND ITS FEEDING QUALITIES.—Mr. T. Eas- dale. of Pepper Arden, Northallerton, writes to The Times: —The great number of letters I have received in cone.- ' quence of your publishing my letter on the above subject, and the number of visitors who have inspected the silos here clearly shows that a very widespread interest is now . taken in this new method of preserving fodder crops. It may be useful to state that Cowton Station on the North- . Eastern main line is within about 20 minutes' walk. As I being a sort of sequel to the former communication, many N.al :,,e interested to learn that two of Mr. Stobaree ensil- age-fed beasts have since been killed, and the result has completely set at rest any misgivings that may have ex- isted in connection with what the quality of the beef might prove to be. Our greatest hopes and expectations are fully realised. Nothing could possibly be finer than its appear- ance, flavour, and tenderness. Our local butcher, as well as one in the neighbouring town of Darlington, both bear will- ing testimony that there will now be no difficulty in die- posing of any amount of ensilage-fed beef at the very best price. To give the public an idea of the solidity to which a mass of ensilage can be, pressed, it may be stated that a cubic foot taken from the large silo here weighed exactly 571 b. The unsold beasts that are under the testing experi- ment were again weighed on Monday last, the result being that the previous report was fully sustained, while Mr. Stobart is thoroughly setiafied that the Whole tterlertaking is a complete success. AGRICULTURE IN JAPAII.-1 correspondent of the Daily News, now in Japan, writes:—" In a journey of nearly 250 miles through this portion of the interior I did not see a single plough. In the course of a subsequent journey through the southern portion of the island I saw two miserable little things which a man could easily lift, drawn by an undersized ox. In almost universal use is the earliest idea of a plough. It is a spade, with a narrow blade about three feet long. The farmer thrusts this well into the soil, and, turning it over on one side, makes a furrow, the action and the result being identical with that of a plough. Only, . watching the laborious process, one thinks of the enormous I strides agriculture will tele in Japan when these rude in- struments are cast aside, and the plough is put to work. i When the rice is cut and dried it is stripped by the simple' process of drawing the heads through a small iron comb, 1 which does i. handful at a time. It is thrashed by a flail i precisely of the same make as that in use in the thrashing- floor of Nachon, at the time tiara put forth his hand to steady ithe Ark of God that David was bringing up from Kirjath r jearim. When the rice is stripped it is laid out to dry on !mats spread in the sun. I ^ FRUIT TREES.—DANGER AHEAD.—Although it may ap- pear little short of presumption to pretend to anticipate the character of the fruit crops of the year we have so recently entered, there are, nevertheleeseunmistakable signs of growth that cannot be ignored by the observant cultivator. Fruit trees are not having the complete rest they need in conse- quence of the abnormally mild weather, and the buds in many instances are commencing swelling. It is well to re- cognise this, as, although it cannot be prevented, the danger which it undoubtedly predicates can in some instances at least be mitigated. Now that both fruit and forest tree planting is being practised to a much greater extent than formerly, and as the work is in full progress, and will con- tinue for two months, it is most important to remember the advanced condition of the trees and act accordingly. When deciduous trees are quite at rest and the sap dormant there is comparatively little danger in the exposure of the rooes to the air in transit from the nursery to the garden or . plantation; but, on the other hand, as is the case now, when the sap has commenced moving, the drying of the roots almost inevitably results in failure more or less marked. Let all tree purchasers, then, now that the sap is already moving, insist that the roots be thoroughly pro- tected by a thick covering of damp, straw or other ma- terial, so that they will arrive moist and fresh. In that state they may be planted with confidence, but if the fibres are dry and shrivelled it is quite impossible that growth can be insured. , FRUIT GROWING.—It maybe interesting to those who are intimately concerned in the cultivation of fruit to know the extent Lord Sudeley is taking up its culture, of which a lengthy account appeared in The Times. We are informed that 500 acres have already been planted by his lordship on his Toddington estate, and 200 more are to be planted with Apples, Pears, Plums, Cherries, Gooseberries, Currants, Raspberries, and Strawberries. It is stated that 130,000 Gooseberry bushes' 228,000 Black Currants, 3,000 Apple' trees, and 32,000 Plums, have been planted. The barns and other buildings on the farm have been converted into a jam factory, which has been taken by Mr. Beach, jam manufac- turer, for 10 years. Ten tons of Strawberries were made 1 into jam daring the past season. About 100 tons of fruit ' will have been grown on the farm the past year, and no trees of any kind were planted until the autumn of 1880. There is considerable economy in having the appliances to convert the fruit into conserves on the spot, the packing and the carriage of the fruit to distant markets being a heavy item in the fruit grower's expenses. It frequently occurs that some days the prices realised will not pay the expenses, and it is almost as profitable to give perishable fruit away in the market as to bring it back and have to throw the best part of it away. But this has been done more than once, with the view of keeping the prices up. What we have briefly stated goes to prove the necessity of a jam manufac- tory in the centre of a fruit growing district, and by fixing the prices at the commencement of the season the growers need not be in a perpetual ferment as to what they will make in the market. We believe the prices have been arranged between Lord Sudeley and Mr. Beach for the 10 REMARKABLE DISAP PE &RANCE! years. ELECTRIC MICROSCOEY.—A number of gentlemen as- sembled at the Crystal Palace recently, by invitation of the directors, to witness the first representation in England of " Les Invisibles," an exhibition of natural objects mag- nified and displayed by means of the great electric micro- scope. The apparatus used in the exhibition is the inven- tion of Messrs. Bauer and Co., and "Lee Invisibles ',' has quite recently attracted a good many visitors to the old Comedio Pariaienne, where, as well as at the Athenreum at Nice, a series of representations has been given. The inven- tion may be described in a few words as being the appli- cation of electric light to the microscope, and the result, so far as the spectacle is concerned, is a sort of improved and enlarged magic lantern. Every one is familiar with the former exhibitions at the Polytechnic and elsewhere of the animalculte in a drop of water, magnified and thrown, by the aid of the lime light, on to a white screen. Precisely the same sort of effect was produced on Saturday by Mr. F. I Link, the London agent for Messrs. Bauer and Co., with this difference, that the magnifying power was enormously in excess of that attained in the old magic lantern enter- tainments. The electric microscope has, in fact, made it possible to exhibit in a most attractive form the appear- I ances presented by minute natural objects when placed under the most powerful magnifying glass. Indeed, the difficulty with which Mr. Link had to contend was the smallness of the screen upon which his pictures were , thrown. For instance, only a small section of a butterfly's I wing could be shown at a time, although the screen was as ' large as the size of the entertainment court‘would permit, whilst the living organisms in a spot of water and the mites in a small piece of cheese were enlarged until they presented a perfectly appalling spectacle to a timid mind. The capabilities of the apparatus may be imagined from the, fact that the eye of a fly was presented in a form no less than four million times its natural size.- The electric micro- , scope, which is worked by an ordinary primary battery, ' may be said to have extended almost indefinitely the possi- bility of presenting in an attractive and instructive manner 1 the wonderful facts of natural science. INTERESTING SCIENTIFIC OBSERVATIONS IN NORTHERN ASIA.—VOLCANIC ERITPTIONS.—Mr. T. R. Green, of Yoko- hama, who has just returned to that city from a prolonged , journey in Northern Asia, has given some highly interest- I ing information respecting recent volcanic disturbances in , Kamchatka. The particulars given seem to indicate that I these disturbances were in close connection with the late I volcanic eruptions in Java, and that the active agency ex- tended over an immense area. It will be remembered that the eruptions of Mount Krakatoa' began early in August last, culminating on the 26th of that month. Mr. Green wiites that at the beginning of July last a cone about 9,000 ft. high by estimation, not marked on maps, but situ- ate near the Kamchatka River, and hitherto supposed to be inactive, if not entirely extinct, suddenly split in two, emitting immense quantities of lava, which poured down its slopes. This phenomenon was not, however, accompanied ' by any very great local disturbance. Mount Siveloch (of Keith Johnston's map), the highest peak of the Kamchat- kan range, 17,000 feet high, was in active eruption through- out the whole month of July, the pillar of flame in calm weather being distinctly visible at distances of from 200 to 300 miles, giving, after allowance for refraction, an altitude above the summit of the cone of between 8,000 and 10,000 ' feet. When the air was still smoke, steam, dm., rose vertic- ally to an elevation of 15,000 feet, where, meeting with a northerly air current, it abruptly took, at right angles, a southerly direction, in a thin, direct line. In this connec- tion it may be stated that Captain Hubbard, of the Toyoshi- mamarn, recently described an eruption which took place at Shibetoru, one of the Kurile Islands, in the early part of June last. Mr. Green further states that in April last the ice in the neighbourhood of the Kuriles was discoloured with volcanic ashes for miles in every directien, indicative of eruptions of unusual violence probably in the north, but of which no report has been violence, Mr. Green was enabled to make some very interesting ebservations on cloud formation in the vicinity of the Cronowtski Peak. He de- scribes this as perhaps the most perfect cone in the world, because it tapers to a fine point, and is of greater elevation than Fujiyema. From 4 a.m. until the sun rose it would show perfectly clear and distinct from the sea like an on- plumed cocked hat. As the sun rose the snow would soften, evaporation no doubt begin, and mists would slowly gather around the summit, giving the mountain the appearance of a gigantic plumed Field Marshal's cocked hot. At daylight on the next morning, as already observed, there would not be a vestige of the plume, but the process of its formation proceeded with unvarying regularity. The information above supplied will probably, attract the attention of learned societies. There certainly now seems an oppor- tunity rarely offered for collectting and digesting the data respecting recent volcanic disturbances, which should be made use of.

leave them power to grind in their turn the most grievous rack-rent out of their tenants, would be to inaugurate the most abominable system of land tenure that the world has ever known. "Progress and poverty" is a grand book ; many of its arguments are overwhelming in force, its illustrations are felicitous, and its general tone of morality —apart from confiscation—is sublime; but its scheme of false land nationalisation is pure bathos, reminding one oforcibly of the saying, "in the name of the Prophet—figs." If tet showing with great power the evils of private owner- ship in land, Mr. George proposes to let it continue in all ite enormity, and only to tax it, thus increasing some of its worst results. The best thing said on Wednesday night was said by the Rev. Mr. Wicksteed, when he pointed out that, although the few can live by robbing the many, the many cannot live by ribbing the few. That was a very neat rebuke for Mr. George, coining as it did from the seconder of a vote of thanks to him for his lecture. If the question were merely one of taking the land from the men who either stole it or had it given to them by a King who had no right to it, restoration without compensation would be fair and reasonable. But there is not only no possibility of so compelling the dead to disgorge their unrighteous gains; it is not even possible to confine the proposed punishment to the heirs of the original possessors of land. Thousands of people have savings as legitimately obtained as most other savings have been invested in land that be- longs to them or to others, and to confiscate the land would be also to confiscate their property. If their property can be taken without compensation, then anyone's property may quite as justifiably be seized, even if it be the clothes on his back.—Mark Lane Express.

DIGGING AMONG FRUIT TREES.—We feel sure the prac- tice is indefensible, and cannot be conducted with impunity. The annual destruction of the best of the roots by digging amongst the trees is something deplorable. Some allege that it adds neatness, and that the ground is free from weeds during the following season, the seeds of the weeds that have fallen on its surface being by this operation buried so deep that they cannot grow. This may appear reasonable to anyone ignorant of the nature of seeds. There seems to be no limit to the vitality of some seeds, including those of many weeds, so that these seeds when dug into the ground are simply stored away to come up again at the next dig- giog, and when brought under the influence of the necessary conditions for germination they soon yield a crop of trouble- some weeds.

THE FRONT GARDEN.—The present is a suitable time for securing briar stems for the purpose of budding roses on them. Select clean, straight shoots, from half an inch to an inch in diameter. It is not necessary to spend much time to secure them with roots, as they are usually trimmed clean off, excepting a few promising fibres thU may happen to be close to the stem. We have planted them with only a knob at the bottom, scarcely as big as a medium size fist, and out of it roots freely emit. We never had a partiality, for standard roses; they are ugly and appear unnatural especially when they are excessively high. But we are compelled to forget all that is objectionable when we see the splendid roses produced for the first year or two in con- sequence of this union with the common briar. Most of the exhibition roses are attained in this way. Those planted now will send forth shoots at the apex,•which must be re- duced to three, and on these budding should be performed next July. Seeds of the briars may be collected now and buried in a heap in the earth, or placed in a vessel inter- mixed with sand, which must be kept wet. This will decom- pose the fleshy outer covering of the seeds, and if they are , well rubbed when taken out to be sown they will be toler- ably clean, and may be deposited in drills one foot apart. They are well adapted for budding, so as to form dwarfs, and some of the finest roses have been exhibited from the seedling briar. THE WINDOW.—The Hyacinth.—On examining these the other day, we found the earliest potted an inch high. We selected the most forward and placed them in semi-darkness for a few days so as to gradually inure them to the influ- ence of the light. To grow them sturdy, they will require watching, and if the foliage appears to elongate in advance of the spike, it is a sure indication that they require more air. There is no altering these irregularities, if they take place. Daily watching and promptness will preserve them at a proper balance. Hyacinths in glasses will require similar attention, and if the water has an offensive odour, or the roots appear unhealthy, change it at once for soft or rain water, and insert a piece or two of charcoal. The bulb and its roots must be disturbed as little as possible in pour- ing out the water, and it must be seen that the fresh supply touches the base of the bulb. Though the hyacinth re- quires a daily supply of fresh air, dry, cold, cutting cur- rents must be guarded against. They are hostile to the well-being of all plants in a growing state, either in a natural or artidcial condition.

A few days ago, a poor Irishman, who applied for a license to sell ardent spirits, being questioned as to his moral fitness for the trust, replied, "Ala, sure, it is not much character a man needs Ito sell rum." A photographer in a country town was recently visited by a young woman, who, with sweet simplicity, asked— " How long does it take to get your photograph after you have left your measure ?" An impatient Welshman called to his wife, 'Come! .„1 come! Isn't breakfast ready? I've had nothing since yes- -terday, and to-morrow will be the third day !" This is equal 0 the call of the stirring housewife, who aroused her maid at four o'clock with, " Come, Mary, get up! Here 'tis Mon- day morning; to-morrow is Tuesday, and nest day's Wed- nesday—half the week gone, and _nothing done yet!" ' '

There was a person Who had a friend who was grasping of disposition, to whom he said one day—" I am going on a journey. Well, you see this ring. Whenever I look at it, I shall remember you." The friend said, "If your finger were bare, you would remember me equally well by that; and I should like someone to give me a ring." The story ends in one word more, which is " Ndad "—i.e., "He didn't give it." PROFESSOR HOLLOWAY AND DICERNS.—He was a shrewd, amusing man, this " Professor" Holloway, and very daring. He once enclosed a cheque for a thousand pounds in a letter to Charles Dickens, which he placed at Dickens' disposal, on condition that one line of complimentary reference to Hol- loway's cures should appear in the book which Dickens was then publishing in monthly numbers. The bearer waited for an answer. "What did you do ?" I asked Dickens. 'Do ?" he cried, "I put the cheque back into the letter, and sent it down to the messenger, saying that was all the answer I had to send !" THE 'TURNING POINT OF MR. GLADSTONE'S LIFE.—In the British Quarterly Review, Mr. Guinness Rogers, dealing with the charge of "instability" so frequently made against Mr. Gladstone says :—He has changed in opinion, but he has ever been constant in purpose. He has been unmoved alike by the fierce gusts of popular feeling or the allure- ments of personal ambition. More than oncele has sacri- ficed office, and, apparently, his hopeiof future advancement, to the love of truth ; but no serious politician will under- take to say that he has ever sacrificed truth for the sake of office. No winds of caprice or popularity have carried him hither and thither, for his course has ever been in one direction: and whatever difficulty or sacrifice that involved he has readily accepted. The crucial period of his history was that which intervened between the resignation of Sir Robert Peel, in 1847, and the formation of the Aberdeen Cabinet in 1853. It was the turning•point in his career, and to outsiders it long seemed. doubtful as to which path he would select. There were combined in him much of the taste and temper of the Cavalier, with the uncompromising love of right and liberty characteristic of the Puritan, and it was hard to predict to which side the balance would in- cline. Church sentiment, msthetic culture, the friendships and associations of his early days, all pointed one way, and there was really nothing to allure him to the other except a deep sense of truth and right. In the Liberal party itself there was little or nothing to inspire hope or awaken enthu- siasm. It was divided by internal quarrels, and those of the meanest and smallest kind—mainly personal jealousies of men, some of whom had but scant claim to be regarded as Liberals at all. A:high-spirited young politician, full of ideas and possessed with ideals, whom events had detached from party associations, and who was burning with desire to do real service to his country, might well hesitate befOre he allied himself to a party which seemed to be all but effete—living on the memories of a glorious past, and led by those who seemed more anxious about the adjustment of their own personal claims than about the pro- gress of Liberal legislation. The remarkable letter in which Mr. Cobden urged Sir Robert Peel to break loose from the conventionalisms of political warfare, and boldly unfurl the standard of a new Liberal party, is one of the clearest evi- dences of the feebleness and degeneracy of a party which only fifteen years before was sustained by the enthusiastic devotion of the entire people, and seemed to have secured for itself an unlimited tenure of power. If Mr. Gladstone hall been repelled by the broils between Palmerston and Grey and Russell, and had been hopeless of any great good to be wrought for the nation by reformers with so little daring, or unity of purpose, or comprehension of Liberal ideas, he would only have shared the feelings of Richard Cobden. On the other hand, if the Tories were divided and dis- organised as the consequence of the triumph of Free Trade, still there was hope of gathering them round some standard which they might regard as the banner of the Constitution. Protection was dead as a principle of English legislation, just as borough-mongering had died before it; but it would have been easy to find something else which might have served as a rallying point. If Mr. Gladstone would have accepted the place of leader, how gladly would he have been welcomed! Those who tell us that it was jealousy of Dis- raeli which made him a Liberal either show their own crass ignorance or are presuming upon ours. They are thinking of Disraeli as he was in two or three of the later years of his administration, not of Disraeli as he was when he en- tered on the hard, steady, uphill work of more than twenty years—all collar work, and often of a very humiliating character, by which he rose to the summit of his'ambition. It was dire necessity alone which made the Tory party ac- cept hint as a leader, and the creation of that necessity is one of the unpardonable offences which Mr. Gladstone has committed. VOLUNTEER PRIZE DISTRIBUTION AT WARRINGTON. The annual distribution of prizes in connection with the 9th Lancashire (Warrington) Rifle Volunteer Corps took place at the Drill Hall, Legh-street, on Monday evening, when our gallant red coats mustered in good numbers, and there was a fair attendance of the general public. Lieut.- Colonel Greenallnccupied the chair, and the other officers in attendance were Captain Ridgway, Lieut. Buchtont Sergeant-Major PenneHy,. and Sergeant Blease. The value of the prizes distributed was upwards of £4O. Previous to making the distribution, Lieut.-Colonel Greenell deliver,.,l a speech of considerable length. He apologised for toe distribution being held so late this year, and said this fact was owing to circumstances over, which he had no muntrol. His wish was that the presentatiOn should', have taken place at the usual time, but his officers very' kindly said that they shoula prefer his being present, even if this involved the ptstpenement of that event. He then alluded to the Volunteer movement generally, directing attention to what Lord Wolseley had said in a recent speech to th, effect that there must be 3 European war before long, and that in the face of this fact ' the public were beginning to realise the value of the Volunteer movement. Many comments had been made upon the shsoting of the Volunteers, and no doubt there was some truth in the criticisms. At the eagle time the difficulties with which they • had to n° tend, in the absence of proper •ranges, accounte,, In a great measure for the low percentage of shooting' It appeared that nearly all the continental natioMf !ere arming, and in the event of war England could not possiblY put more than 60.000 troops in the field. Then they would have to fall back IIDOII the militia, which would be called up, leaving our barracks to be occupied by the Volunteers. The speaker dwelt upon the fact that the local corps irae very much short in its equipment; especially was this the case es to knapsacks and valises Tttey bad for some time been promised the Martini-Henry ride, but had not yet get it. The organisation of the corps general' was faulty', and they required a scheme by which they would be mobil- ised, and would be so called up at any moment. ' Captain EIDoWAY (who was loudly cheered) addressed the men, and referred to the 'fact that they had Only at present a range of 400 yards. The Regimental Committee hoped to increase the length, and it was a question tiurieg the next month or two whether they would get the Sanction of the Government and of Others intarested. He Aiought that this was really a question the Government ought tc take up, especially as there was a depot in the district; The depot had bad every year, owing to the shortness 01 the range, to send large numbers of men to PleetWood an Altcar, which meant a heavy expenditure. An altered range to suit the new regulations would mean a cost or several hundred pounds, but it would soon be eavhZ9 tb! non-payment of the railway fares and 'other t a 'great deal would be saved by the Government before long. LORD CARNARVON ON GENERAL GORDON'S MY stow.— he Earl of Carnarvon, speaking at Taunton on Saturday, referred to the despatch of General Gordon to Egypt which he considered was a wise resolution on the part of the Go- vernment. His only regret was that the decision had been taken so late. He should like to know, however, what were the PoWereentrusted to General Go. don. Her Majesty's Government were responsinle for the administration of affairs in Egypt; and if Khartoum, with its mingled pepelatiou ot loyal Egyptians, Hellish Christians, Englishmen, Germans, and French, fell, and some terrible massacre were the couse- Iltietece, it was on the head of the Government that the re- sponsibility would rest. JAMES ON A MUNICIPAL CORRUPT Petecricus A deputation from the London and Counties Liberal Union waited upon the Attorney-Gene i el, on Tues- day afternoon, at the Royal Courts of Justice, to urge upon aim the necessity of extending the operation of the Cor- rupt Practices Act, passed last session, to municipal elec- "'ems. In reply, Sir Henry James said he had more than °Pee made an attempt to draw up a bill applicable to both r arliamentary and municipal elections but found difficul- ties in the way. lie hoped, however, time appf oacn- ing Session to introduce a bill applicable to inuoicipal elec- tions. There was a great deal to be said in support of the view they took, and he did not doubt that Her M tjeety's Government would give their suggestion very favourable COnsideration. SIR CHARLES EMILE ON PARLIAMENTARY REFORM.— Sir Charles Bilks address, d a meeting of his constituents on Tuesday evening. Speaking of Parliamentary reform he thought that the details of redistribution should be deferred till the registers under the new franchise lied been com- Pleted. In any case redistribution could not long be de- layed. If the House of Lords should as some predicted, threw out the Franchise Bill and the London Government sill, in what stronger positior could the Goverauneut stand before the people—hindered in their work slier it had re- ceived the approval of the Commons of England by a hand- ful of peers, voting against their own better judgement under the leadership of Lord Salisbury. If the Conservativeecar- ried out their threat of forcing a dissoltition lay rejecting all Cioverunient bills the result would be a triumph of Radical opinions such as the country had not yet seen. Turning to EgYptian affairs, Sir Charles said the Government had great confidence in the advice they had received from tx eneral Gordon. The Government first suggested the sending out of General Gordon to the late Egyptian Government many Months ago, but at that time their own advisers in Egypt thought that under the circumstances he had better not go there. SIR STAFFORD NORTHCOTE AT BARNSTAPLE.—Sir S. fforthcote was the chief speaker on Thursday night at the &rat annual dinner of the Barnstaple and North Devon Con- servative Association. In responding to the toast of the ifouse of Commons, Sir Stafford remarked that it was one of the first obligations imposed upon those who were mem- bers of that House to endeavour to maintain in every way its credit in the eyes of the nation. Referring to the pro- Posed measure for reform, be said the Conservative; were desirous of having the franchise on as large and firm a basis al possible; but when they considered the proposals Shadowed forth to them they saw it was not merely exten- *ion of the county franchise, but destruction of the county , franchise. The proposal to postpoae redistribution until 1 after the Franchise Bill had been pawed mean that the j Government either had in their minds some plan of a Character they did not like to disclose, or they Mee no ulti- mate plan at all, therefore it was the bonnileu duty of Con- ; Servatives before they in any way assented to, or coMmitted I themselves to any principle of reform whatever, to tie made acquainted with the whole character of the plan the Govern- ' naent would bring forward, otherwise no sooner would this measure be passed than a further agitation would be set on fOot. LORD RANDOLPH CHURCHILL ON THE EGYPTIAN POLICY. , —Lord Randolph Churchill made a great speech at Black- Pool on Thursday night. He condemned the Egyptian j Policy of the country as one which had only been under- taken in the interests of Jewish bondholders and i Stockjobbers. This was the first time that England's Power had been exercised for such a despicable Fause, and he trusted that the people, by examine l ing into the matter for themselves, would put an end to such a state of affairs. Instead of attempting a I Stupendous programme in the coming session, he thought that what Parliament should do was to inquire into the con- dition of the finances and into the management of our great Public departments. If committees of experienced members j eware appointed he was sure that a -great saving of expendi-• j lure might be gained. The noble lord also advocated an inquiry into the et sto of British industries, which had been ' brought as low by a miseakeu • policy of free trade, which imposed a burden On necessaries coining from abroad while it admitted luxuries and manufactures free. In mi brilliant Bud effective passage his lordship showed. lio'w Mr. Glad- etone'e policy, like his amusements,. had been one of chips. His lordship advised the country to return to the Tories as the party who really tried to secure the greatest happiness be all homes. MR. SHAW•LEFEVRE AT MANCHESTER The Right Hon. J. G. Shaw-Lefevre, M.P., was the principal guest at I a soiree held on Wednesday evening at the Manchester l Reform Clubnand delivered an address on political topics. Iu reference to the franchisa and redistribution questions, he pointed out that the cooling Franchise Bill will be a larger measure of enfranchisement in point of numbers than either of the preceding Reform Acts. The number to be admitted (if the borough franchise in Ireland was also ex- tended) to the enjoyment of the suffrege could scarcely be lese than two millions. The extension of the franchise would involve some difficult questions—such as that of the freehold votes in counties, in regard to which it would he necessary to proceed cautiously, and with conciliation. Redistribution, whether it be concurrent with or, as is far More probable, a measure subsaiquent to the extension of the franchise, was obviously a most difficult task, involving as it did the necessity of dealing with so neany places which now have no 3Pecial representation. He expected uncompromising Op- Position to the Government proposals from the Tory party, but did not anticipate that any of the fallacies which in 186 G succeeded in driving a Liberal Government from Power would serve the same purpose again. On the ques- t,i,on of redistribution Mr. Lefevre expressed his opinion that equal electoral districts, each returning one or two Members, were scarcely within the bounds of practical Politics. Apart from the populous districts of London and ' the larger county constituencies, he could not but think that we should preserve two of the esse,ntiel principles of Otlr present system—namely, the representation of commit- ldties and the separation of the urban from the urral ConT- %unities. Ireland, if we were not prepared to concede onie Rule, should be treated with absolute fairness in the Imperial Parliament, and equality of representation in some reeelect seemed to be an essential condition, and one from I'lli-eh the Liberal party could not depart with safety to its Own principles and its own existence. A vote of thanks was Passed to the right hon, gentleman on the motion of Mr. R. Leake, M.P., seconded by Mr. B. Armitage, M.P., and sup- ported by Mr. W. Agnew, M.P.

IRELAND. A Treasury warrant appears in last night's Gazette pro hibiting the transmission by parcels post of any firearms ammunition, or other explosives to any proclaimed district in Ireland. A STATIONMASTER SHOT.—The stationmaster at Bailin - grave, county Limerick,' was fired at about nine o'clock ratuFridaY night by some person unknown, and died on rday from his iniuries. The cause of the crime is not apparent.
•A MYSTERICMS
-Within the last few

clays a respectable young girl, the daughter of a police. sergeant, has mysteriously disappeared in Dublin. A club house waiter has been arrested. It appears the girl left her home about seven o'clock in the evenine. on some text, and and the accused was observed to meet and away with her. The prisoner is a married man with 't o Children. ORANGEMEN AND NATIONALISTS.—The Orangemen apf N.eorY. county Down, and Armagh, at Newry, on Tuesdax night, arranged to send a thousand men to the counter demonstration to the Nationalist meeting at Castleton on Xneiday next. Orange placards have been posteditxten- aiyely in county Down, calling on Orangemen to make a -counter demonstration against the forthcoming Nationalists' Meeting at Castlewellan. ROMANTIC ELOPEMENT FROM Dinsmx.—An elopement Is reported to have taken place from Dublin within the Past few days. The lady, who lived in the suburbs, is the possessor of £3OO per annum in her own right. Her father 1.8 owner of considerable property, and was in favour of oer union with a gentleman of means, but the proposed 'watch did not meet the daughter's approval, and she dis- appeared from Dublin in company with the 'object of her affections—a shop assistant in the city. SYMpitH7 FOR JAMES CARRY'S ASSASSIN:A London- ',err! correspondent reports an extraordinary scene from Lnarrybeg, county Donegal. An immense crowd of peasantry "er,nbled at that place, and, after assisting at amass offered t.;P for the repose of Patrick O'Donnell, h4nged for the mur- oer of Carey, they pruceedea with a coffin to the graveyard. Where it was deposited in the family burying plot. The People all knelt round the grave in prayer. An intsiorteies rested on the coffin, which bore a plate with the inscription, Sacred to the memory of Patricia O'Donnell, executed in t'clnclop, Dec. 17tb, 1883." A sum of £35 was subscribed for a monument. Resolutions were passed by the people thanking their Atnerican friends for the,r assistance,and also thanking Victor Hugo. Smith's visit to that City, and said he was surpristd that any Tory tactician o the smallest sense would lend himself to the policy begu by Sir Stafford Northcote, for the only hope of a return Power by the Conservative party lay in the continued an-. tagoniena of the Irish National party to the English Whigs.

He did not attach enormous importance to the extension of the franchise in Ireland. Whatever might be the effect upon the ,Nationalists strength of an extension of the fran- chise in England, he believed that an extension of the franchise in Ireland would not make a difference of more than four or five votes. At the same time, if England was given an extended franchise Ireland must have (quality with England in this matter. MR CHAMBERLAIN AND IRISH OPINION.—Mr. Chamber- lain has forfeited the good opinion of the Parnellite journals by his recent vindication of Earl Spencer and Mr. Tre- velyan. The Irishman coolly remailts that all that has been said in denunciation of the Executive is justified by the f icts. "If Earl Spencer and Mr. Trevelyan could only boast that they had exterminated a million of the mere Irish, their countrymen would cheer them to the echo and decree them a national triumph." If "a man so fair minded" as Mr. Chamberlain is admitted to be could stand up for the present "despots," what, asks the Irishman, can be expected from "the common ruck of English boors? " This is good, but it is almost better to find the Irishman protestine, that in Ireland "the public press is being throt- tled witlirthe grasp of a garotter," and that the country is every day getting deeper into the depths of "political serf- dom." A FIGHT FOR A FARM—What is peculiarly an Irish scene is described by a Tipperary reporter. While the body of a widow named Byrne lay in the house awaiting burial, the friends" of her late husband on the one hand, and the next of kin on the other arrived, each party being 40 or 50 strong, and took up their ciparters in separate apartments. The object was to fight for possession of the farm, but actual hostilities were prevented during the two days' wake by the presence of a large force of polies,. After the removal of the body one party "made a rush" on the other and ejected them. Then the police applied themselves to keeping one lot inside and the other outside, and when they had been re- inforced sufficiently for the task they cleared out of the place entirely and put into possession a man who is said to be entitled to the farm under the will of the deceased woman's late husband. No land act Can be framed which can suit the Tipperary taste for settling questions of title.

A criminal couit at Pesth has sentenced Dr. Rosenberg to two years' imprisonment for killing Count Stefan Rat- thyany in a duel arising oat of a "love affair." Notice of appeal was given on both sides against the judgment. SUSPICIOUSLY FOLLOWING KING ALFONsO.—A French- man and a Portuguese were arrested on Monday on the Retiro l'romenade, Madrid, on the charge of attempting to approach the royal carriage. The suspicions of the police were aroused by the circumstance that the two individuals in question have been noticed constantly following the King during the last few days when his Majesty was driving or

CUERDLEY. FATAL ACCIDENT AT CUERDLEY. Joseph Oliver, 70 years of age, who has been in the service of Mr. W. Taylor, brewer and farmer, Crterdley, for a considerable number of years, died at the Warrington Infirmary, on Tuesday morn- ing. It appears that on Saturday afternoon last the de— ceased fell from a large boiler to the ground, a diitance of six feet six inches, breaking his right leg and sustaining other injuries. He was at once conveyed to the Infirmary, where he died about 2.30 a.m. on Tuesday. FARNWORTH. •

--- BREACH or Co/imam—At the Manchester Asaizes, on Tuesday, before Mr. Justice Brett. John Richardson, a wholesale potato dealer in the Manchester market, claimed fro:n William Grace, a farmer at Farnworth, near Warring- ton, damages for breach of contract to supply him with a certain quantity of potatoes.—Mr. Fleming appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. J. W. Hamilton for the defendant.—The plaintiff alleged that the defendant had failed to fulfil a contract he entered into to supply him with 20 or 30 tons of "magnum bonum" potatoes at 8a 61 a load, and a similar quantity of "champion" potatoes at is 6,1 a load, to be put on the railway at Farn worth Station.—For the defen- dant it was contended that he only contracted to sunly the plaintiff with £5O worth of "magnum bonum" and "cham- pion" potatoes, and that he had fulfilled the contract After hearing the evidence, the jury found for the plaintiff —damages £ll 16S Scl. FRODSHA.M. SERVICE OF Soo.—On Monday evening a service of song, ent•itled " Pilgrim Street," a story of Manchester lib, was given in the Town Hall, Frodsham. The merits of the narrative and music were deserving of a larger audience. Mr. Jones,of Runcorn' gave the connective readings, and under the influence of Mr. liolford's baton, the choir acquitted themselves exceedingly well. Miss Clough accom- panied on the harmonium. SOCIAL GATHERING—The anneal social gathering of teachers in the Trinity Wesleyan Sunday School and their friends was held on Thursday evening, when the Rev. G. L. Allen presided. The programme was a very lengthy one, and consisted of songs by Miss K. Rigby, Mies Manton, and Mr. Harrison; botanical lectures by Mr. R. Holland and the Chairman, the lecture by the latter being illustrated with the aid of a magic lantern; recitation by Mr. Rhodes; an organ recital in the chapel by Mr. A. H. Walker; pianoforte duett by Misses Turner and Booth; and anthems by the choir. SauviosO SONG.—The new service of song, entitled, "Pilgrim Street; a story of Manclieeter Life," compiled by Mr. B. Moore, of Runcarn; was given at the Town Hall on Monday night. Owing to other attractions in the town the audience was small. The various pieces were well rendered by an efficient choir, composed of ladies and gentlemen from various congregational choirs in Runcorn. The solos, duets, Arc., were placed in competent hands, and met with a good reception. Mr. John Holford (choirmaster of Ellesmere- street Chapel) was the conductor, Miss Clough was the accompanist, and Mr. J. D. Jones read the connective readings.

THE WAR IN TONQUIN: FRENCH ADVANCE ON BAC Nietn.—A telegram received at Paris from Hong Kong, dated Thursday, contains advices from Hanoi to the 19th Inst., stating that a strong reconnaissance has been made in the direction of Bac Ninh, and that the enemy were found in great force at the junction of the Red and Black river. They fired upon the reconnoitring party, without, however, the:r shots taking effect. It is expected that the French will meet with strong resistance. A singular case has been heard at Moscow. An action was brought against the children of the ex-treasurer of a fouadling hospital to recover from them a large sum of money which, it is alleged, their father had embezzled from the funds of the institution. The jury found for the de- fendants, and if their verdict be right children in Russia are not liable for the defalcations of their deceased parents. An a tpeal to a higher tribunal has, however, been lodged by the Public Prosecutor against the finding. SAFETY OF PART OF HICKS PACHA'S ARMY.—The news is confidently given that a large part of General Hicks's army is at Lake Rahad. It was probably left there by him when he went on to make a strong reconnaissance with his stiff when he was attacked at Malbeis. General Coetlogen telegraphs for instructions as to how they are to retreat. A Renter's Cairo telegram says that Geneial Gordon has arrived at Port Said, where he was received by Sir Evelyn Wood. In consequence of information that the road to Khartoum via Korok is the only practicable one at present, General Gordon has abandoned his intention of proceeding direct to Khartoum via Suakim. AFFAIRS IN MADAGASCAR: ATTEMPT TO CdRRY OFF THE QUEEN.—The Temps of Wednesday publishes advices from Madagascar to the 27th ultimo, stating that the sani- tary condition of the troops was satisfactory, notwithstand- ing the occurrence of a few cases of fever. Nothing what- ever was known reguarding the fate of the Hove ambassa- dors. The garrison of Tatnatave had made several sorties. A body of 500 Ilovas attacked Majunga on the night of the 13th November. in order to carry off the Queen of the Sakalaves, but they were forced to retire after sustaing a loss of sixty killed. The American corvette Brooklyn ar- rived at Tatnatave on the 13th of December, and greeted the French flag on shore with a seine of twenty- one guns. On passing behind the French cruiser, Naiade, the band on board the Brooklyn struck up the Marsellaise. A CORIOUS TRAGEDY.—Tne Ame.rican newspapers record the conclusion of a criminal case which has attracted much attention. About a year ago a man named Dukes deliberately murdered I Treasury officer named Nutt, the father of a girl to whom he had been affianced. Dukes had not hesitated in order to obtain a release from his engagement to bring a scandalous charge against the young lady, and when her father resented it he shot him dead. For this crime he was tried, but several of the jurors were bribed, and to the in- tense indignation of the community a verdict of acquittal was returned. One of Mr. Nutt's sons, however, declared that be would kill Dukes "at sight," and the miscreant fled from the town. He could sot, however, elude Nutt, who overtook him and shot him dead. A jury of Pennsylvania citizens have now acquitted Nutt of the charge of murder, on the ground that when he shot Dukes he was "under an excess of temporary insanity." THE SOUDAN: GENERAL GORDON'S MISSION.—The news of General Gordon's miesion to the Soudan has been re- ceived in Egypt with great satisfaction. " Authentic par- ticulars " of the General's instructions informs us that he will go at once to Suakin:, via the Canal. At Suez he will meet Sir Evelyn Baring, with whom he will come to an un- derstanding as to the co-operation of the English authori- ties in Fgypt. On reaching Suakim ho will bring into play his knowledge of local characteristics and his personal in- fluence with local chiefs. The road from Suakim to Berber passes through the domains of tries with which he is on friendly terms. The Hadendowa chief will be summoned to Suakim, and under his escort General Gordon expects to proceed at once to Khartoum. " When there he will as- setnble the head of the neighbouring tribes and announce to them that be has come on the part of the English Go- vernment to restore to them their liberty, and to remove the swarms of unpaid soldiers and adventurers of various kinds who have been the curse of 'the country. He will also have another communication to make, which they may find less agreeable, but which they will have been taught by expe- rience to respect. He will inform them that the slave trade must positively cease, and that as soon as he hes finished what he has to do in the Soudan he is going round to the Congo to deal with slavery at its headquarters." SHOCKING MURDER IN NAPLES.—Meneignor de Cesare, General of the Olivetaus of Monte Vergine, near Naples, was murdered at Rome, on Thursday night last week, under horrible and mysterious circumstances. He had re- turned in the morning from Naples to his usual winter quarters, in a house in the Via Della Purificazione, accom- panied by a man-servant, whom he greatly trusted. In the evening the neighbours were disturbed by stifled cries and sounds proceeding from the Moneignor's apartment, and as the cries were son hushed, only a servant girl had the curiosity to go down and inquire what had happened. The man-servant answered her call by showing his hand ban- daged and his body smeared with blood. The girl, terrified at the sight, wanted to send for the police, but the man-servant begged her to desist, telling her that Monsignor had been surprised by the hus- band of a .woman he had brought into the house, that there had been a row, but that now the three, together with two brothers-in-law of the husband, were supping together amic- ably. When the girl went downstairs in the morning she found the door of Monsignor de Cesare's apartment open' and proceeding to the manservant's room found him in bed. He rose and went to look after his master, saying that the guests of Thursday night were to have left for Naples in the morning. Monsignor was then found lying in his bedroom in a pool of blood, his throat and chest horribly gashed, and his shirt torn to shreds. In the room adjoining, the chests and cupboards had been forced and emptied. In the dining-room were the remains of a supper. The police were sent for immediately, and the manservant was arrested. The deceased was 72. TERRIBLE WRECK ON THB AMERICAN COAST: LOSS OF 97 LIVES.-A very deplorable calamity occurred on the coast of Massachusetts early on Friday morning. The steamer City of Columbus, from Boston to Savannah, was negligently run on to a terrible ledge of rocks daring a heavy gale, and became a total wreck. There were 81 pas- sengers on board, most of them women and children, and a crew of 45 men, and no fewer than 97 were drowned. The wreck occurred at a distance of one mile and a half from the shore. The passengers rushed on deck on feeling the shock, and were swept overboard by scores. Others who took to the rigging soon died from the intense cold. All seamen familiar with the locality affirm that the steamer must have been very much out of her course when she struck. The survivors assert that while they were in the rigging they saw two steamers, but both failed to notice the wteek. The mate of one of the steamers referred to declares that although he inspected' the wreck with a glass he saw no signs of any human beings. The hull of the City of Colinnbus is intact, and it is expected that many bodies will be found between decke. A number of those who were lin the rigging were frozen to the ropes to which they clung. The night was clear and all lights were visible. The disas- ter is attributed by all the newspapers to gross ignorance or carelessness, and a rigid inquiry is demanded. They especially condemn the captain's conduct in going below before all danger was passed. The captain asserts that both the second officer and the quartermaster were in the pilot house at the time of the disaster. The City of Colum- bus was a steamer of 1.900 tons register. The majority of 1 her passengers were in delicate health, and were going south to recruit. .

The lifeboat Albert Edward, which went out from Clacton- on-Sea, on Wednesday night, returned on Thursday with the loss of two men, the boat having capsized and subse- quently righted herself. Some delay to traffic Iv's caused by a collision between the Midland train and a goods train at Swinton Junction, near Rotherham, early on Thursday morning. The guard of the express was injured. A vessel laden with sugar—the New Union. of Faversham —was, on Thursday, destreyed by fire off Sheerness. The fire broke out at three o'clock, and at five o'clock the crew took to their beats, and stood by the burning vessel until rescued by the coastguard. When Serjeant Maynard, then ninety years of age, came at the head of the lawyers to congratulate the Prince of Orange, the Prince having paid him this compliment on the vigour of his age, "That he outlived all the men of the law of his time," Maynard answered, " Had not your High- ness come over, I should have outlived the law itself." THE STOKE NEWINGTON MYSTRIZY.—With regard to the theory that Mr. Power committed suicide and was not murdered, Mr. Ernest Cogden, the intimate friend of the deceased, and the last person known to have been in his, company, is confident that his friend was murdered, and that,.instead of the police having decided to take no further action, redoubled vigilance will be displayed by someone who he knows is actively engaged in attempting to solve! the Stoke Newington mystery. POST-OFFICE ROBBERIES BY Lans..—Three boys, named Gretton, Smith, and Forester, whose ages ranged from nine to fourteen, were charged at Hanley, on Thursday, with stealing letters from the Handley Post-office. The smallest boy put his hand through the slit of the letter-box and reachrd the letters, which was afterwards opened, and cheques amounting in value to over £2O were in one day stolen. The eldest boy (Gretton) was • sent to jail for a month, and to a reformatory school for three years. The other boys were each fined 20s. and costs. div.head: HALTON.
div.p: HALTON.

HALTON MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.- At the weekly meeting of this society, held on Monday night, a paper entitled "What is Man?" was read by Mr. J. W. Boyle, of Runcorn, and was criticised by Messrs. J. H. Gamer, R. Hughes, and S. Barrow. The Rev. S. Mees melded. LYMM. ENTERTAINMENT.-Mr., W. Johnson gave his popular entertainment, entitled "A. merry evening," at the Plough Assembly-rooms, Lymm, on Monday evening. His varied representations of character kept the audience in a con- tinuous vein of laughter, and provoked great applause.

div.head: WESTON.
div.p: WESTON.

WESLIIIYAN DAY 5ca0.07.----A-dis-tribution of prizes, con- sisting of framed and Unframed illuminated certificates, took place on Friday evening, preceded by a tea. Thomas Norman, Esq., of Runcorn, presided. The rewards were handed to the scholars by Miss Norman. A number cf books, kindly given by Mrs. Kirkham, of Weston, were also distributed. Mr. Norman spoke in high terms of the master and. mistress, Mr. and Mrs. Dunbobin. He congratulated them On the present state and efficiency of the school, and urged the parents to assist them in every possible way theV could, for the work of educating the young was a noble one. He was certain the children sent to this school would re- ceive a first-class secular education, as well as thoroughly grounded in morals and the principles of religion. The kind of work in this school shows for itself. Everyone present cannot but be pleased with the results, and the manner in which the children had gone through their exer- cises that evening E. M. Sneyd-Kynnewley, Esq., Her Majesty's inspector, in his report of the last inspection of this school, says :—" The school is row doing much better; the children are in good order, and both in the elementary and olass subjects the work is very creditable. Paper work generally neat. Sewing very fair." Mr. Kirkham moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman and Miss Norman, and after being responded to the meeting closed, the children receiving fruit as they retired.

WESTON POINT. DROWNING FATALITY AT WICSTON POINT—On Monday, an inquest was held at Weston .Point on the body ot sailor named Carl Oscar Johanson, who was dr.wned at Weston Point on Friday night. The deceased was a sailor on board the schooner Perseverance, of Foy, which was lying in the docks, and when returning to the vessel from Runcorn, along the canal side, he fell into the water. A woman saw the accident, and reised an alarm, but the body was lifeless when recovered. A verdict of "Accidentally drowned" was returned. ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS. •

TFIE CHARGE AGAINST A CHESHIRE CLERGYMAN.-011' Saturday at Great Neston, the commission of inquiry by the direction of the Lord Bishop of Chester, for the pur- pose of investigating eleven charges of drunkenness which had been brought against the Rev. John Aldom, M.A., in- cumbet*of the church and district of All Saints, Thornton Hough, in the diocese of Chester, was concluded. At the close ot the evidence on both sides the court were unanim- ously of opinion that there was sufficient evidence to justify further inquiry, and it is possible that both parties may agree to refer the case to the bishop, whose judgment would in all likelihood be final. THE DESECRATION OF A CHESTER CHORCHYARD.—At Chester, on Saturday, Mr. Ellis, solicitor, appeared on be- half of John William Carter and James Dean, charged with desecrating a churchyard at Boughton, Chester. Mr. Ellis said that Mr. Carter, one of the defendants, was the owner of a cottage contiguous to the graveyard. The sanitary authorities reported that the cottaga was in an insanitary condition, and Mr. Carter sent Dean to attend to it. In ex- cavating he unearthed certain bones and skulls of persons who had been buried there. Seeing these bones Mr. Carter ordered the workman to desist, and had the bones covered up; but some mischievous boys discovering the remains unearthed them, and began digging at the skulls with their sticks.—The Magistrates' Clerk stated that Mr. Carter had given up the ground to the Corporation, and the prosecution would be withdrawn on payment of costs, which was acceded to by the defendants.
