she went to live in Elieemere-street. It was unfortunate that the child had been , born, but he submitted that no mother in the world could have made the child any better than it now was. He thoroughly believed that the state of the child was brought about by constitutional disease. He sabmitted that the woman was not guilty of wilful neglect. If she had been, would she have taken the child to Dr. Richmond ?—Emma Yughill said she was the mother of the woman now charged, and lived in Lisberne- lane, Tuebreok, Liverpool. Her daughter was mar- ried to Mr. Irwin, but some dispute had arisen between them and divorce proceedings were now pending. The child was born at witness' house, and was weakly at its birth, and used to scream night and day. During the three months her daughter stayed with her, the child had witness, her two daughters, and two servants to look after it. It was in a very weak rotate and its eyes were affected. t,he had two doctors attending i-. One was Dr. Lupton and the other was Dr. Edgar fitown, of the Eye and Ear Infirmary, one of the best doctors in Liverpool she be- lieved. The doctors told her th it if the child's eyes got better in all probability the disease would go to seine other part of the body. The day her daughter went to Manches- ter she had business with her lawyers, and witness Was with her and stayed with her all night. The-post-card referred to was posted at night and ought to have reached Mrs. Thomason's the following morning instead, of noon, but the delay might be accounted for by it being Christmas time. Her daughter in her letters to witness Mways spoke in affectionate terms of the child. Witnestealways thought that her daughter was too anxious about her children, and she believed she was so anxious to fatten the child that she gave it a great deal too much food. Her daughter left her (witness's) house intending to go to a situation, and she left the child with Mrs. Moseley, who was one of witness's old servants. She had been very unhappy for some time past, and thought if she went to some employment it would occupy her mind. She did not go simply for the wages. Her daughter was- allowed 15s per week by Mr. Irwin. (Major Cartwright : Whew! Is that all?) Witness replied that it Was, but that ehe helped her when she thought proper to do so.—Mrs. Moseley, of 7, Wakefield-stteet, said that the prisoner and her child came to her house on the sth of October. She had seal the child that morning, and she did not think there was any difference between its state now and when she first Saw it three months since. The prisoner staved with her a week, then went away into a situation, leaving the child with witness and plying her 63 per week for look- ing after it. Witness had received several letters from her while she was away, and she always told her, to take the greatest care of the child. The child need to be continually crying. At the prisoner's request she gave the child milk from a special cow, and she had often seen that cow milked. When she had been away nine weeks she returned and took the child away.—James Moseley corroborated the last wit- ness —Dr. Richmond, for whom a messenger had been sent, said that he remembered the prisoner coaling to the Infir- mary with a child, but he could not soy when it was. He had no record of it because she did not bring a recommend with her. He remembered prescribing for the child, bat could not remember what the child was suffering from, as he had such a large number to deal with. The child was here shown to the witness, and he said it was quite poseible that it might have been properly fed, and its present state might have been brought about by constitutional disease. The child was not in a healthy state, and there was nothing in its appearance to show that it had been neg- lected. (Mr. Sutton: I think that the medical profession is a profession of mysteries.)—Before the magistrates retired to consider their decision Mr. Sutton addressed them on , their sentence in the event of a con.viction. In many of the similar cases in which he had prosecuted, the women were properly sentenced to six months imprisonment with hard labour, for they were women beyond the control of their husbands. He felt that in this case the position of the woman, who, as respondent in a snit for divorce would need to meet the suit, was one to command consideration and sympathy. However degraded or guilty she might be; it was fair to think her mind had been greatly harrassed and distressed by her unhappy position, and that to this sad condition might be attributed much of her neglect. He, therefore, asked the justices to deal lightly with the case, and treat it as one exceetiontl to the class of cases he had before appeared in—The Beneh then retired with the clerk (Mr. H. B. White), and on returning Major Cartwright said that the case had been a very painful one. The Bench were satisfied that the prisoner was guilty ef negligence ; but after taking into consideration all that Mr. Davies had brought forward in her favour, and after hearing the appeal which Mr. Sutton had just made, they had decided to deal leniently with her. She would have to pay £3 and costs, or go to prison for two months.—Mrs. Yughill : Thank God !—A very touching scene was then witnessed. The mother and daughter embraced each other, the latter weep- ing aloud for several moments, and exclaiming " Never again!" The mother, who was evidently agreeably surprised with the sentence, afterwards patted Mr. Davies- on the shoulder.
FATAL ACCIDENT ON THE CHESHIRE LINES RAILWAY.

Mr. Samuel Brighouse, the newly-appointed coroner for the West Derby Hundred, held an inquest at the Rain's Head, Warrington, on Tuesday, on the body of Jos. Kelly, a widower, aged 35 years, of Silver-street, who was killed on the railway, on Saturday morning —The body was identified by Mary Kelly, daughter of deceased.—James Moody, 134, Battersby-lane, stated that he was foreman for Sir Robert Pitt, contractor, Liverpool, in connection with the Cheshire Lines Waggon Works, Warrington, and the deceased had been working under him. On Saturday morning deceased, , with others, was engaged discharging waggons on a new line in progress of making, and the gang then left in order to unload a second set in the Central Station yard, about a , quarter of a mile distant. The men were in the habit of getting over a wooden rail which fenced the line, but wit- ness had warned them, deceased among the rest, not to do so, as they could get to the yard another way. Witness was 80 yards nearer Warrington Station'than deceased when he saw a passenger train passing on the up line. He heard the driver sound the whistle and then saw the deceased fall from the rails as if shot from a gun. The engine caught him on the bead before he could get out of the way, and killed him instantaneously. A luggage train was passing on the down line, and the goods van was just coming by when deceased came off the rails. Deceased's attention had been directed to the goods train and not to the passenger train. and when the van of the former passed he thought the course was clear. Kelly had been in his employ about six weeks, and be knew him to be a steady man.—Peter one of the deceased's fellow-workmen, said that after they had finished their work on the new line they proceeded to- wards the station yard by the fence. Witness had got over on the other side of the line, when he saw deceased on the top rail. He saw him looking in the direction of a luggage train which was approaching,.but he did not notice the pas- senger train, which came up and killed him. The trains I almost met, but he was positive deceased did not observe the I passenger train. They had been cautioned not to go on the I main line.—Alfred Cooper, 8, Blackburn-terrace, Toxteth. park, Liverpool, in the employ of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway, deposed that he was fireman of the passenger train in question on Saturday morning last. He was about 200 yards off, when he saw a batch of men get over the fence. The whistle was sounded. On corning up a man (deceased) in getting off the fence stumbled through his boot heel catching the rail, and he came on the side of the up line. He seemed to stand still for a few seconds, and then turned his head, when the engine buffer of witness's train caught him. The engine was stopped, and witness went to him, but he found him to be quite dead. One side of his head was knocked in, his right arm broken, and his breast and side badly injured.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."—We believe the deceased, was a member of the Refuge Assurance Company, of which Mr. H. Thornton is the district manager. Though deceased only entered the society in December last, and had paid but Is 24, his relative, received £lO 2s.

The usual fortnightly meeting of this Board Was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday, there being present Messrs. Greening (chairman), Derbyshire, Caldwell, Broadbent, Jolley, J. Houghton, Hunt, Greenell, Brown, Grange, Owen, and Major Cartwright. HOME COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee, which contained nothing of pithlic interest, were adopted on the motion of Major CART WRIGHT, seconded by Mr. JOLLEY. THE STORY OF A WORKMEN! WAIF. M. Danarrsnana, the chairman ,of the Schools Com- mittee, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said he would like to refer to a case, the particulars of which, if they came before the public,Might be the means of afford- ing assistance to the Guardians in the matter. They had a boy named John Warrington, a foundling, wile was brought • up at the Workhouse from hie infancy, and when he was old enough he was transferred to the schools at Padgate. , There he was almost an incorrigible. There was not a wall I around the whole of the school premises, and the tad, who , was between 10 and 11 years of age, was in the habit of getting out of the place unknown to the officials and of visiting neighbouring houses, the occupiers of which treated him so kindly that it made him go again. He wished that those neighbours would not do it. They not only gave him lumps of plum pudding—(laughter)—but they gave him pence, which prompted him to repeat the visit, and consequently the school authorities could not keep him in bound. On one i occasion, Mr. Reynolds, "father" of one of the homes, hear- ing that the youngster was intent on paying a visit to a neighbour, hid his clothes, hat he was not to be out-done by ' this, but presented himself, clad only in his shirt, at the house of a person named London not far from the residence of the Rev. H. Williams, vicar of Padgate. Here lie was treated most hospitably, his clothes were sent for, and he was then brought back to the schools. (Laughter.) He thought the neighbours around were doing an injustice to the boy, and if, instead of treating him so kindly, they had given him a few strokes of the birch rd and sent him back directly, it would have been better. One dark night he went two or three miles away to a house where there hap- pened to bean evening party going on. Young Warrington went straight into the house, walked up to the piano, and Joined in toe singing and merriment. When the company Came to know who he was, they treated him hospitably, al- lowed him to take part in the festivities, and sent him beck to the schools on the following day. That was at dollies Green.—Viajor CARTWRIGHT : What A Christian country th,et is, to be sure. (Laughter.)—Mr. DARBYSHIRE, continuing, acid the boy was continually running away and giving the Superintendent (Mr. Mines) a great deal of I trouble. They tried the rod, but as that appeared to have no effect the committee had instructed the Superintendent to see on what terms the lad could lee got on a training shin, and a report would be rqade to the committee. The boy said he would like to go—he did not care what it was so long as be was set at liberty. The neighbours could help the committee if they sent Warrington away from their houses immediately, and not coax him in his pranks. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Bnomometrr thought that from what he had seen end heard of the little fellow he was not a bad lad. The Chairman of the Committee complained' of people giving him coppers, but he did not know whether the Chair- man had not been guilty of that himself. (Laughter.) But passing that over, it struck him that the boy was a nice little fellow, and under suitable canditions might be made a useful man. He believed it would be a good idea to put him on board a training ship, where he would have no op- portunity of returning to a neighbouring farm, but might be turned into a sailor.—Major CARTWRIGHT considered the lad would make a good seaman. The best thing would be to take him entirely away from the school, because in carrying out such Jack Sheppard and Dick 'Lupin business —(laughter)--he was encouraging others to do the same, because other lads seeing the good treatment their com- panion had met with would follow his example. They should send him away to a place where he would prove useful in the future, as they would never manage him at the schools.—The CHAIRMAN also thought the Board should place the boy on board a training ship, where he would have no back door to run out of. This waif was one of those in- dividuals whom the committee found it very difficult to manage—in fact he did not think it was possible to manage him. Mr. Mines had bestowed every kindness he could upon him, but his only reward was in the lad at once setting off to do some kind of mischief or damage. (Laughter.) Mr. Mines had been very kind to him one day, and soon afterwards be found that his protegi had been to the schoolmaster's desk and mixed together all the pens which the master had only just previously arranged in very neat order. - (Renewed laughter.)—Mr. CALDWELL did not believe Warrington was a vicious lad, and if he was sent to a training ship he might yet prove a credit to the school. He thought the Clerk should be instructed to place him on board a training ship at once.—The CLERK said he must make enquiries first, as he was not sure of the terms on which the lad could be taken.—lt was then agreed that the Clerk should make the necessary enquiries with the view of placing the lad on board a training ship as soon as pee- sible.—The minutes of the Schools Committee were then adopted. -

div.head: RELIEVING OFFICER'S DIFFICULTY.
div.p: A RELIEVING OFFICER'S DIFFICULTY.

The CHMRIIAN said the relieving officers had mentioned to him that they would be glad if the Schools Committee would report to them at any rate once a week as to what children had left the schools, and whether they had been apprenticed or taken out by their parents. They com- plained at not receiving such a report, and Mr. Shearer was placed in a peculiar position in A case in which he was pro- secuting the other day through not knowing as to whether certain children had left the schools.—The Board resolved to instrupt Mr. Mines to give the necessary particulars, and the subject dropped.
THE VACCINATION QUESTION AGAIN: A. GROAN FROM THE NEW OFFICER. The CLERK read the followins, letter addressed to the Board:—
Eldest° wn, Jaluary 22n1,

Gentlemen,—When von honoured me by ele :dog me to the office of vaccination officer for the Newton district your chair- man said that I should be expected to work up the arrears as far as possible. Gentlemen, I think that neither you nor ' I bad a clear knowledge of what the arrears amounted to. I had been to d before the election that the number of the arrears was about 200, but since my appointment I have carefully gone through the report book with the (-flowing result :—The total number of entries are 1 062, and I classilled them as follows: Vaccinated and insus- ceptible 424, dead 42, removed to other towns and the vacci- nation officer acquainted 32. removed where relieving officer not acquainted 65, removed to piaces unkown 200, unlit 46, postponed and otherwise not accounted for 241, objections to vaccination 1, and been once summoned 1, total 1,062. To sum up there are 476 cases which are settled, and 586 which require looking after. In addition there are about 150 cases in the register which have not been in the report book, so that the arrears insteal of only amounting to 200 are in fact over 700. 1 trust, thereihre, gentlemen, that you will take the above statement into your favourable consideration with reaard to Ithe extra time which will be requisite to give the matter its fullest effect.—Your obedient servant, A. COOPER

—The Cumulate asked whether they had not agreed to pay Mr. Cooper at any extra rate for the arrear cases.—The CLERK : Nothing was said to him definitely, although you told me you would take the subject into consideration. It simply mesas that the late officer has taken all the eight- pencas for cases about which he had not toe least trouble in the world, and he has left the other cases for the neWofficer. -The CHAIRMAN said that when the other officer was elected they gave him something more than 83 for working up certain arrears.—Mr. CALDWELL, considering the great work which would be involved, thought the arrear cases should be allowed to .pass over, but that should support their officer in preventing others setting the law at defiance.— Mr. JOLLEY said the law should not be set at defiance, and they should pay this man a little extra to energetically work the arrears to the best of his ability.—The Cumulate remarked that he was not a strong advocate for vaccination, but was almost inclined to be an anti-vaceinator—{MajoT CARTWRICIAT : If this is reported in the papers anti-vacci- nators at Newton will rejoicel—but if he was to aclmms- i ter the law he would do it so far as it came under his juris- diction. (Rear, hear.) The officer had been appointed to work up the cases of arrears and fresh cases, and any extra time which he devoted ta the duties they had consented to pay him for it. The vaccination question was one which should be very carefully dealt with. lie knew that very great and bad results had attended vaccination, but never- theless he was not going to tell the officer to be lenient with would-be offenders in this respect.—Major WP.iGasT: Then we'll set you down as a middle man—just as much on one side as 03 the other —lt was eventually agreed that the Clerk should write to Mr. Cooper giving him instructions to deal with the matter, and stating that they would take the subject of compensation into considers- doz.

MR. DARBYSHIRE AND THE ROYAL AORICUTUELL SHOW. A leter was received thanking the Board for signing; a memorial in favour of the Royal Agricultural Society's next show being hell at Preston.—Mr. DARDESSITELE ex- pressed an opinion that he did not think many of the mem- bers knew what they were doing in signing the memorial. —Mr. JOLLEY : You signed it. (Laughter.)—Mr. DA.RBY- SHIRT{ indignantly denied that he did so, and in reply to Major Cartwright said he belonged to the county ef Che- shire, and Chester was a very strong competitor in the matter. OLT-TOWNSHIPS AND Ina" CALLS" Major Cenrwmany drew attention to the .` calls "owing by the out-townships, and moved that unless they be met within a reasonable time that the Clerk sh.uld seethe over- seers in the matter. Whilst Warrington and Latchford. which paid five-eights of the poor rates of the Union, met their calls so promptly it was unfair that the out-townships should keep so much 'behind--Mr. JOLLEY seconded, con- sidering that other townships should follow the good example of Warrington and Latchford.—Mr. licwr : They are not all tradesmen in the country--they are °nIV poor farmers.—Mr. JOLLEY: They are bettor off than tradesmen. —Mr. DARBYSHIRH said ‘he observed that Gracpenhall was three calls behind, but he lam it mas not the fault of the overseers or the ratepayers, and be hoped the Clerk woald instruct the parties concerned to pay a c3uple of calls at once —The Citatintax said that Grappenhall and South- worth were three calls behind....-Mr. BROADBENT was in favour et punctuality being insisted upon, otherwise it opened the door to irregularity. (Rear, hear —Major , Cartwright's proposition was ultimately carried. rROPOSED WEEKLY MEETINGS Or THE BOARD.
Mr... BROADBENT wished the Board to cwnsider_the advis:
ability of meeting every we in-stead of-fortnightly as at present, and whether there was not sufficient business fot a k weekly meeting. He thought it would be much better for

/official and rend business if the Guardians met weekly. lienot did wish to raise a discussion lin the ;natter that day, his only object then being that the Chairman and members of the Beard should consider before the end of the Board Year whether such a change would be desirable.—Major CArrrerruourr : It will be time to discuss that on the 21st April.—Mr. BROADBENT : You can consider it in the mean- time.—Mr. CALDWELL thought such A proposition would be negatived_...The CHAIRMAN said that formerly the Beard was in the habit of meeting, weekly.—The subject then dropped. There was no other business ef interest.

"THE -TRUE HONOUR OF NATIONS.' LECTURE Ar wARRINGTON. A lecture on the above suite:- was deliven-d at Wycliffe. Hall, on Monday evening, by the /Lev. J. Freeston, of Stalybridge, in connection with the Peace 'Association. Lit the absence of F. A. Roberts. Esq., who Tlt4B announced to have presided, the chair was taken by Councillor walling,. tnn. There was a fair attendance.

The Cwaintrare, in intreaucing the lecturer, referred to the previous able addresses given in Warrington by Mr. 'Freeaton, and speaking especially of a lertuee on " Astro- nondy," he took occasioa to ask the yeung men present to take the first opportunity to study toe starry sky, as there were now constellations to be sees, which wuald prove most interesting for reflection. The subject of, ttre lecture that- evening was •• Tne true honour of ustione." • There was a reference in scripture which said " Righttouesess, or right doing, exalteth a nation," and the question might come as to what was right doing, there were so 'limy differeut epinions.on that point. Ye thought, however, it might be explained by another scriptural quotation—" Whatsoever you would wish others might no unto you, you do unto . them." That would really guide them to do what was right in the matter. (Hear, hear.) foe Lire.ruenn, in commencicg his address, observed he had noticed that when men spoke of tie honour of their country they used the term honour" in quite a different sense to the way.they used it in reference to their own con- duct or in regard to their private a ipacities, but it seemed to him that moral laws should apply to natioos in precisely the same sense as they did to individuals. It was dishon- ourable for agich man to oppress a pour man, and so it was equally dishonourable for a powerful nation to take advan- tage of a weak one. As a first illustration of his meaning he referred to recent affairs in South Attica, and said that when the Government made peace with the Boers accord- ing to a previous arrangement, they were charged with having trailed British honour in the dust,. and that they had done a dishonourable thing. In what sense, be asked, was the word " honour " used in that respect? He could make it to mean no other sense than this, that their British honour was their power and willingness to fight, that after the defeat of Sir George Colley they ought to have gone on fighting the Boers and showing the power they had to subdue-such a cemparatively small body of people. The word "honour "in that case was misused as it woad not have been honourable for them to have continued slaughtering hundreds and perhaps • thousands just tuprove that they could do it, a fact which no one doubted not even the Boers themselves. (Hear, hear.) If they bad done 80 such conduct would have been dishonourable in the highest degree. (Hear, hear.) A few years ago their Government. was anxious to extend their boundary of the north-west portion or India, and believing they wanted a more scientific frontier—(a laugh)—they came to the conclusion that they must take a large piece of teriitory from their neighbour, Afghanistan, He would express no opinion as to whether they really required a more scientific frontier, he would take it for granted they did—but was it right to go and attempt to steal the terri- tory ? He c iuld not sea on what ground of common sense or of moral principle that they would tell him he was dis- honourable if he stole a single yard of land irons his neigh- bour, and yet be considered right and proper for a great nation like England to go and steal miles and miles of ter- ritory from a weaker nation. , He said that was diehonour- able conduct. (A,- voice: Undoubtedly.) Yet because the owners of that country should fail in carrying out what , they in England desired they tired up • their dignity, they said, was disgraced, and to maintain their honour they mast fight the country and not only take the few hundreds of miles they originally wanted but invade the whole country. That was again dishonourable. Instead of attempting to steal the land they required why did they not go to the Linear of Afghanistan and try to negotiate with him for the purchase of the land instead of stealing it ? Suppose that they had offered three millions for it, they would see that doing the right thing meant doing the best thing, for they would have obtained the land they wanted, extended their frontier, and made it more "scien- tific." Instead of doing_that, however, they went to fight, for which they had to pay close upon 20 millions of money, they had murdered thousands of men, and even then did not get the land after all, and the frontier remained the same as before. (Laughter.) It was weakness, folly, and dis- honourable for a nation like theirs to treat a neighbour in the way they did, and his contention was that they should be honourable in their conduct nation to nation as they expected between gentleman and gentleman. (Hear, hear.) Ia such cases as-he had illustrated it was there, he main- tained, that the tree honour of nations ought to have been shown in doing that which was right and just, and, as the chairman said in his opening remarks, it was righteousness that exalted a nation. As righteousness exalted a nation, so unjust measures degraded it. and as far as his memory was concerned he did not know of. anything that had occurred within the last forty years that had so degraded and so dis- honoured the English name as their attack upon Afghanis- tan. (Hear, hear.) Of course they had their own self- interest to look after in the struggle for existence, but there was a limit, and that limit was between "thine and mine," by moral law. That moral law should be applied to nation in the same way. Not a century ago, not in the dark ages, and not even in the middle ages, but only five years ago there were the leading newspapers in London and leading statesmen publicly declaring that Government had nothing to do with morality, but what they an a nation and a Government had to do was 0 look after British ineerests— they were simply to spread Imperialism. He confessed being positively shocked and surprised when he read lead- ing articles giving expression to views of that kind. The lecturer next spoke of our action with respect to China and the opium trade. They knew perfectly well that opium had a weakening effect on the human constitution, how at firat it gave a pleasant excitement and then a counteracting in- , fluence by means of whichahe nervous system got ruined, and all manliness wee gone. The Chinese Government saw the ruin the drag was working, asked the Indian Govern- ment not to bring any more into the country. What did they do? They sent their ships.to war, their soldiers bom- herded the Chinese forts, killel thousands of people, and compelled. the Chinese Governmera to take their opium. That, he submitted, was dishonourable conduct from one nation towards another. It was dishonourable and unwise. Although they had up to then been getting a profit of from este eight millions annually by the trade, he believed they would have been gainers in every way if they had given it up, and instead of using so much land in India for the cul- tivation of the opium, plant, if they had cultivated rice or wheat for the food of the people and induced the Chinese . to spend six millions say in buying Lancashire manufac- tured goods—(applause)—it would have been better for China, better for India, and better for England. (Hear, hear.) Having spoken of the matters leading to the. Crimean war, which he pointed out would have been avoided if common sense and justice had been exercised, he adverted to the action taken with regard to the Alabama dispute. There were many. who said it was dishonourable and lowering the dignity of the English nation by settling that dispntethy arbitration„ instead of by fighting. Oc what principle was it dishonour- able, and how did it differ from the action of two honour-. able individuals? He contended it was one of the most bononrable things that their Government had ever been en— gaged in, and in this as in the other cases, be asked if the honourable action was not the wise and good action. (Ap- plause.) To those. who said it was dishonourable. to pay three millions of money to the American people in. settlement, what would it have cost them if they had gone to war with America? In his concluding remarks, Mr. Freeston spoke 'of the country's extravagance iimaintainings standing armies, and the desirability of establishing Inter- national Courts of Arbitration for the settlement of the In looking round the monuments erected in St. Paul's Cathedral lately, be was struck with the fact that they were almost all sacred to the memory of fighting men, and be conli not but feel how incongruokus it•was that in that glorious temple whcre week after week clergy- mendt therein and peace in were the fmelemlnorww. Hhcroeeonswurtyelrre,2ol3o:Bana in towards men, that Christianthe great dmoecttr hi doctrine oo of teen; they celebratedhad d efeerrothyeednum(aleeeraro,fhleharesr.)of their prcposing.a vote of thanks to the teat he had also been struck with the the minuments erected in St. Pand'S, The, Celeihicautrurarel'ire'rat:s2.f:the Army as professions had gone arm in arm too long; the alliance he thought was an unholy one, and the sooner the nation expressea its opinion to that effect; the better. The vote of thanks having been, seconded by it was supported by the Rev. John it-I.NGormoe o.w the': aree Jentatne there were not more ladies present, because lie thoeght if the fair sex were educated in the principles the lecturer had expounded thou evening, they would have coneiderable influence in guiding the politics of - men in this question. (Hear, hear.) A vole of thanks ta.. the Chairman for presiding concluded the proceedings.

mE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, JANUARY 26, 1884.

! THE decision which has this week been. , given in the Queen's Bench by Mr. Baron PoLLocK. in the action brought by Mr. PER- CIVAL HEYWOOD to compel the Bishop of MANCHESTER to institute the Rev. HARRY , COWGILL to the living of St. John the Evan- gelist, Miles Platting, will be received, we believe, with general satisfaction by the clergy and laity, to whom the decision must . commend itself as the common-sense view of the question at issue. The circumstances under which the Bishop refused to institute , are we should think, familiar to all. Sir PER- CIVAL HEYWOOD is the patron of the living, which was formerly held by the Rev. SIDNEY FAITHHORN GREEN. He was admitted in 1869, and he very soon not only made himself notorious, but, what is worse, he materially , assisted to bring the service of the church into something like contempt by the vest- ments which he wore and the many ritualistic practices in which he freely indulged. Mr. GREEN'S behaviour was, at the ir stigation of the Church Association, brought under the notice of Lord PENZANCE, who pronounced the Rector's mode of conducting the services in the Church to be illegal He was conse- quently duly admonished, but notwithstand- tag this he continued his illegal practices, : and it was in consequence of disobeying tne I order of Lord PENZANCE'S Court that he I was for a lengthened period incarcerated in ' Lancaster Gaol and subsequently deprived !of his living, which became vacant in 188 z. Now, let it be noted that Mr. GREEN'S con- duct met the approval of the patron of the ; living, Sir P. HEYWOOD, a most uncom- promising ritualist; and also that the Rector of Miles Platting was assisted in his nonsen- sical manoeuvres by the Rev. HARRY Coworm., who was curate from 1877 to 188 z. While the latter, too, was in charge of the Church during Mr. GREEN'S imprisonment, he wore the unlawful vestments; during the com- munion service he administered wine mixed with water; he used lighted candles when they were not required for the purpose of light; and the customary genuflexions were observed during the consecration prayers. In fact, he endeavoured to perpetuate all the illegal practices for which his Rector was sent to prison. Mr. COWGILL was therefore as great an offender against the ecclesiastical law as Mr. GREEN, whom Mr. COWGILL seems to have aided and abetted at every turn. This, then, is the gentleman whom the patron presented to the living of which Mr. GREEN had been deprived: and these being the circumstances, the Bishop very properly required of Mr. COWGILL some guarantee that if instituted he would conduct the ser- vices in accordance with the requirements of : law. Mr. COWGILL declin ed to give any pledge as to his future action, and the Bishop ' thereupon refused to institute a clergyman whom he knew had violated the law, and who was likely to continue so to do. It must 4 appear clear that if the Bishop had assented to Mr. COWGILL'S institution he would I not only have stultified his previous action towards Mr. GREEN, but he would have , been countenancing Mr. COWGILL' S illegal conduct. It seems equally clear that . Sir PERCIVAL HEYWOOD by present- ' I ing Mr. COWGILL to the living threw down a challenge to the Bishop, a , challenge as unnecessary as it was . indiscreet, and one, too, which the , Bishop could not safely recline. ALLEGED THEFT OF A HORSE BY i RUNCORN BOAT- MAN—At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday' before Mr. H. Reynolds, Moses Littlemore was brought up on remand charged that he, being the bailee of a horse belonging to William Yarnell, did feloniously steal the same.—Yarnell is the captain of a canal boat, upon which the prisoner had been " hand " for the past three months.' On Monday, the 7th inst., the boat left Runcorn with a cargo of sand for Heywood, in Lancashire. Attached to the boat was a horse Yarnell bad purchased from Edwin Tucker. When they had reached Linnet's Lock, which is about seven miles past Manchester, Yarnell found the horse was not working satis- factorily, but he managed to complete the journey with it, and started on the return trip. At the expiration of the third mile, Yarnell asked the prisoner what he had better do with the horse. He agreed that the best thing would be to take it back to Runcorn, and he consented to ride it. He mounted it about nine o'clock on the 11th inst., and Yar- nell travelled by train to Runcorn in order to purchase another horse, The prisoner did not turn up that day, but at noon on the 12th Yarnell saw him in a house in Stone street, and asked him where the horse was. The prisoner replied that the animal had "dropped dead" with him on its back, and it had required the strength of three men to pull him from under. He added that he had " knackered him" for 10s, and he produced half a sovereign, which, however, he declined to give his master. Later on the same day he handed Yarnell 7s 2d, which he said was all that was left. On the 17th inst. Yarnell saw the horse alive in Tuckey's stables, and a warrant was issued for the prisoner's enerebension, which was effected by P.S. Walley. It tran- spired that the prisoner had sold the horse to Robert Dut- ton, horse dealer and slaughterer, Altrincham, for 24' s and this person afterwards sold it to William Heaton, a boat- man, living in Gilbert-street, Runcorn, for £2 178 ed.—The prisoner was committed to Chester Assizes for trial.
