RUNCORN Y.M.C.A. HISTORICAL i'.CLAss.—Mr. J. Craig, principal of the Runcorn Collegiate School, lectured to the members of this class on Thursday evening on " The Stuart family." RUNCORN RATEPAYERS' ASSOCIATION.—It is stated that representatives of this Asseciation will appear before the auditor at the forthcoming audit in order to test the liability of the ratepayers to pay the costs incurred in the recent action, Beasley v. Commissioners. Loa]) WINMARLEIOII AND FARNWORTH GRAMMAR SCHOOL.—The Right Hon. Lord IViumarleigh has written to the Rev. George Bond expressing his gratification at his recent visit to Farnworth' and forwarding £lO. half to be given to the Grammar School for prizes or something use- ful, and half to the fund for restoring Farnworth Church. THE HALE-DAY HOLIDAY MOVEMENT IN WIDNEs.—The Half-day Holiday Association have appointed Mr. F. H. Pankhurst president, Mr. E. Warham treasurer, and Mr. Peate secretary. The committee consists of Messrs. Read, Sandland, R. Booth, Melvin, F. Tebbutt, S. B. Stringer, and S. Guy. With the exception of grocers and butchers, all the tradesmen will close their establishments on Thursday, the 7th February, at one o'clock, and at the same time every following Thursday. The movement which meets with much favour, is to be inaugurated by a pic-nic. WIDNES PARISH CHURCH ENTERTAINMENTS. Under the presidency of the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, the third entertainment of the present series was given on Tuesday evening, to a good audience. An excellent programme was gone through in capital style by the following ladies and gentlemen :—Miss Fairley, Mr. Appleton (Runcorn), Mr. Annett, Mr. Craig, Mr. Moulson' and Messrs. L. and J. Kil- cross. The glee class, conducted by Mr. Crawford, acquitted themselves in their usual efficient style. RAILWAY FATALITY AT WIDNES.—There died at Widnes Accident Hospital, on Wednesday night, Frederick William Gough, a joiner, who resided at 44, Warrington-road. On Wednesday evening, the 26th December Gough was found , on the St. Helens railway, near Ann-street level crossing, with his leg in an awfully mat.gled condition, and it is sup- posed he was run over by two two trains that had passed a few minutes previously. He was conveyed to the hospital, where it was found necessary to amputate the limb, and the ' operation was performed by Drs. Cooper and McLennon. The injured man became unconscious, and be remained in that condition until his death. He was only 24 years of age. An inquest will be held to-day. SAD END OF A WIDNES FLATMAN.—Mr. Btighouse, coro- ner, held an inquest at the Main-top Hotel, Mersey-road, i Widnes, on Tuesday afternoon, touching the death of John Davies, a flatman, whose body was found in the canal at I Widnes. on Sunday morning.—Thomas Davies, of 26,j White-street, deposed that the deceased was his brother, and I he was 41, years of age. He last saw him alive between I eight and half-past on Friday night, the 18th inst.—George 1 Whyment, waterman. of 64, West-street, said between nine and ten o'clock on Fridry night, the 18th instant, he called! at the Main-top Hotel, and saw the deceased there. He was then drunk, and lie enticed him to go on board the flat I with him. He saw him safe in the forecastle. The next morning the deceased could not be found, and a search was I , made, in which he assisted. He saw the body recoved from the canal on Sunday by a man named John Mason.—The I I jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned." DINNER TO POOR CHILDREN AT WIDNES.—On Satur• I day afternoon, 160 poor children partook of a dinner in the , Widnes National Schools. They had been invited to the r . repast by the Vicar of Widnes, who had been assisted in his labour of love by Mrs. J. W. Williams, Mrs. Thomas, Mrs. Fairclough, Mrs. Cane, Mrs. Hunt, Mrs. James, Mrs. Eaves, I Mrs. Shaw, Miss Fairley ; Messrs. J. B. Imison, Atherton, Cane, Watson, Hunt, Beattie, and Starkey. The funds!. obteined from various sources would only permit of the ' number Mentioned being fed, and a COMmitiee, ef Which Mrs. Williams was the head, had no difficulty in distributing ' tickets to that number of poverty stricken children, who are very numerous in Widnes. Huge quantities of beef and potatoes and platm pudding bad been provided, and each 1 child was allowed to fully satisfy the cravings of hunger. ' As the children left the room after their meal, they were each presented with an orange and a bag of sweets. WltlifEs POLICE COURT.—Yesterday, before Mr. John : rStock and Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun., Henry Stowele and i James Quinn, labourers, were charged with sleeping in the I works of Messrs. Hutchinson and Company on the previous I evening, and, on the evidence of P.C.'s Townley and Black. I hall, were each eentenced to seven days' bard labour.--e James Edwards, an old man, was charged with begging.— I P.C. Blackhall deposed to seeing the prisoner enter several I shops in Waterloo-road. He emerged from one with a bun 11 in his hand, and the constable went in and addressed vari ' I ous inquiries to the woman behind the counter. In the presence of the prisoner she stated he had been begging, and he was taken into custody. Upon the prisoner was found!, 2s 33 in copper, and upwards of a dozen boxes of matches. ' —The prisoner stated he was a licensed hawker, and pro- I duceel his certificate. He contended that he went into the I shops to sell matches —The Bench discharged prisoner. 1, ACTION BY A WIDNES BUILDER. At the St. Helens j County Court, on Wednesday last, before Mr. T. P. G. I , Thompson, Judge, Mr. Thomas Sadler, of Widnes, builder, ' sued Mr. William Wood, of Crow-wood, contractor, for £32 18s. four and a half years' ground rent, from March, 1879, .1 to September, 1.°83, at £7 103 per annum, for land at Ander- son's corner, Widnes-road, Widnes. It seems that the defen- dant had agre-d to tike a sub-lease for 997 yea's of the land ; in question and had signed agreements to that effect. No lease hid been signed. Mr. Knowles, solicitor, Widnes, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Hardy, of Liverpool, Barrister-at-law (instructed by Mr. W. T. Husband, solicitor, , Widnes), appeared for the defendant. Objection was taken by the Court as to the sufficiency of the stomp on the agreement., and eiltimately the case was adjourned for pro- ; duction of the plaintiff's title as the lease of the land to ; him was not produced in accordance with a notice to pro- duce given by the defendant's solicitors. The Judge allowed 1 defendant's costa. THE COUNTY CORONER AND UNPROFESSIONAL REPRE- SENTATIVES. —At an inquiry at the Main Top Hotel, Mersey-road, Widnes, on Tuesday, before Mr. Brighouse, Inspector Shaw appeared to represent the London and North-Western Railway Company.—The Coroner said that 4 Inspector Shaw could not crosieexamine any witness, and , he was of opinion that a rich company like the London and North-Western could afford to pay to be represented by a solicitor, and Mr. Shaw had better retire and the result of 1, the enquiry would be communicated to him. Inspector Shaw then withdrew. The Coroner said he might say that I he had quite made up his mind that he should not allow un- professional gentlemen to appear before him on behalf of anyone. He should insist upon companies whose interests were attacked being represented by a solicitor or barrister. He felt this to be a duty owing to the jury, so that their I time might not be t Alton up to the extent it would be if he allowed any but a solicitor or barrister to be present. Pro- fessional gentlemen were versed in the rules of evidence and the modes of cross-examination, and knew how enquiries were conducted in as short a time as possible. If he allowed unprofessional persons to appear before him it would not only annoy, but get the cross-examination into a wrong channel, and might take up a great deal of the valuable time of the jury. JUVENILE THIEVES AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, yesterday. Mary McLoughlin and Mary Cummins, aged respectively 11 and 12 years, were brought up charged with stealing a man's shirt from the shop of Mr. Joseph Littler, draper, Widnes-road. Mary Elizabeth liamblett, assistant to Mr. Littler, identified the shirt, which was valued at Sc 61. In was safe in the shop at 1-45 on the 23rd inst., and half an hour later it was missed. It had not been sold to the prisoners.—P.C. Walker deposed to appre- hending the prisoners on Wednesday afternoon.—ln answer to the charge, McLoughlin alleged that she stale the shirt I at the instigation of Cummins, and that she pledged it and gave the latter 4d.—The prisoners were each fined 10s.— McLoughlin was further charged with stealing a pair of drawers, the property of Mr. Littler, but she was dis- charged.—Patrick Mitchell, 11 years of age, was brought up charged with stealing 15Ibs. of coal, the property of the London and North-Western Railway Company. The pri- soner was caught in the act of stealing the coal from near the steam crane on the canal side lw P.C. Murray.—Thos. Carter, railway inspector, said all the coal near the steam crane belonged to the railway company.—The boy was Ordered to receive three strokes with the birch rod, and his father, who was in court, requested Inspecter Wood to "lay on heavy," as the prisoner was a "bad un." ODEFELL3WS' TEA PARTY AND BALL AT RIINCOML--The members of the Loyal Wright's Pride Lodge of Oddfellows held their Bth annual tea party and ball in Runcorn Public Hall on Thursday evening. About 280 persons sat down to the tea, which was provided by Mrs. Waterworth, of the Anchor Inn. The tables were presided over by Mrs. R. Wright, Mrs. C. Cooke, Mrs. T. Burrows, Miss Wright. Mrs. T. Lydiate, Miss Lydiate, Mts. Molvneux, Mrs. Weedall, Mrs. Saunders Mrs. Griffiths, Mrs. Davies, Mrs. Pye, Mrs. Dykes, Mrs. Holt, Mrs. White, and Mrs. J. Whieyates. Pre- vious to the ball, a meeting presided over by Dr. MacDou- gall was held. Letters of apology for non-attendance were . read from Captain Hazlehurst, J.PC, Messrs. C. Reynolds, J.P., H. Reynolds. J.P., j. Brundrit, J.P., W. Whittaker, and Dr. Steele. The Chairman delivered an address on the advantages of friendly societies, with which he had been identified for 15 years, making special reference to the one whose Bth anniversary they were celebrating. It must be admitted, he said, that the flower of the working classes of Runcorn were members of friendly societies, with great ad- vantage to themselves but greater advantage still to the welfare of the community.—Dancing commenced shortly after eight o'clock, and was continued for many hours, to the strains of Mr. Ward's quadrille band. Messrs. J. Pritchard, R. Gorst, and W. Wright officiated as M.C.'s. POPULAR EVENINGS FOR THE PEOPLE. These f ertnightly entertainments still continue to maintain their popularity among the inhabitants of Rain bill and the neigh- bourhood. This was fully proved on Wednesday evening last, when, dispite the violent gale blowing, a large and appreciative audience assembled. The chair was taken by the Rev. J. Barton, Miss Ashton acting as accempanist. The following programme was performed :—Pianoforte selection, Miss Ashton; quartette, "0 hush thee my baby ;" song, " The village blacksmith," Mr. J. Rudge ; duet, "Over the waves we float," Mrs. Thomson and Miss Kempton ; song, "The railway porters" Mr. U. Hartland ; Lancashire reading, Mr. Stoba ; song, " The wedding bells,' Mr. G. Hurst ; Yorkshire reading. Mr. Thompson; song, " Mrs. Brown's adventures," Mr. J.- fledge, song, coming ‘t'obWie. wTohne'tcgonochlu°dnline'g" tmla rro'lithwes tr y; eL,"a nMcriss.hTi rheorme apdeionng;, smo nr .g s, remarks of the Chairman brought to a close a most enjoy- able eimning. All the performers acquitted themselves well, and were deserving s of the applause and appreciation their effort received.

good. Kyrie Bellew is to me the most disagreeable actor of promise we hive. He is stagy, stilted, mannered, con- scious of his good looks, and—l do not like to say the word —but, on the stage, caddish. Miss Lingsrd was very con- scientious, and very self-conscious. Sophie Eyre was extremely good. But the team was not in hand. The play did not act itself. There were drags, aim illusion was broken. One of the most iinpoi rant membetv of the com- pany was the iron cui tain, which did ye ann.'s service at the end of the performance by rolling doss ii the most tractable way, vibes the ordinary drop curtain refused to work. If we are to have a theatre on fire, and if Mr. Itruce is insured, I hope it will be the Prince's. That curtain should not be kept out of work. But the great event of the week, literary, social, artistic, scientific, everything in fact except legal, has been the ar- rival and the reception of Mr. Barnum's elephant. The great authority on humbugs has made his greatest coup, and as nothing more was possible in that line, he has crowned the glory of his life—and made his will. Every kind of judicious trumpeting was sounded for this animal who was at once an Albino and a god. It seems now lee is not an Albino and he is not a god. Whether Barnum will make a new will, I cannot say ; but he certainly will not have his money returned. The doctors are delighted with the elephant—but I think they are the only people who are. Long names and incomprehensible ex- planations won't make a dirty-coloured lump look white. He certainly has white toes—his bitterest enemy must admit that—but so we have many guinea pigs and some fox-terriers. Soap may do much, and bleaching powder may do more. At present he is a dirty kind of grey with pink blotches. If in his anger he had swallowed some reams of blotting paper, and this foreign matter had "come to the surface" under vigorous medical treatment, his present ap- pearancs would be explained. Still at the private view he was looked at with great interest. I saw Mr. Briton Riviere contemplate him as a good subject for a new picture. The skin doctors are quite excited, and if he were a devil instead of a god the attendants in waiting on the other elephants in the gardens do not hate him snore keenly. On Monday the public came. The enterprising Barnum had the omnibuses labelled, "This way for the sacred elephant." The shilling public came in their thou- sands, more than 5,003 of them. Two hundred and fifty pounds worth of believers in the white elephant. When they found him dun ducketty mud colour relieved with pink, instead of being a dazzling white that would bring tears into their eye spotches, the 5,000 were disheartened, and , when the God was not allowed to eat buns the 5,000 were angry. I think Barnum is not very popular just at present, and that the cockney public would rather have a Jumbo than a God.

And here, now, is an ,ther disappointment for us. If there is one thing in which we believe, if in this age of sham and ' impostures we can point to one article of cur own growth, of absolute originality and undoubted worth, it is our ex- cellent Oscar. We know him in life with that long,great coat, redeemed from mere utility by its capacious and un- necessary for collar, with his still more remarkable frock coat, executed by an mstbetic tailor from the poet's ov n design, with the long thatch of dishevelled hair, framing a f”e which some ladies have said to be beautiful, with h'S Oracular utterandes, Ms affeetations, and his stupid bOTZ ItIOtS. We have produced him, we have ad. mired him, we have worshipped him, we have sent him across the Atlantic, as a specimen of what young Eng• land can do, and now there comes an answer from Yankee. land that he is not original after all. A man named Barony. an obscure photographer, whose wares are in tie windows of every capital in Europe, claims the creation of our Oscar. It was he who arranged those graceful knicker- bockers, it was he who settled the falls of the seductive drapery, who gave expression to the collar ot the coat, and invested the poetic £o3thete with artistic merit. The matter is to come before the ourts. It will be a proper precedent to Belt v. Lewes.

div.head: FURIOUS GALE AT RUNCORN AND . WIDNES.
div.p: FURIOUS GALE AT RUNCORN AND . WIDNES.

A storm of great violence, increasing in intensity to- wards evening, broke over Runcern on Wednesday morning. The tide began to flow two hours before the expected time, anal was several feet higher than its proper level. No craft of any description ventured from the port. A number of houses were pirtially unroofed in the town, and signboards and slates were flying about in all directions. In the even- ing a flat was observed at Weston Point to be labouring heavily, and to those on shore it was evident she must sooner or later sink. The three men on board were con- tinually drenched by the heavy seas that broke over the vessel, and they could do comparatively little to save the flat. Eventually the waves brought the vessel opposite the pier at Weston, when she went down. The piermen im- mediately threw ropes to the men, who were struggling in the water, and succeeded in dragging them on shere. Later a flat was seen to ground off Hale Head, and the wave washed furiously over the deck. There were on board five men who jumped into the small boat and pulled across the river towards Weston Point. After almost superhuman ex,;rtions they reached the pier, and were rescued from their perilous position. One of the number who was an elderly man, was so exhausted with the effects of the storm that he swooned away immediately he was taken to a hut on the pier. He was attended to lay some kind hearted people in the village, and was able to leave for home on the following morning. The flat was the Kid, be- longing to Mr. Cooper, of Widnes. At Widnes the storm, although raging with great violence, did little damage compared with previous occa- sions. In the evening the wind blew in gusts so strong that pedestrians had great difficulty in walking, and were in great danger from falling slates and chimney pots. A shed at the works of Messrs. Hutchinson and Co. was partly wrecked. The new copper works, which have been twice demolished, escaped uninjured entirely.

div.head: AN INCORRIGIBLE YOUNG ROGUE AT WIDNES.
div.p: AN INCORRIGIBLE YOUNG ROGUE AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. F. H Gossage and Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun., Henry Mather, a boy, 13 years of age, was brought up in custody charged with stealing an overcoat of the value of 155., the property of Sarah Mather.—Mrs. Mather said she was a grocer and provision dealer, Mersey-road, and the prisoner was her son. On the 28th December he left home with the overcoat in his possession. He returned on the 30th of the same month without the coat, which he informed her he had pledg,cl for ss. He gave her no portion of the money nor the pawnticket. He had no right te take the coat. The prisoner was a very bad lad and entirely beyond her con- trol. He bad not previously stolen anything from the house, but he had frequently left home for a week without her permission.—The prisoner pleaded guilty, and he was then charged with stealing a suit of boy's clothing, value , 63.—Mrs. Mather said the clothes were safe in a drawer in the bedroom, on the 13th inst. On the following day the prisoner left home, and on the 16th instant she missed the articles. She did not see the prisoner again until Satur- day when he was in the custody of the police. In answer to Mr. Lewin (deputy clerk to the indices), Mrs. Mather said she had frequently locked the prisoner in a room for days together in order to cure him of his bad habits.—PC. Blackhall deposed to apprehending the prisoner on Satur- day afternoon. He charged him with stealing a suit of clothes, and the prisoner replied, "I took the clothes and gave them to a boy! did not know to pawn, and he gave me the ticket and the money."—Mr. Reeney, pawnbroket, was then called into the box, and in answer to Mr. Lewin, s-dd the boy who pawned the articles seemed to be about 12 years of age.—Mr. Gossage: You should have made some inquiry before you took clothes in pawn from a lad.—Mr. Lenin: Did you know the boy at all? No, sir.—Mr. Gos- sage: It is a very careless way of conducting your business, I think. Stand down.—The prisoner pleaded guilty.—At an invitation of the Bench, the Rev. J. Wright Williams, , vicar of Widnes, made a statement to the effect that every effort had been made be reform the prisoner by Mrs. Mather, but without success. A few months ago his father died suddenly in America, and since then be bad been much worse. He (Mr. Williams) knew the boy had stopped ont night after night, and at the mother's request he had talked to him again and again. It was only in the boy's interest that the case was brought before their worships, in order that be might be held by a stronger force than his mother found herself able to exercise.—Mr. Gossage said the boy had behaved in a disgraceful way to his mother and all belonging to him, and he would be sent to gaol 14 days, afterwards to be committed to a reformatory school for five years. He would then be 18 years of age, and be would have a chance of behaving himself properly

RECITAL AT THE EARLESTOWN CO-OPERATIVE HALL.— Last (Thursday) evening Mr. Robert Hall, of Manchester, a noted elocutionist, gave a second recital in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown, under the auspices of the Earlestown and District Liberal Club. Mr. Hall has attained considerable success as an elocutionist and reciter,and it is to be regretted that so few persons were present last evening to bear so ac- complished an artiste. His selections were given with marked emphasis and effect, but one or two seemed unsuited to the tastre of his hearers. CLERKS DINNER AT NEWTON.—Tbe clerks employe& by the London and North-Western Railway Company at the Viaduct Works Eatlestown, sat down to their first annual dinner at the Leg!) Arms Hotel, Newton, on Friday eywinng last. The repast was .a most excellent one, snd reflected the highest credit upon the host (Mr. Mralmsley). At the sal- secimmt proceedings the toasts Prosperity to th Londou and North-Western Railway Company," and " Health of "e the officers and clerks" were duly honoured, and several • songs, readings, ac., were capitally' rendered.

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday under the presidency of Mr. Jno. Ashton. There were present :—Revs. J. Lockwood and J. IV. N. Tanner Messrs. Pickering, Weir, E. A. Wallington, Hamilton J. Darbysbire, C. Rigby, Stokes, T. Norman, W. _Handley, Campkin, Acton, H. Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk.) SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE'S MATTERS. The Rev. J. Lomtwoon said the chairman (the Rev. !Canon Barclay) had written to him that the doctor had for. bidden him to go to the Workhouse, and he would thank him to take up the resolutions which stood in his name. He (Mr. Lockwood) did so with great pleasure, regretting the indisposition of their respected chairman, and hoping that he would soon be restored to his wonted health and strength, and be able to preside over the meetings of the Board. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Lockwood then moved that Mr. James Collier, assistant overseer for Weston, be appointed school attendance officer for Clifton and Weston, at a salary of £lO ' per annum, and that Mr. Albert Woodier, assistant overseer for Halton, be school attendance officer for Ilalton, Norton, and Stocaham, at a salary of £lO per annum. Mr. Lock- wood pointed out that under this arrangement the educa- tional interests of the district would be better attended to. —Mr. NORMAN seconded the motion. He was sure the two gentlemen would do their duty, and the expenditure of a few extra sovereigns was not lost if the children were made to attend school.—Mr. DARBYSILIRE pointed out that Mr. Wright had performed the work for £l2 10e. per annum, and as the two gentlemen had other duties which would compel them to go over the same ground, he did not see why the Board should exceed the sum previously proposed by Mr. Lockwood, namely, £7 10s. each.—The Rev. J. LOCK. WOOD said Mr. Woodier would not accept that sum, and drew attention to the fact that the districts bad been enlarged by the addition of several townships.—Mr. NORMAN : You must look at this point; that the work has not been done before. It will have to be done properly now.—The motion was carried without disseat.—lt was reported that the ex- penditure of the School Attendance Committee for the past quarter had been £l7 I.Bs. 101 The estimate for the current quarter was £29 7s. 6d. MAINTENANCE OF CHILDREN AT SCHOOL. Mr. HANDLE?, in ptesenting the report of the Finance Committee, s iid there was a special account of £l9 6s for the maintenance and clothing of the children that were sent to Pantasaph School. It was recommended to be paid on the consent of the Local Government Board being obtained. Two of the children at Pantasaph had a father living, who is able bodied, and he believed in full work. He thought it was rather too bad that the Union should bear the ex- pense of the maintenance of his wife and other children in the house and two at Pantasaph. The father, Patrick Baxter, ought to help to discharge some of the liabilities, and he moved that they proceed against him for the re- covery of the money.—Mr. E. A. Wataaworote seconded the Motion, which was carried. • REJECTED APPLICATION. The CLERK read a letter from Dr. F. S. Boreham, the medical officer for the Great Budworth district. He said he had been a medical officer for nine months, and now thoroughly understanding the amount of work required to be done, he found it impossible to continue in the post at the present salary of £6O per annum, the expense of keep- ing a horse, drugs, (tc ,being greater than The amount. He therefore applied for his salary to be in- creased to £l2O. (Laughter.) He was sure they would give this matter fair consideration, and they would mutually agree that it was a just application.—Mr. C. RIGBY: I propose that the letter lie on the table.—Mr. EIANDLEY moved that the Clerk reply that the application was inopportune, as the appointment was of such a relent date.—Mr. NORMAN seconded the motion, which was car- ried.—lt was stated that Dr. Boreham's predecessor only received £6O per annum.

APPOINTMENT OF A SCHOOLMASTER. The Board had personal interviews with three applicants fOr the p9St et Schoolmaster, named W. F. Birch, Thomas Stubbing, an W. Clark.—The Rev. J. LOCKWOOD moved, and the Key. J. W. N. TANNER seconded, the appointment of Stubbing at a salary of £35 per annum.—Mr. WEIR moved, and Mr. RIGBY seconded, an amendment that Birch be appointed.—The original proposition Was carried by Seven Totes to five. A GUARDIAN AND RI! ERRAND BOY. Mr. and Mrs. Humphreys, of Runcorn, brought before the Board a boy named Clacus, who 18 months since was sent to the farm of Mr. Charles Rigby, guardian for Acton Grange. On Sunday, the 13th inst., be ran away and made his way to the house of Mr. Humphrey, at Runcorn. He alleged that he had been improperly treated, and Mr. and Mrs. Humphreys having befriended the lad previously, took I him in, and now came before the guardians to say that they would maintain him if Mr. Rigby would fit him out with a snit of clothes —ln answer to Mr. W. H. Linake; and Mr. Rigby, the boy, who is 16 Tears of age, admitted that he had no complaint on the score of food, and that he WAS well housed. He alleged that be had never had any money given to him.—Mr. Rigby explained that the lad had an idle, dissolute father, who had frequently been to the farm to endeavour to obtain money, and that the boy had also asked for mmey to give his father. Mr. Rigby had there fore thought it best to save the money for the lad, and he had done this.—lt transpired that on the Sunday when the boy ran away Mrs. Rigby had spoken sharply to him for letting the brush fall when cleaning the shoes, and told him to go away and never return.—Mr. RIGBY said the cheek and impudence of the lad was something awful. He had make his milk cart into a veritible parcels post, by which he had gathered three or four shillings a week, and many odd pennies. He took good etre that the boy spent the money in shoes and such like things for himself. Although the boy had not been of much use to him until six months ago, he was willing to allow him to go, and would buy him a suit of clothes.— Mr. NORMAN observed that it was a great hardship upon a farmer or any other person who had for 18 months main- tained a boy, who when he beca:ne useful to his master, should run away, and he thought there shoula be some pro- vision by which this could be prevented.—Mr. JONES (the master) said he had previously suggested that boys should be apprehended.—The subject then dropped, and the ordinary relief business was proceeded with.
THE CAREER OF A YOUNG RUNCORN THIEF.

Thomas John Oliver, 10 years of age, was brought before Captain Realehorst and Mr. James Handley, at Runcorn Police Court, on Saturday. charged with stealing half-a- crown from the person of Jane Eccleston. Eccleston is a domestic servant at Messrs. Howard and Pearson's, Church. street, and on Friday evening she was given half-a-crown with which to make some purchases at Johnson's shop. She wrapped the coin in a piece of paper and placed it in her pocket. On her way she stopped at a shop window, and whilst standing there she felt someone tug at her pocket, and turning round she saw the prisoner standing there. She found that her money had been taken, and she said to the prisoner " Have you been in my pocket ?" He replied that he had not, and she had come to the conclusion that he was speaking the truth when a waterman named John Picker- ing-, who lives in Bridgewater-street, seized the young 'robin, who thereupon dropped the money. He was subse- quently apprehended by P.C. Morris—Mr. Superintendent Williamson said he was always sorry to bring children be- fore the Bench as felons. He was sorry to say that was not the first time the prisoner had been before the court. Only on the 6th November last he was tried, with another boy, for stealing a florin from a stall on the fair ground. The other boy was sent to a reformatory, but Oliver was ordered to be whipped. Subsequent to that time the boy was again brought under his notice. He attended Trinity School, where he was noted as a bright boy who always did his lessons well and attended school regularly. The school- master noticed that the boy was spending money very freely and brought him to him (the speaker) who found that he had lOs in his possession. The boy stated that he had found a half-sovereign in the street, and being unable to discover anything the police handed the money to his parents. It afterwards transpired that a half-sovereign had been stolen from a shop in Percival-lane. The police had received numerous reports of women's pockets having been picked, and curiously enough the prisoner had always been seen in the locality. 'The boy's father was an industrious respectable man, and up to a short time ago he thought the same of his wife; but he could not imagine that a little boy would rob pockets, sometimes to the extent of £3, without there being a receiver in the affair. Sometimes people had gone to the prisoner's home and been blackguarded for their pains. The prisoner was a very sharp fellow, and a very sharp thief too.—The Bench sentenced the prironer to 21 days' imprisonment, afterwards to be sent to a reformatory school for five years.

JUVENILE THJEVES AT WIDNES. At the Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, before Messrs. G. Pilkington, and Holbrook Gaskell, jour., James Millard Smith, aged nine, and. Peter Connolley, aged seven, were brought up charged with stealing five india-rubber rings, of the value of 10s, the property of the London and North-Western Railway Company.—Benjamin Tushington, foreman shunter of the railway, said about noon on the 21st met, be saw the prisoners on a siding. He saw them come from beneath a wagon, each carrying rings in their bands. They placed the rings beneath a wagon and covered them with a piece of slate and paper. The rings were used in wagons at the place where the draw-bar went through the plate, and if the "cotter" was not put in properly, the wagons, when running, were very dangerous indeed. Thefts of this description had taken place for the past two years.— Mr. Joy:3,3°n, the school attendance cancer, said the boys at- tended school irregularly. The Bench sentenced Smith to receive six strokes, and Connolley three strokes with the birch rod. Corbett Ciaroner. 11 years of age, was charged with stealing 30 lbs. of coal, the property of the London and Company.—r.c. Murray deposed Not th-Western Railway that on the 17th inst. the prisoner was near the steam crane on the canal aide, where he was picking up coal and placing it in a basket. The buy stated that his mother bad sent him for -some coal. The coal the boy had collected weighed 30 lbs.—The mother admitted that she had sent the boy for cinders.—The Bench considered the mother more to blame than the boy. They would deal leniently with him because they thought he was more sinned against than sinning.— The boy was sentenced to receive four strokes with thebi rod.

A WINDFALL FoR Tax POP,—We are informed on good authority that the Honourable Mrs. Stapleton-Bretherton, of who recently died, bequeathed to his Holiness the Pope the munificent sum of £4OOOOO. and that Mr. Erring- ton, M.P, has been entrusted with the pleasing task of con- veying the good tidings to his Holiness.
_A CANAL BOAT i MEAN.

BRUTAL ASSAULT ON A WOMAN AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Police Court, on Saturday, before Captain Hs zlehurst and Mr. James Handley, Robert Jones, captain of the flat "Cricket," belonging to Mr. C. T. Faulkner, of Manchester, was charged with assaulting a young woman I named Annie Cody.—The complainant said she was a single woman, and her borne was at Broadheath. near Altrincham. For the last three weeks she had been living with the pri- eoner on board his flat. Oa Seul3.7 niges the 13th inst. they went down to Liverpool with the flat and on the way be abused her in a shameful manner. He pulled Lei about by the hair and tried to kick her. He then fastened her in the cabin, and on coming back to Runcorn he again savagely assaulted her, and teking out a knife he threatened to des- troy her. She got the kuJe from him and thrust it in her bosom. The black mark on her arm was caused by the pri- soner's violence. When the flat arrived at Runcorn she went ashore being afiaid to stay longer with the prisoner. When he was beating her she asked him to spire her life, and he retorted that he would make her a " coffin suit." She was carried into a hut in an insensible state frhen at Runcorn by some lock porters. Examined by Mr. Suberina tendent Williamson : When she ran from the fiat the pri- soner followed her and said he would drown her. He kicked her several times with his clogs and said he would finish her. Complainant further stated that when her mother knew she had been liv.ing with the prisoner she refused to allow her to remain at home.—Cross-ex ,mined by prisoner. She did not come on board the flat at Manchester and ask to be allowed to ride to .A ltrincharn. When ehey left Altrincleam she did say she would go to Runcorn. She did so because her mother had tcld her she would not have her at home. She did not sly at Liverpool that she would drown herself when she got off at Runcorn. She dLi not about that she was mad —Mr. Superintendent Williamson observed that the complainant had been so injured about the he td tE:It she was not exactly elesr about the dares of the assaults; but she had been the victim of the prisoner's vioienee on three separate days.—Prisoner (to complainant) : Haven't you been following the flat up and down P—Complainant : No, I have not, and I will stick to Superintendent Williamson: You have been sufficiently long with the prisoner to be dishcnoured and beaten in the bargain.—Com- plainant (crying): Yes.—Peter Lowe, a labourer, said he lived in Mersey-street. On the 13th inst. he helped the prisoner with his boat down the locks. He saw the prisoner go to the cabin, and shortly afterwards heard screams. The mate told him to stop where he was, as the affair had nothing to do with him. When the prisoner had finished his tea he wanted to go on deck, and as he came up the cabin steps the complainant kept pulling him back, and the prisoner fell on complainant's breast witkhis knees several times. The prisoner asked complainant several times if she would go ashore, and then dropped with his knees on her breast. The woman aggravated him to it.—Mr. Super- intendent Williamson: Did be drop with his knees on her purposely P-Witness : I could not say. Every time she pulled him down he dropped with his knees upon her breast. —Mr. Johnson: Did you see her struck at all ?—Witness: I saw the prisoner pull her out of the bedplace, and knock her on the floor.—Mr. Stiperin- tenderet Williamson: When all this was going on, did the woman say anything? Witness: Only scteamed.—Mr. Superintendent Williamson: What age are you now? Wit- ness: 19.—Mr. Superintendent Williarascn : And could you stand there and see the woman abused without taking her part? Witness: There were two of them, and I was afraid of interfering myself.—Robert Brown, a lock keeper near the Tidal Dock, said the prisoner's was the first flat that came through the locks on the morning of the 1511 inst. When the flat entered the lock he heard some one moaning. He said to the mate of the flat that there must be some one in the water, but he made no reply, and witness went to where he thought the sound came from. He saw the com- plainant standing on the deck moaning. He told her that if she was afraid of the prisoner she had better come into his hat, and he would see that she was protected. She said she wanted her clothes, and left him. The flat went on through two locks, and as near as he could guess had entered the fourth, when the compleinaat came running hack, screaming loudly. He crossed the lock to meet her. Before be could get to bim she fell to the ground. If she had not fallen she would certainly have run into the lock. He asked two men who were there to take care of her, while he weet for a watchman. When he returned they curled the woman into his hut, and as she was hungry he gave her his supper —Mr. Superintendent Williamson: Did she appear to. have been abused ?—Witness: She was deathly.— Inspector Ilollingworth said on Tuesday morning he was told that a woman was lying seriously ill at a hut at Bottom Locks, and on going to that place found the com- plainant in a very weak state and moaning very mach. She was seen by Dr. McDougall, who said the woman had been very badly abused. By the doctor's advice the woman was removed to a lodging-house in Mersey-street.—Mr. Superin- tendent Williamion said he had not called the doctor on ac- count of the expense.—The Chairman thought medical evi- dence unnecessary—The prisoner in defence denied that he struck the complainant. He alleged that she persisted in cemieg to the boat and annoying him.—Mr. Superinteadent Williamson said the prisoner ought to know well enough what to do if he bad been persistently annoyed, and under no circumstances ought he to have assaulted the woman. He could have obtained the assistance of the police, and he was sure he had made no application or he would have heard of it. He had tried to stain the woman's character, and had made some allusion to drink, but he wished to point out that the women was perfectly sober when she came to the police station, and he had learned that she had never taeted ' drink in her life. After what he heard of the prisonet be had scarcely patience to address their worships, and be could not help losing his temper. The prisoner was said to be one of the most brutal men on the Bridgewater Canal aed was a terror not only to women hut to men as well.—The Chairman said the Bench considered the case proved. The prisoner's conduct had been brutal in the extreme and no would be sent to prison for three months with hard labottee At the expiration of which term he must find sureties to keep the peace for six months, failing which he would be imprisoned for another month.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

THE CABINET COUNCILS-THE CRIMINAL PRO- CEDURE BILL-THE BISHOP OF CHESTER- THE NEW ROAD UP CONS TITUTION HILL- MRS. LANGTREY-GERM AN OPERA-PAULINE LUCCA-A NEW THEATRE-Mr. EGAR BRUCE- OUR BARNUM ELEPHANT-OUR OSCAR WILD.
LONDON, nicriesDAT.

It is satisfactory to know that the Government are deter- mined to meet Parliament with a strong suit of tramps in their hand. No one can tell what opposition or obstruction may effect. But, if Government have their way, the next session will not be a single-measure session. The Franchise Jilin, of course, is well in the van of party prospects, but the Gobernment of London will not be allowed to slip into the possibilities of some future Parliament. Sir Henry James will be prepared with his Criminal Procedure Bill. I under- stand that all the correspondence started by Lord Bramwell in the Times, signing his letter "B," on the subject of the defence of prisoners by counsel, and their use of unsupported statements of the prisoners, will not have passed without effect. These difficulties which have led to so much subtle argument will not occur again. A more important question will be the Continuance of the winter assizes. At the present moment most of the Judges are away. There are only two courts trying little trumpery claims before Common Juries. The Special Juries cannot be taken till the 15th of February. This is what London loses. Now, what do the provinces I gain? Litigation has not had time to ripen in the country, as it used to do when the assizes were held in the spring. The jails are certainly more speedily delivered. But much is lost to gain this, and what is gained might be achieved much more simply. I hear it is proposed to increase the jurisdiction of the Courts of Quarter Sessions, and of the Recorders, and thus take some extra work off the already over-burdened skoulders of the Judges.

Who is to be the new Bishop of Chester? The Primate is bothered with his Church patronage. All sorts of in flaences are brought to bear upon him, and in Church matters he must be general. Latterly the high church and the broad churchmen have had their tarn. It is said that the former have had more than their turn. This is a rea- son why we should look for some preferment going in the direction of the Evangelican party. Certainly Canon Fleming is at present the favourite. Between the vicar of St. Michael's, Chester-square, and the late vicar of St. Peter's, Eaton-square, there used always to be one friendly bit of rivalry kept active year after year by the same event. Which of them would have the largest collection in a Lon- don Church on Hospital Sunday. The present Bishop of Truro generally beat the Canon of York by a heavy score. Even when Dr. Wilkinson changed surplice for lawn sleeves 9,!, rivalry continued between these two, the most fashion- able churches in West 'End isondop, This time Canon Fleming's congregation won the blue ribbon of charity by a considerable figure. Next to Canon Carpenter and to Canon I Farrar be is the most popular preacher in London. It was pleasant to see the Prince and Princess drive up , the new road over Constitution Hill this week. At last ' the great improvement has been made, and, perhaps. we will soon see the lesser improvements carried out also. The Duke's statue must be made to move on. We are getting so accustomed to its imbecility that we forget how other people laugh, and the untidy delta'opposite the hospital is to be sodded over, and the whole place put into some kind of order. The plans are all made. The drawings are on paper. We are only waiting till the season shall begin, and then, true to old traditions, Piccadilly will be torn up and dismantled. At least one thing is happily settled. Mr. Ayrton is not going to succeed Mr. Lefavre. That would indeed be a calamity. The rumour that has gone about is not int",

Mrs. Langtrey has ban so long away that we will be glad to see her back. but I hear she intends to reserve her- self for the provinces. he is now in New York, and ker tour here will conatnZnce just as the London season con- cludes. She left England with only three or fourcharacters in her repertoire. She returns with more than a dozen. She has wisely avoided Shakespeare, as making rather too heavy demands on her powers. I bear from America that she has greatly improved in her acting. American critics gush a great deal, but there are some good judges who have the courage of their convictions. When Mrs. Langtrey was told that her performance in Rosalind proved her to be a very pretty woman and no actress, the lesson started her on the road to improvement. It would be well if English critics were as judiciously unsparing. At last it has been settled we are to have our German opera this season, and I am glad to say not too much of it. Twelve representations will suffice. Wagner is, of course, the staple, but Fidelio will be given, and two of %Veber's operas as well. The management have secured Alban', who is splendid in Lohengrin and Tannhatiser, and we shall also see our old favorite Pauline Lucca. Years ago, when Wag- ner worship was not yet quite catholic, LUCCA was singing at Berlin. She took the old•fashioned roles Faust. Don Gio- vanni, Diuorah, &c. She would not sing Wagner. The Press urged her on, but she was inexorable. Then someone —perhaps Wagner himself, perhaps the manager of the theatre. She would not, because she could not. Lucca was furious. She ordered Tannhaiiser to be put in the bills, and three nights afterwards she came out in the opera. Never had there been such a success. The house was choke full, and everyone was enthusiastic. Next day Lucca sent word to her critic—l think it was the composer himself—that she hated his music, and would never sing in it again. But in the lapse of years she has thought better of it, and we I shall certainly hear her this summer.

-- - Since my last letter a new theatre has been added to the long list of new theatres. In au age of scepticism there seems certainly no want of faith in the class who risk money to amuse the public. The fact is there are two things, merit and fashion. Pot a good play on, have it well mounted and well acted, and it will take. But these managers find it impossible to get a good play written, and when it is written they can't tell whether it is good or not till the public come to their aid, and the public verdict can't be pronouced till after the play has been seen aid all the expense of mounting, of dresses, of music, of scemery has been inearred. The public are quick enough with their verdict, and have latterly taken to damming plays with great sincerity and gusts. Indeed a failure seems to give greater pleasure to the gallery on a first n;ght than a success given to the stalls. If the manager can get merit, he may perhaps get fashion. and fashion is even a greater triumph than merit; because it dispenses with Merit. Take the Gaiety; anything at all will pay there. A couple of dozen fairies, with distinctly human outlines, pull the piece through, no matter what it is. Irving and Ellen Terry are fashionable. If they appeared in Saidford and Merton the public would still go for a time. Now nothing is so fashionable as novelty, and people will go to see a new theatre, because it is a new theatre ; and a clever manager, if he can once lead the stream into his box office, might to be able to keep it going. That is the secret of so many new London theatres. The Imperial is closed; the Globe is closed; Her Majesty's is nearly always closed; and yet another is built about as big as the first two put to- gether.

Mr. Bruce's career has been singular. If Ido not mis- take, he began management with the smallest theatre in London. He brought out "Crutch and Toothpick" at the Royalty. It was an unexpected success. Then be took the next smallest theatre in London—the Prince of Wales—and brought out "The Colonel." it was an unexpected success. Luck followed him; for the Board of Works insisted 03 that theatre being pulled down, so he was driven to build the Princes, and he has built it large and handsome, and in a good place. Quite a bunch of theatres are now grouped round, Leicester-square. There's the Comedy, the Criterion, the Pandora, the Alhambra. Mr. Bruce's is the stateliest of them all. The Prince of Wales was there to open it. There was nothing but titles and celebrities in the stalls and private boxes. The play was "The Palace of Truth," Gilbert's fairy piece, that his name in the old days of the Haymarket when Willie Kendal was slight and Madge Robertson was slippy, and poor old Buckstone had not yet gone over to the majority. There is great difference of opinion as to how the play went. To me it seemed thin and poor. The I subject was too slight. And then the east was not -very

AT RUNCORN. The first meeting of the 22nd year of the existence of this class took place on Wednesday night, at Brunswick School, when the Rev. George Rack delivered a lecture on "The Bible, the Word of God." lie commenced by asking the question—Was the Bible true? Some people had said that it was only a human composition, having no higher authsrity than the poetry of a Scott or the philosophy of a Carlyle. While admitting the morality at its precepts, the profoundness of its truths, the beauty of its poetry, and the grandeur of its eloquence, such people denied its super- natural character. If such a view were true, then the teach ing of the Bible became mere speculation. The talent „ self-sacrificing labours, and honesty of the writ, a; of the books of the Bible stamped it as Divine. Sir Willi am Jones said "The Bible contained more true sublimity, r Lion! important history, and finer strains of eloquence and p, than collected from all other books in any age or lang, a„„ei. Milton said: "There are no soags comparable to the , 8-OZ,e of Zion, no orations equal to those of the prophets, and no politics like those the Scripture taught." Sir Isaac Newton said: "The Bible contained the most sublime phi Amoy?: St. Paul was a striking example of the self-sacri' Acing zeal of the writers of the sacred Book. The hor ..esty of the', writers was apparent in the biographies they or rote. Abra- ham's deceit, David's adultery, and Peter's d , anial were all remorselessly narrated. The lectuier next proceeded to dwell on the internal evidences of Divine authority the Bible contained, such as the agreement of the varic,r writers the adaptation of Scripture to the race and the inexhaustible character of , ts tre Prophecy was then dwelt upon as ag. conclusive deuce of Divine revelation. The lectr rer than dwelt upon the influence the Bible bad exercised in the past and pre- sent times on the hearts of men and nations. For such wonderful effects there must be aCF AISC. The authors were reckoned great whose writings swa- red the nation; but they passed away to be followed by others, whose works in tarn found their last restingplace in t' .3e world's waste paper ban- ket. But the Bible lived, becan .se of its Divine origin. It had lived through the oppositi on of the priests of Paganism, Juda;sm and philosophy. It had lived, though corrupt and degenerate Rome had emplo, her imperial power to crush it, and though Infidelity hr employed all its ingenuity to overthrow it, and to ins., igurate an " Age of Reason," as opposed to an "Era of daith."—A vote of thanks to the lecturer was then unan amously passed.

PRICES OF JAM. 61r,-11?.ferring to Mr. Hartley's letter on the jam ques- tion, we should like the public to know that he has stretched a great deal in saying raspberry jam can be bought at any retail shop dat, 61, black current at 5-kd, and plum at 4d par lb. Although large buyers of jam, we cannot purchase it at the price mentioned. We wish Mr. Hartley would sell us twc, or three gross It) plums at 4s, we should then be pleased to let the public have the benefit. Hoping Mr. Hartley will see his way clear to rectify his mistake, as it causes the public to think that retailers get a large profit on this commodity, we are yours, &c., LAWLESS BROTHERS. Warrington, January 22,1884.

RUNCORN POLITICAL LIFE. Sir,—l am pleased to see that at last the Runcorn Liberal Association have commenced real work. Ido not flatter myself that it is in consequence of my. letter. to VOU mane- many months ago that an attempt has been made in the direction of educating the electors and non-electors of Runcorn on the great questions of high political importance. Be that as it may a start, and a very good one, has been made. The lecturer on Tuesday night, on the subject of the franchise' was very opportune. Dr. Langford must have felt enconrged as he proceeded with Isle lecture when be saw how quickly his points were picked up and applauded. lie could not have had a better proof 'of his remark, that the voteless dwellers in county constituencies were Neal in intelligence to their more fortunate brothers, whom accident has placed in a position to vote in a parliamentary election. The hall was nearly full of grown men, everyone of whoee faces showed an eager appreciation of the subjects that were being dilated upon by the lecturer, yet not more than 40 of them were voters With the exception of half-a-dozen well-known men of business, it would have been impossible for a person not familiar with the register to have singled out the voters from the non-voters present. But the time has gone by for arguing on the subject of the franchise, the right which has been so unjustly witheld for so long is about to be taken by the people for the people ; for we cannot speak of the Legislature giving anything that belonged by right to the peeple. I earnestly hope that the series of meetings so successfully begun on :Tuesday night will be success- fully carried out. And this can only be brought about by each Liberal doing his utmost for the association, whether in supporting the funds—always an important matter in strengthening the hands of the indefatigable secretary, or in making known to all with whom be came in contact the 11.)rk and aims of the Runcorn Liberal Association. The Tories are on the alert, and though they cannot speak, they can bribe, and cozen, and cajole, aad intimidate; and these are difflicult influences for honest men to tackle and over- come.—Yours, Jrc., JUNIOR LIBERAL. Runcorn, January 22nd, 1884.

FARNWORTH GRAMMAR SCHOOL AND THE LATE HEAD MASTER. Sir,—lf • you wilt kindly permit me to occupy a small portion of your space this week I shill feel obliged. In your account of the opening of the new Grammar :School at Farnworth, you state that the late Head Master built a suit- able residence and premises for the school, but that an un- fair price had been asked for them. I now wish, with your kind permission, to give you a clear account of the negotia- tions for the purchase of these buildings, and also of the facts which have reference to my (so-c died) resignation. There are two periods of time which it will be necessary to keep in view, (a) from July, 1876, to July, 1878; (8) from October, 1880, to November, 1881: and for the sake of clearness I will deal with the latter first. At the end of October, 1880, the trustees made enquiries about the price of the building, together with 5,600 squire yards of free- hold land. The sum of £3,500 was demanded, which I may say was fully £7OO under the cost price. Unfortun- ately, at this juncture. I was suddenly taken with a second and very severe attack of the disease which had already prostrated me for two years, and was for a time physically and mentally incapable of attending to business of any k-ind. When at the end of a few weeks , I rallied somewhat, I learned that the trustees I had offered £3,000 for the premises and land. The small- ness of the offer caused me much anxiety, and I confess it did nat seem to me right under all the circumstances of the ease, that I should be called upon to submit to so serious i al toss, for it must be remembered that the trustees had had I the use of the buildings during five years qaite free of cost. They had not contributed a penny towards their erection, and had ref tiled to build themselves. Tnev had moreover put a clause in my agreement compelling me to raise a re- spectable boarding school in connection with the Grammar School, and, indeed, it was this clause which determined me as to the form the building should assume—a form which, while admirably adapted to its purpose, renders it unfit for anything other than a school, hotel,lodging-hense, or public institution of some kind. Taking these things into con- sideration, and the fact that the money hal been expended, not as a speculation to secure profit, but for the purpose of developing the school and placing it in a position to perform its part in promoting the higher education of the neigh- bourhood, I thought it hard to be compelled to submit to a direct loss of £1,200, and wrote to the late Vicar of Fern- worth to see if more just terms ceuld not be arranged, but the reply was that the trustees were not in a position to give more. It was necessary for me at this time to remove from Tunbridge to the neighbourhood of London, to be near tae phyeicien who had my case in hand, and feeling much e- , pressed a: his report and at the prospect of never being able, although relatively a young Man, to earn another penny for my wife and children, I thought it better to accept the £3,000, and wrote to Major Cross to that effect. To my astonishment the answer to this was that the trustees would then give only £2,800, and in two or three days another letter came from Major Cross stating that the trustees had further resolved to reduce their offer to £2,500, arid that they must have an im- mediate decision. I scarcely remember now what I did, I was a helpless log in bed, very weak, and often in a state of scull-consciousness; I feared that the intention was to ruin me, and think! wrote to my solicitor leaving the matter in his hands. From that time, January, 1881, I have heard nothing further from the trustees. The offer of 4500 was, I believe, indirectly renewed in November, 1881; but as this was not very much more than the value of the land and the bricks, the offer could net be accepted. The statement, thee, that an unfair price had been demanded amounts to this; that the trustees were told they could have the pre. ; mines at their own price within two months from the time their offer was made; and that their own departure from the. terms of that offer Was the cause of the failure of the neg,o. tiations. I find my strength is failing me, and so with your permission 1 will defer until next week etitering upon explanations of my resignation and of the negotiations which were somewhat informally carried on from 1876 until 1878. There was then a school of 90 boys, nearly 40 of them boarders, and! tried to induce the trustees on ac- count of my failing health to become owners of the pro- perty. and permit one to retire. After 16 years' hard work, almost ivithout holidays,! felt a firm conviction that com- plete rest and change could alone restore the health I was . gradually bat surely losing. I think I may say that, during my mastership, I bad done what I could (as much, perhaps, as any one Titan not wealthy could do) to advance higher education in Widnes. I had spent all my money when no one else would Tove a penny. I had given all my strength working early and late ; and now my reward is that the £5,000 I had in- vested—the trustees had no school fittings nor utensils of my ki, od—is virtually confiscated, and! am left ill, helpless, er.id almost penniless, with a wife amt four delicate children. I am, sir, your faithful servant. - JAMES Ra.yEN Late Head Master of the Grammar School, Fern' worth. 31, Park-road, New Wandsworth, S.W., 22nd January, 1884.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL
BILL.

The Manchester Ship Canal Bill came before the Ex- aminer on Standing Orders of the House of Commons on Thursday. The opposition was confined to the Mersey Docks Board, the Corporation of Liverpool, and the London and North-Western Railway Company. The chief obj-ction to the scheme urged by the Docks and Harbour Board had referenoe to what is known as 'the Works Clause" of the bill, which would give the company proposed to be incor- porated power to make and maintain certain estuary works. viz, the forming of a low-water channel, to commence in the bed of the estuary of the Mersey near Eastham and ter- minating at Runcorn. The ground of objection is that the plans do not specify the line of the work, inasmuch as the limits of the low-water channel are not in accordance with the standing orders indicated is the plans deposited, and do not show what the width of the low-water channel will be. It was also contended that the bill does not comply with the standing orders' in that the works proposed to be made come within the second class of private bills. There was, of course' a long legal argument, and,Mr. Lys- ter, engineer to the IVlersey Dock Board, and Mr. Leader Williams, engineer of the Ship Canal scheme, were exam- ined, but their evidence was of a purely technical character, and of almost exclusive interest to experts. The Examiner decided thy the question of limits of deviation was one entirely for the Committee on the Bill, and had nothing to do with what was proposed now. He thought the width of the channel was distinctly shown on the plan, and said he could hardly say more than that it ITO shown as clearly as it possibly could be shown. Tee promoters proposed to make a certain channel, on which their estimates and every- thing else were based, and whether they should be allowed to depart from the proposed lines of the channel was a questioned to be considered afterwards. The Bill was there- fore declared to have complied with the Standing Orders.

MR. E. WHITLEY, M.P., AT DITTON. Last evening week, the annual distribution of prizes to the scholars in attendance at Ditton National Sunday School took place. The event was preceded by a tea meet- ing, et which a considerable number of scholars were present. The public meeting was presided over by the Rev. J. Cas!ells Brown, the pastor, and he was supported by Mr. Whitley, M.P., and the Rev. George Bond, MA., (vicar of Farnvvorth); Messrs. Joseph Longton, W. Fergu• son, T. Booth, and Kilshaw. A short programme of musi- cal selections was gone through by the children in a deas- ing style, and Mr. Davies, of ', Hues, caused much amuse- ment by bis comic songs. The Rev. J. Cassell s Brown ac- companied on the piano.—Mr. WHITLEY in a speech of considerable length, dwelt upon the importance of religions 1 education. For many years he had taken a deep interest in Sunday School work. He had done so because he be- lieved .that upon the instruction which they I received in Sunday school, depended in a great 1 measure the course of life which many )of them led in their after careers. (Hear, hear.) And as time passed on he must cenfess that the feelings of his early days had been deepened with regard to Sunday school work. Education of every kind was good. He did not , undervalue secular education. He believed it was a neces- sity of the days in which we lived. At the present time there was a great cry for education in every parish, town, and city, and, aye, in almost every family. Children were being educated now in a way that it was almoet impossible 30 or 40 years ago. He was sure of this, that unless a girl or boy received a good education it was almost impossible in these days of competition and active enterprise to get along in life simcessfully. But beyond and above the study of secular subject?, there wastan education against which no other educational instruction would avail. Secular educition might fit them to be sharp and intelligent, and to get on in life to a certain extent; but, after all, unless they i had received instruction n God's Holy Word he felt persuaded that neither his young friends behind him, nor anyone else in that room however young or old could get ou in life weheut the teaching and the guidance and the direction of God's Holy Word. (Ap- plause.) For the welfare of his young friends in that room it was absolutely necessary that they should be taught in that Sunday school Sunday after Sunday. He also im- pressed upon the parents the Incalculable results which of assembling their families iwnotuhldeirfoltloomwesfroonmeetheae cPti.:aScatbic Sabbath to join in devotional ex- ercises, for the eetly impreseions of good which the children received would remain with them through life. The longer he lived,and the more he was persuaded of this fact that upon their fealty to God and their observance of God's Holy Day depended the future prosperity of the country. 1 (Applause.) He had often thought that E. i Englishmen were ' blind to the privileges they had long enjoyed n God's Holy Day, but it was a striking fact that while every other country that he knew had been invaded by foreign foes or had been the scene of an intestine war, England had been preserved for long centuries from the foreign invader, and while there were many differences and some discord amongst the people, yet England had been at peace within herself. The maintenance of peace in any country depended upon the religions tone of the people. They found among the anarchists of France men with distrust and hatred; they found them amongst men with no religion ; and depend upon it the great enemy of this country was the man wlio had no settled religious belief; a man who had no belief in God's providential care. (Hear, hear.) A country grow- ing up without religion was on the way to national ruin. (Hear, hear.) He was rejoiced to know that a large propor- tion of the children of the parish of Ditton were in atten- dance at Sunday school, where they would learn lessons which, when old men and women, they would never forget. The bon. gentleman then urged those present to gather rosnd the Vicar and aid him in the good work he undertook for the good of the parish. (Applause.) On the motion of Mr. KiLsnew, seconded by Mr. W. Gunk, a vote of thaaks was heartily accorded to Mr. Whitiey for his address.

div.p: THE 14',XAMINElz, SATURDAY, JANUARY 26, 1884.
CHAPTER Hu FAMILY COUNCIL.

Maher of the man spoke, or could speak, but waited, in somewhat grim humour, the approach of the Countess, which promised for them a new period of exceeding un- pleasantness. As she ntered, Miss Vandeleur, addressing her said,*as if determined to leave them no loophole for escape, perhaps again to carry out their fell purpose, "Your sons wera proposing a trip to France, and had not the gallantry to allow a lady to go with them, even though she condescended to ask."

The Countess gased excitedly on the three faces in rapid succession, and saw there the confirmation of the frightful truth, she hardly ventured to suspect befure. "And you?" she said inquiringly to Miss Vandeleur, hardly knowing what to say, or if it was safe to say any- thing. Stephen saved Miss Vandeleur from answering, by himself saving with a smile, "Miss Vandelear, mother, effectively convinced as we had better stay at home." The smile, and the seemingly light-hearted indifference with which Stephen treated the whole matter (but only in the hope to conceal its true character from his mether) impelled her to cast aside all pretences, and to exclaim : " Ah, heaven! I understand. But for this brave girh you would now have been moving swiftly to the work of I mutual slaughter! Deny it if you can !" There was no such denial forthcoming; and after a pause the Countess again spoke with an extraordinary change of nsanner ' " But it is no time to dwell on the offences of others when the acknowledgment of our own is justly due. In my over- weening desire to keep secret a matter seriously affecting the honour of the fatnily. I failed to see how you its chief members might all be compromised. Before God and man I beg pardon of all!' " Mother !" said Stephen, " my very dear mother, is this necessary ?" "I ask the same question," said the Earl," and with the deepest concern." " Judge from the story I have yet to tell." Turning to Lord Harlaxtoh who still held the packet of papers in his hands she said : "Do you know that it is your mothers's testimony you bold there among the rest, and which includes mine ?" " My mother's !" echoed Lord Harlaxton in the greatest astonishment. "Are you then not my mother ?" "You have often in childhood heard me speak of a dear sister, of her extraordinary beauty, and premature death soon after her marriage. Twelve months before that event I was called to her in the dead of night. I found her in a state more awful thanl can even now venture to recall, much less to describe. Bit by bit I got from her the sad details. She had been reduced under a solemn promise of marriage, knowing the truth of her lover's statement that he would be disinherited if he married her before the death' of the rich invalid to whom he Was heir.

"In one and the sarne day she discovered the death of the invalid some weeks before ; the marriage of her lover to another woman ; and that she herself was destinetl to bring into the world an evidence of what she felt to be her shame.

"It was then she sent for me. I arrived just in time to prevent her suicide or insanity, by pledging myself—a childless woman—to receive the babe at birth as my own, my husband's prolonged absence abroad giving the oppor- tunity. "And so it was. And the kindly doctor. who was in the secret, who had known and secretly loved her lonebefore, and been rejeeted by her, eventually again wooed and won her, but only to Brid her die, broken hearted, in his arms, within three months of their bridal." In a voice half-stifled with emotion, Lord Harlaxton said "And the name of the man?" _
"The hour for vengeance has passed away. Re is dead. The good doctor has also followed. All the rest you know,
