CHAPTER LXXL-THE ARREST.

As the bailiff watched the approaching victim, who cams along a path, the full breadth of which was partly hidden from his sight, he communed with himself enjoyably: Hengaging liinnocent ! He's a coming as hunsuspici- oils as a new-born baby into the werry jaws of the lion, where he'll be made a lion of himself as we law jokers say. What! The devil There's two,on em! Ow am Ito dis- cover which is which ?" He moved towards the arch to follow Gentleman Jack, and cried,
"I say !" as loudly as he dared, but saw it was no good. "Hots; of sight! Hof course!" and then, in bitterness of spirit, he hid in the Alcove to watch, and consider how to act.

Presently Stephen and, a friend, a Diplomatic official, cams to the broad walk, and there stopped, the latter at the time saying— "Oh, lam only here for my brother's wedding. I am to be his best man.'7. . _ .
"And in what direction of activity do you think to move?" • .

"If the offer you once so kindly made me, and which I was not then able to accept, of an introduction to diplomatic Lie, is still available, I should gladly embrace it," responded Stephen. " Hum ! Ha! lam most willing. But things are a good deal changed since then. However I will see what can be done, and let you know." Such was the cautious reply of Stephen's diplomatic friend, and in return Stephen drily expressed his thanks, "I suppose you know," added the official with a laugh, " the old de- finition of an ambassador—one sent abroad' to lie for his country ?" "Yes," responded Stephen ; "and of all the sayings that degrade official life, this is, I think, the most corrupting and mischievous!" . .

• " Really ! Why 2" was the amused rejoinder. " Because it so perfectly hits off, and excuses the beset- ting sin of the vocation—to daily with the convenient false- hood, while appearing only to disseminate enjoyable truth." ' Aad Stephen looked as if he were indulging himself with some of the enjoyable truth of which he spoke, at his friend's expense, who quickly said, as he looked at his watch, "I am delighted with your explanation, and will take care you shall have an opportunity to carry your views into action, the very first time an embassy goes out—on your principles !" "Which ?" said Stephen to himself, as he looked after the departing officifi ; "he sees were meant as a satire upon his own !" And again he went on his search through the garden for Lord Harlaxton, taking a different route from the Diplomatic official. Seeing this, the bailiff rushed forth, exclaiming— " D—n it! I can't harrest 'em both till I know which is the right man! Ha! One of 'ern comes back," So he retreated under the arch, to prevent a passage that way to the village and the open country without his knowing. "It was Stephen who returned,weary and irritable at the growing belief that Lord Halaxton WAS determinedly keep- ing aloof. The bridegroom is nowhere here," he said to himself. "So I must seek him in the house, surrounded perhaps by the wedding guests, or luxuriously reclining at the feet of the bride." He was about to move through the arch as the shortest way to the front qf the house, when the bailiff met him and said, hurriedly, . "Beg pardon. sir, but that gentleman who left you a mi- nute or two ago was the Honourab!e Stephen Froude, wasn't he ?" _

Stephen looked at the Bailiff, suspected his quality and business, but thought of his friend, and at once said "No, I am he !" " That trick's rayther COO stale !" cried the Bailiff, grin- ning from ear to ear; and setting off at once in pursuit of the Diplomatic Official who had gone through the arch. Stephen laughed heartily as he thought, "If my Diplomatic friend could have overheard, he would almost have been tempted to try in future Truth as the only deceiver. Now, then to use my freedom." As he moved through the arch, be wss obliged to add—" Devil take him, he's here again, and stopping the way.!" So he retired a little to avoid notice. "I must give it up," the Bailiff was saying to himself as he came back from his unsuccessful pursuit of the Diplo- matic official, who had gone into the house, where the Bailiff knew well he must not attempt to follow him. " I must give it hop. My. bootiful perfession. My legs is a turnin' rebels." And he went to the alcove to rest them. • Stephen now tried to pass him by unnoticed whilst his back was turned; but whether, the attitude itself were a trick, suggested to the bailiff by seeing stephen waiting about as if to get away; or that he heard the step and was instantly roused, he moved directly so as to confront Ste- phen, and then a second time addressed him— You say your name is Honourable Stephen Fronde ?" "Yes," Stephen could not but say. The bailiff smiled a benevolent smile, approached Stephen in a friendly and familiar manner, so that Stephen really thought some very different and much pleasanter communication was forth- coming. But suddenly the bailiff made a rush at him, shouting at the same time— "l got you. You are my prisoner. I'll knock you down if you resist." "Don't make a fool of yourself, and pray keep your hands by your aide. Pve no intention to resist, as you must have seen.' " Then I arrests you at the suit of George Baldercomb for six hundred and fifteen pounds ten shillings and sixpence. And ha! ha! ha! I begs pardon for doubtin a gent's word. But it's so precious seldom, the law finis sitch willin as- sistants in sitch quarters, that I was quite taken in. Ha; ha! ha! You see we isn't use to it." And therewith the bailiff wiped away the moisture in his eyes. "This has happened at a most unlucky time," said Step- hen, half to himself.

"Right as a trivet !" ejaculated the bailiff, triumphantly slapping his knee. "That's always the f ust obserwation." *1 must seek a friend who will help me," remarked Step- hen, who was all the while meditating how to extricate himself.
0, it's ball right!" cried the bailiff, in fall satisfaction be had got the tree man. "The friend is inwariably the second deloosion . .

" I see Lord Harlaaton is coming this way," said Stephen. "He is, I believe, seeking me, as kave long been seeking him. I must now speak to him, and alone. You can wait where you like, close by, only keeping out of sight and hearing. Take this." Stephen removed from his finger a ring of some value, and handed it to the bailiff : " I give :sou this, and with it my word of honour, that you shall be paid before you leave, or you shad take me with you." The bailiff looked bard at him, and then turned away as if to reflect. This he did two or three times, before he took the proffered ring, and said— " I Myer did such a thing in hall my life before, but, damme, I will do it for you now !" Stephen thanked him, and as he was going, stopped hint to ask— "Do you mind telling me Whether anyone beside your employer' Baldercomb, has interfered, and so contrived that I should be arrested just now ?" The Bailiff looked cautiously round before answer- ing, then came back and came elose to Stephen and once more the hoarse whisper was beard noisily saying— " I believe the Head did it hall !" And then with various nods, winks, and knowing ges- tures, he went to his place of waiting and watching. "Jack," thought Stephen, as though addressing him, "I beg your pardon for thinking it possible you could be so treacherous! Still, let me suspend judgment. Lord Hatlaston may be as innocent of this ruse as he must be of the burglarious seizure of the papers. "And even were he guilty of both, I have something•to think of at this moment infinitely more precious than his exposure and punishment, supposing my mother's state and his present relations with Miss Vandeleur admitted of either.
"He approaches. And, is it possible ?—.l packet, doubt- less the stolen one, in his hand!"

CHAPrER LXXII.—THE MErrtwo OF THE BELLIGERENTS. As Lord Ilarlaston carne from the garden, out of the broad sun, he was surprised to find Stephen there; for he had come to the only sequestered part of the grounds to read the papers obtained Prom Gentleman Jack.

" We'll, you have got back?" he said i.o Stephen, as he I recovered from his momentary embarrassment and held out his hand. " Glad to see you." • "And I you," said Stephen, taking the proffered hand I after a brief hesitation. . "But dismissing to a more con- ' venient time all matters that can wait, I wish to say a few words on my own position and your relations with Miss Vandeleur." "Stay!" cried Lord Harlarton. "As to your position I am most ready to listen, and respond in an amicable spirit to anything reasenable; but as to the young lady who is I presently to be my wife, I prefer to discuss our relations only with her." "No, Philip, that cannot be," said Stephen, with an air of stern decision. "You will talk them over with me, and now, unless you prefer a discussion on a different theme, which Will certainly be now. " Really !" replied Lord Harlaxton, in a tone of irony. "Do things go with so high a hand? Is it this packet of papers, which I was about to read, that-- "I see, then, you do understand the nature of what I was about to say on my own part," said Stephen. "Are you sure you understand it yourself ?" retorted the Earl, growing more and more angry. "Try me !" responded Stephen. "But pray be careful. I did wish—: do still wish—that we should take counsel together in a friendly spirit." "1 respond to that. ' said Lord Harlaston, "but request that the name of my bride may not again be mentioned." ' "You must really allow me to take my own c3urse in Opening my mind toyou," urged Stephen, in a temperate tone. "And if I will not ?" demanded the Earl. "What then?"
"Then. my lord of Harlaxton," exclaimed Stephen, losing temper, and throwing away all the restraint he had been struggling to keep up, "1 give you that title for the last time unchallenged." _

"My good fellow, I am really concerned for yourself," I responded the Earl, "in having to say the title does not really depend on your benevolence, however charming." The E irl apparently knew he was adding fuel to fire by his every speech, and was not unwilling to give way to the impulses that possessed him. Nor was Stephen by this time loth to follow the ex- ample "You compel me then to go on. I wanted to be silent, for your sake, for my mother's, and for the salvation of the family's honour. I was content to leave you in the fullest enjoyment of all you possess, asking only in return one I thing: the lady to whom I have given my whole heart, and whose affections I have reason to believe I have won."

"Choose your path, this way or that l" said Lord Harlax- ton, in a voice of suppressed fury', as he pointed in the two opposing directions; "and I will take the other. I hold no longer converse with you." "So be it !" said Stephen. "Meantime Ido not yet ask you how you obtained the papers in your hand. but simply say they are mine—are addressed to me byname—l demand them P; .
"And I ref use to give them up till at least they are read !" said the Earl. . . _
"I can wait," rejoind Stephen.
"Read them now. I

, will not leave without them !" "But what if they should prove of such a character that I am bound to detain them in the interest of justice for the prosecution of their author ?" This provocation was unendurable, and was responded to in the same spirit by Stephen. "Do you thus refer," he said, in his quietest but most penetrating and insignificant of tones, "to a packet stolen from my mother's jewel case, and which is now f And on you ? " "It is time, I see, to throw off the veil, and acknowledge ourselves for what we are," said Lord Harlaxton, mortal enemies! There is my yacht. The wind is favourable. Three or four hours will take us to France. There are weapons in the cabin. Paper or no papers, right or no right, I offer you that solution. "I accept," said Stephen, who had by this time recovered all his natural coolness of demeanour, when confronted by dangers, or their equivalent. So he added, " We had better leave a message that we are going away together, to discuss in privacy, our affairs." Lord Harlaxton took a note book from his pocket, tore a leaf out, and handed it to Stephen, saying : Write, then, and we will both sign it, to give the ladies the more certain satisfaction." When Stephen was thus engaged, Lord Harlaxton opened the packet, took out and glanced over the contents, and began to read; but seeing there was no time to do more, re- placed them, as Stephen spoke : "I have signed." And he gave the paper to Lord Har- laxton, who appended his initials. "How shall this be de- livered ?" Lord Harlaxton hurriedly answered him, "Miss Vandeleur is coming. She must not know or sus- pect. What's to be done ?" asked the Earl, greatly dis- tressed at the interruption. "Make a virtue of necessity," rejoined Stephen, "and get her to be the bearer. That of itself will stay sus- picion." As she drew near, Stephen advanced to meet her with a smile, and said, " You will not wonder, Miss Vandelear, that Lord Har- laxton and!, having many and important things to talk about, are going for a short Bail in his yacht. Will you kindly, after readinl-r, give that to my mother ?" As be handed the paper to her, which she glanced at, but hardly took time to read, her thoughts being otherwise engaged. She looked frotn one to the other, with such a Penetrating glance, that Lord Harlaxton could not stand it, so turned away. Stephen's eyes confronted hers, and made no sign. Presently she said, and smiled for the first time in her turn. "Ladles do not usaally invite themselves into the society of gentlemen; but the day is so fine, the air so enchanting, the water so refreshing to one's senses through all, its heav- logs and murmurings, that I am inclined to petition to go with you. I will nestle in a corner, and if I grow tired read myself asleep over my book—a perfect one for the purpose —it is so deliciously dull." . . .

The; two men exchanged glances, and Stephen again I spoke : "Miss Vandeleur cannot doubt that her society is to be preferred before that of any other person in the world, but business is business, and must be done in a business-like manner. So I beg her to excuse me just now." And he moved slowly towards the yacht. "I appeal to you, Lord Ilarlaxton." cried Miss Vanda- leur, in anxious tones, forgetting all her previously assumed gaiety. "He does but say what I can repeat," cried Lord Harlem- ton. "Adieu, for a little while !" And he too went towards the yacht, turning once to kiss his fingers to her, but receiv- ing no reciprocating sign. But she followed swiftly upon them, so that they had scarcely jumped upon the deck, and shouted to the men to "Let go !" before she was on the edge of the Terrace Quay, and crying aloud to them in ringing tones, "You may get off before I can descend in safety, but not so far but I think I can reach you by a bold leap. I will certainly try, if you do not stop !" In another moment she would have been as good as her word, and perhaps have fallen into the sea, for the yacht was tossing about, when Stephen's voice was heard in stentorian tones to the sailors, ' ' " '
"Stop! stop!" And he was just in time—the vessel hapi not actually quitted her moorings; the ropes were agaih made fast.

Seeing their chance was over, both the gentlemen as- cended to the quay, looking a little flurried, and ashamed of the position in which they now were, but prepared to carry it off by a humorous bravado. But the reception that awaited them put them in a very different frame of mind. •

"Do you really think," asked Miss Vandeleur, looking from one to the other, "you have deceived the poor simple girl who so wanted and tried to put faith in you? Your false message has been wasted. I spare you both the offence of its delivery to the Countess. Take it, in all its worth- lessness!" .

She then tore the paper into small pieces, her vehe- ment fingers seetning to take a sinister 'pleasure in making them as small as possible, and then she threw them at their feet. "But the Countess comes. Perhaps she may be easier of belief, if you will again try the deception on her !"

WINSFORD SALT TRADE, The early months of the past year urought about again one of those most extraordinary ruptures of the good understanding which had prevailed for the previous year amongst the members of the trade. "Excessive and incon- trollihle greed of same few, submitted to in the first instance by the red, very soon produced the inevitable result: The association collapsed, and prices have remained in core- queues ever since at starvation poiat." If we add to this cause of bad trade the phenomenon of the failure of the brine springs, which has produced for four months compul- ' gory stoPpage of many works; and though that evil has ' departed, yet it requires a hold imagination to predict a continuance of such departure. Bence that no wonder that while it lasts some are doing all they can to grasp results. Prices in the early part of 1.`:132 ruled at 48 to 5s (work price) for common and Calcutta salt, in the summer theY declined to 4a, but in autumn, when the brine failure pro- duced compulsory stoppage, a short season of 5s 61 again ; intervened. At present we are with moderate stocks and a 1 very small demand again at the lowered figure. The demand 1 has been prodigious all over the world, there is a decided ! increase in the consumption everywhere, and although other countries are extending their production of salt, our ocean carriage facilities will ever give us the lion's share. India especially is beginning now to respond to the equalisation of the duties. Rough fishery salt was an article difficult to I obtain last year, and high prices prevailed throughout. Rock salt has remained at its now perennial model figure. Agriculturists have realised the fact that it is the onIV proved preventative for the prevalent cattle disease, and there is a great demand over all America and Australia. England and Scotland will shortly follow no doubt. Pricss I for contract deliveries of 1884 are as follows :--7Shippel 1 f.o.b. Liverpool per ton of 20cwts. ADRIFT ON THE MERSEY. A BOAT GROUNDING ON FRODSHAM MARSH. A boat ,containing 18 persons, from the training ship " Akbar." stationed in the Mersey, Was adrift in the river and exposed to the pitiless fury of the storm on Wednesday night. e We e are thankful to be able to relate all load a mar- from a watery grave, the boat grounding, on Frodshantise;lpe to ctoolndeapnoderxelpoitofilsetlrefeallfotewr, Duck- worth, succilaMbseld; narrative o structor William Roxburgh, ore, lannadmiendg.Duckk: tethsurvivors, gave our correspondent a very clear ontight of suspense and suffering, and stated a--‘• I am infetrue °or. on itytehaea Wednesday ship A.kbar,, and left the training ship afternoon in the usual four o'clock boat, a 10-ea'red cutst ay but in consequence of the unfavourable weather we t:roli; two extra oars. The boat contained 1$ lads, and five officers and others, including a female. It was intended to land at Rockferry slip. After shoving orff the wind collie:lanced to blow heavy from the westwarkso that we could not get the bows of the boat towards the shore, and it being flood tide at the time the current took Us up the harbour. All efforts to pull the boat towards the shore were without avail, the wind blowing the oars out of the boy's bands. We Persevered until darkness set its and then dropped anchor; but, fortunately, the anchor dragged, or the heavy seas Which we afterwards experienced would have swamped the boat. As it was we-were drenched to the skin, and when the storm lulled at intervals baled the water with our hats until we found Ourselves aground, and, lifting the boat as high as possible, waded to land. We had no idea where we were, and wandered about until daylight, crossing the fields , and ditches as best we could. The weather was not so rough when we left, the training sfiip, but after- warda blew a perfect hurricane. The boy Duckworth did not belong to the ship, but he landed with the rest, and on being missed a fruitless search was made, and he was afterwards found lying down and lifeless." A man named Joseph Falkner, of Marsh Green, Frodeham, was the first to meet the weary voyagers when going shooting down the Marsh,ibout a quarter to eight on Thursday morn- ing, and took four lads he met to his home, where his mother gave them every attention. He then took a can of warm tea.down the Marsh, which he gave to those he met, and afterwards, with others, carried others to places of abetter, where they speedily came round with care and attention which sets generously forthcoming, and all were able to return to Liverpool by train except a lad named Reeves, who, under the care of Dr:Robinson and Mrs. Falkner, is progressing favourably. The body of the boy Duckworth awaits a coroner's inquest at the Queen's Head Hotel, Frodsham.

Messrs. Joseph R. and W. P. Baines, share brokers. 1 , Queen's Chambers, Market-street, Manchester, write cJan. 24th):— There is no phenomtnal feature to record as presentirg itself since we last wroe. A moderate business has been concluded, a• d prices show no general inclination, the changes that have taken pace being result of individual influences, which have affected the several stocks irregularly. What approach•to tone of market there is is towards ease, which may be attributed possibly to the slight upward movement in the value of money and reports of railway meetings recently held. Foreign Stocks have a good record, as with the exception of Peruvians, which are and Turkish stamped lower, all the alterations marked are favourable. Egyptian Unified are U. ditto pref, •, Laira, I; Italian, 11; Spanish, ; and Russian, I higher, Mexican Railways fluctuate a little, and on balance are about 1 better than last week, but another decrease (Ji,HO). The future prospects will hardly, we think, be viewed with equanimity except by bears. Suez Canals have moved backwards and forwards a little, finishing with a rise of j to 1i on the week. Miscellaneous investments have changed nands to an extent about the average for some time t ime back, but with t la a x - ception of Banks lower prices predominate.

SAD RESULT OF Iron=Artos.—Another sad instance of the effects of drunkenness has occurred in the neighbour- hood of Sheffield. A farmer named Thomas Trickett, who lived at Loxley, has been found lying drowned in a pond near, his house. He was the worse for liquor when last seen. A: death under like circumstances occurred a few days ago in another suburb of Sheffield. • DEATH OF EARL GROSTRNOR.—EarI Grosvenor, the eldest son and heir of the Duke of Westminster, succumbed at an early hour on Tuesday morning to the attack of con- gestion of the lungs which suddenly manifested itself on Saturday. The deceased nobleman, who was only ix his thirty-first year, married in 1.1174 Lady Sibell Mary, young- est daughter of the Earl of Scarborough -, and their son, Viscount Belgrave, now four years of age, becoraes heir to the Westminster title and estates. The Queen, the Prince and Princess of Wales, the Duke and Duchess of Albany, Mr. Gladstone, and many other personages, hare telegraphed their condolences Is the Countess Gresvenor and ,the family. WIDNES LIBERAL ASSOCIATION. MR. J. MORRISON ON THE FRANCHISE. On Wednesday. evening the annual meeting of the East 'Division of the Widnes Liberal Association was held at the Albert Hotel, Simms Cross, Mr. J Morrison, the chairman of the division, presiding. Although the night was very stormy, and it was almost impossible to walk along the streets, there was a fair attendance, amongst those present being—Messrs D Wright, J. W Carlile, T Crosier, George Rae, H Hartland, and H B Shores (the general secretary). The minutes of the last meeting having been read and con- firmed, the appointment of committees was proceeded with. —Oa the proposition of Mr J W Camara, seconded by Mr T CROSIER, the committees were appointed as follows: Messrs J L Mnspratt, T Crosier E, D Wright E, R Fogg E, Hamblett E, S Kidd, S Robinson E, P Talton, D Hirst E, T Deakin, C Stout, J W Carlile E, W H Kershaw, W Pritchard, J Leathwood, J W Wareing E, J Leatherbarrow, J Y Dale, J W Davies J Horrabin. S K Muspratt, J Mor- rison E, J Davies, J 1:1 Lewis, R Mercer, G Rae E, D Forster, T Dennett, A Cowley, J Brock, A Walker, H Hart- ley, J Hargreaves' J Newell, D Stowe, W Mounfleld, R Ratcliffe, T Reay,J McMahon, Dr Cooper. Mr. J Heaney was appointed the representative of Cuerdley. Those per- sons with E affixed to their names are members of the Executive Committee. The CHAIRMAN proposed that Mr. Rae be re-appointed honorary secretary, observing that be deserved the thanks of the Association for his past services. He was always anxious to take part in anything that would forward the interests of Liberalism in Widnes. The motion was seconded and carried. Mr. J. W. CARLILE then proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Morrison for the able manner in which he had presided over their meetings during the past year. He also moved that he be re-appointed chairman for the ensuing year, as he was better acguaiiated with the duties than anyone else. Mr. D. WRIGHT, in seconding the motion, said they had worked ilniCabi y tog,ether. Mr. Morrison had presided over all their meetings often at great inconvenience to himself, and Ise had done all in his power to forward the interests of Liberalism in Widnes, and in the endeavour to educate the people in Liberal principles. The mation was carried. Mr. Siloam then read a report of the work of the Associa- tion daring the past year. The Ceternacas said he must in the first place thank them for re-appointing him as their chairman for the en- suing year, and he must particularly thank Mr. Carlile and Mr. Wright for referring to his services in the way they had done. He was sure the report which they had heard from Mr. Shores must be highly gratifying to every Liberal in the own. (Hear, hear.) The success they had achieved in the Revision Court was due, he thought, entirely to the eiertion of the principal officers of the Association, par- ticularly to the vice-president and their indefatigable and able secretary, Mr. Shores. To them alone, he believed, was due their satisfactory position in that department of the work of the Association, because he did not think they had been called together once daring the past year. With re- gard to finance Mr. Shores had informed him that they were in a better position this year than they had been for many years. They bad paid their way, and they had something they had not had for a great many years—a balance in the bank to the credit of the Association. He was pleased to see that there was more activity in the district, and a greater desire amongst the members not only to werk, but to give their means in order that the work of the Association might go on prosperously. This activity was due in a great measure to a fear that the Reform Bill to which the present Government were pledged to bring in might be thrown out by the House of Lords. Liberals were determined that they would be prepared for the issue if an appeal was to be made to the country. Now the reform that most concerned them, and to which it was necessary to refer, was the giving of a vote to householders in the county. And in his limited experience he had found many Liberal-minded Conserva- tives, and even Liberals, who opposed the granting of votes to householders in the counties. They did so on the ground that it was unfair to give .votes to workingmen equal to wealthy men who had large interacts at stake in the shape of land, house property, or manufactures. That on the face of it was a plausible argument they must be prepared to meet as far as they in their humble means could. The reply to that was this. The granting of votes to people was sonply a means to an end, namely, that the House of Com- mons should faithfully reflect the wishes and aspirations of the great balk of the people, because -it was an admitted principle in this country that the majority must govern. Yet they all knew that in the beginning of this century the voting power was in the hands of a very few. The aris- tocracy had it all in their own hands, and at that time the House of Commons did not reflect the interests of the great bulk of the people. They knew as a matter of history it was not a mere statement of his that legislators in their own interests removed the burden of taxation from their own shoulders, and placed it on the shoulders of the working class. He referred more particularly to the land tax. Many of the largest landowners in the country bad got their land, given to them by the State on condition that a certain tax he paid. They removed this burden from their own shoul- ders to the shoulders of the workim class by taxing the ' 'hinge that labourers chiefly consum d, namely, tea, to- bacco, and other articles. The tax on the working class on commodities chiefly used by them amounted to 30 millions last year, whereas the land tax was only one million. People got dissatisfied with that state of affairs, and an agitation commenced over all the country. Previous to 1832 all the country was aflame with agitation, and it was only when on the verge of revolution that the House of Commons gave way, and the Reform Bill of 1832 as passed. Since that date the franchise had been enlarged until in their own time they got household suffrage given to the boroughs. Now they had given household suffrage to the boroughs he did not think anyone would contend for a moment—he had not heard a Conservative mention it—that the present House of Commons was not a better representation of the people than it was in the olden time, when the franchise was in the hands of the upper classes. There seemed to be a fear in the minds of many that the labouring interest would swamp all other. But he did not think there was any fear ot that, because the labouring interest had now the power in boroughs, and the representatives they sent up were very few indeed. They could be counted on the lingers of one hand. There was Mr. MacDonald Mr. Burt, and one or two others, and be was sure the way iu which these men bad worked in reforming the relations be- tween employer and employed in making mining more safe and in passing the • Factory Acts, the way which these men had conducted themselves merited their warm admira- tion, making them wish that there were more such men in the House of Comm ins He did not think there need he the slightest fear that granting household suffrage to the counties would deprive any other interest, but they might depend upon it the representatives they sent up to Parlia- ment would always be men who had come to the front, men of educition and ability. He.therefore, thought that as they had got household suffrage to the boroughs, it was a Perfect anomaly to refuse it to the counties. He could not see what argument there was against it, for a man in a county was quite as able to exercise the franchise as a man who lived" in a town. Thee, as Liberals, were determined that this injustice should be re:moved. There was some idea that this Reform Bill, which would, he believed, be oise of the first measures of the next session, would be thrown out by the House of Lords. He saw in an organ a few days ago that the House of Lords would throw the bill out if it extended to Ireland. It also stated they would throw it out unless it was accom- panied by a redistribution of seats, and, thirdly, they would throw it out because it would disfranchise a great number of the small boroughs. If the bill was thrown out, and Mr. Gladstone was compelled to appeal to the country, they would be determined, as far as in their humble way, to use every means in their power to send Mr. Gladstone back with a greater majority at his back than he " had at present (hear, hear) in order that that he might be enabled to pass those reforms to which he had promised to devote the declining years of his illustrious career. There was every indication that whenever the Liberals of Widnes were called upon to exercise their rights with regard to sending a member of Parliament they would work as one man in order that they might achieve the re- forms in which they in the counties were very much in-1 terered. After again thanking these present for electin,r. him chairman, Mr. Morrison resumed his seat. SPEECH BY CAPTAIN BRUNNER. _ .

-- --- On Thursday evening the annual meeting of the West Division of Widnes Liberal Association was held in the officers' room of the Volunteer Hall, Widnes. Captain H. Brunner, the chairman of the division, pre- sided, and he was supported by Messrs S Owens, H B Shores, D W Hunter, Reddiman, T Jones, W Kerr, &e. --On the proposition of the CHantsfax, the general com- mittee was appointed as follows :—Dr O'Keeffe, Messrs J Latham, J Bray, J Dagnall, S Owens, H R Colquitt, G 8 Wharton, R Baker, C Short, J Anderson, B Brown, S B Stringer, G Hesketh, T Robinson, N Mathieeon, George Davies, .J Bennett, U Ogg, T Ramo, J H Lee, R Booth, J Midwood, V C Driffield,D Gill, J Tailon, Job Ward, John -Oriffitbs, John Phillips, and A Powloon. Mr. S. OWENS moved, and Mr. REDDIMAN seconded that the following gentlemen form the Executive Committee:— Messrs. J Taylor, 8 Sadler, W Sadler T Sadler, F H Pank- bnrst, R Webster, T Hughes, and F Lawrinson. MC, SHORES moved the re-appointment of Mr. D. W. anYatet tO the position of hon. secretary in corupli.ramtary tr.rins. • Mr. T. JONES seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously. Mr. OWENS proposed that Captain Brunner be re-elected was Chairman for the ensuing year, observing that his liberalism was Mr. W. Ksunegoaestsioectuoteecitypteh.e proposition, which

carried. The Getarearsiv, in making his acknowledgements, de- livered a speech of considerable length. He observed that he hoped to have been able to bring a friend to deliver an address, and he regretted his absence on their account, and to a certain extent upon his own, because spelcuil was not a thing which he cared for particularly, and it was always rather a trouble to him. Nevertheless there were times when people with any political opinions at all ought to express those opinions and give a reason for the faith wh:c'a was in them. There were a great number of things whicl• r, night have spoken to them about, but one thing had s him in particular as snitaLle for saying a few wards upon that might, and that was the coming tession. On the sth of February Parliament would be opened, and of course, as usual, when Parliament met the Government would have to bring forward certain proposals. These pro- trsals would be criticised, and possibly carried, possibly rejected. The things which they had to expect during the outing session were first and foremost the Franchise BiU,

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: secondly the Municipality of London Reform Bill, and thirdly the County Government Bill; and then probably some measures for the relief of the poor. A great deal was said about the extension of the Franchise Bill; they knew thit in that bill househole suffrage would be extended to the counties; that was to say, every man living in a house and paying rates would have a vote for the county. Well, now, what was the reason? Why should they want at? In the first place, they wanted it because it was atsnrd that men who lived in a borough in houses, and paid rates, should have votes, while men who lived just outside the Parliamentary boundary should have no vote, although' they lived in as good houses, and were perhaps just as good an and in every way fit to exercise the franchise. That absurdity must be done away with. But there were other reasons why they wished to extend household suffrage to the counties, Since household suffrage was givea to the boroughs there had been a very great ettension of the Educetien Acts, and people residing in counties had beea very little consulted as to their ideas about the matter—at any rate they had had no possible chance of expressing an opinion about the Acts. There was this difference between the people living in towns and those living in the counties, that the wages of the agricultural labourer and others trying in rural districts were leas on the average than those ef workmen living in towns, so that the cost of education pressed very mach . more on the agricultural labourer than it did on the artisan. Now they ought to know whether these people were satis- fied with the Education Acts as they had been passed. Whether they thought Parliament had been going too fast, or ought to go faster still, because the majority of the voters might before long declare that instead of hiving to pay for education as they had now, education should be free to all. ' They ought also to expect from their rural voters what they bad got to say about the depression in agriculture,and what they would proposed to remedy the state of affairs. Possi- bly they might hear something from them about greater freedom of trade in land, and through their representatives might have some proposals to make in order to remove the great depression which no doubt at present existed. Whatever measures for the relief of the poor had to be taken it seemed to him that the rural voters would have something to say on that subject because there was no doubt the overcrowding of large cities had arisen in a great • measure through the emigration of poor people from the rural districts. Wages had fallen so low, land had been . thrown out of cultivation, and these poor labourers bad had to go to London, Liverpool, and Glasgow to try to mend their position. The Toriee had one or two very great ob- jections to any bill for the extension of the franchise. They contended that the country had not demanded it, that the people did not require it, and that it could not be extended in Ireland—they said in fact—it would be wicked and foolish to extend the franchise in Ireland at the present moment—therefore it was not right it should be extended in England, Scotland, and Wales. The answer to the first , objection was that whatever proposal of reform was made the Tory always said "Nobody asked for it, and that it was not necessary"; but the vary essence of Toryism was that they would never listen to any proposal of reform until they found themselves face to face with rrvolution. They ob- jected to the extension of the franch7se to Ireland on the ground that it would give Mr. Parnell such a tremendous increase in his Parliamentary strength. But supposing the whole of the Irish members were Parnellites, he did not see that that was any reason for them to be afraid. What bad they got to be afraid of? Liberals and Conservatives alike had quite made up their minds upon this point that there should be no separation whatever between England and Ireland. He believed that the feeling of the greater majority of the people in this country was that Irishmen in Ireland Bhould have just as much liberty and enjoy every freedom . that Englishmen, Scotchmen, or Welshmen enjoyed, and no Irishman in his senses would ask for more. Lord Salisbury would be perfectly satisfied to extend the franchise if he thought his party would gain anything by it, and the rea- son why Tories objected to the franchise to Ire'and or any- where else was that it would be w ,me for them. If they were to wait for an extension of the franchise until Irish- men loved Englishmen, and loved Eriglish rule as they ought to do, they might, he was afraid, wait for a great length of time. Certainly, so long as there were differences in representation, it was not likely that Irishmen would love England. With regard to the County Government Bill and the Bill for the reform of the municipality of London, these ought not to be party questions, but being brought forward by a Liberal Government and criticised by a Conservative Opposition, they would he made party questions. There was, no doubt, some government wanted ter counties. It seemed an absurd thing on the face of it that if they wanted to make a new railway' from Widnes to St. Helens they could net do BO without going up to !Parliament to ask for it. There were many small matters which concerned only one county. Why could not those matters be settled in that one county without going up to Parliament about it. Parliament had already far too much to do, and the County Government Bill was intended as a measure of relief for Parliament. After referring to the London Muni- cipal Reform Bill, the speaker said the Conservatives thought that if there was a dissolution of Parliament next session the present Government would be replaced by a Con- servative one. Ile dia not believe it. When people wanted a change of Government they could generally see some reason for it. What were the people disratisfled with the present Government for? Was the Government blamed for doing things which they ought not to have done, or leaving undone things which they ought to have done? No fault could be found with the Government either on their home (Or their foreign policy. A dissolution might take place this session, and what they had to do was to be prepared for it. It was for that ream they had those meetings in the various divisions, and eleeted committees, secretaries, and chairmen se that they would be on the watch and be prepared when the time came to vote as they should do, and endeavour to the best of their ability to uphold the prin- ciples they professed. ( Applause.) A vote of thanks having been accorded to the chairman for his able address, the meeting then terminated.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, en Tuesday, under the presidency of Mr. J. Ashton. There were present :—The Revs. John Lockwood, J. W. N. Tan- ner, Messrs. Pickering, E. A. Wallington, J. Darbyshire, C. Rigby, Stokes, H. Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk), Dr. Adams (medical officer's deputy).

sERIGUS Mut:BEAK OF FEVER AT -FBODSHAM. Dr. ADAMS presented the following report :—I have to , report an outbreak of scarlet fever at Norton on a cottage ' occupied by Thomas Wyche, and situated between Norton ; Crossing and Norton Station. Three persons have been at- tacked by the disease up to the present time, viz., Henry Wyche, aged 18 years, Thomas Wyche, aged 27 Years, and Elizabeth Wyche aged 54 years. The drioliing water supply is very defective, and the water contains vegetable matter and living organisms. I have to report a further ex- tension of the outbreak of typhoid fever at Frodebain Bridge. Mrs. Glaspool was attacked by the disease, but was removed to the Dutton Workhouse Hospital on Friday last, the 18th inst.—ln answer to Mr. Derbyshire, Are CLERK said there were three cases of typhoid fever In the House. He added that there were ten persons suffering ,at tbe diseasendfouratß arose if rtowmast suggestedhesa m e d sebays npart. FAroDdAta mt that at Frodsham from a defective water supply which was ob- tained from the "pipe on the quay" and " smallbrook pipe." The Doctor said this WI). p ismd under several pub- lc urinals in the township, which were not drained. He was afraid the water supply reps was only an ordinary drainage pipe, and that the water from the urinal thus was able to contaminate the wamr.—Mr. WALLINGTON: Have we power to close that pipe without any analysis being made F—The CLERK: No. You must have proof.—Mr. WALLINGTON thought the best plan would bs to have an analysis of the water made as quickly as possible. He hai had the opinion of a doctor, who firmly believed that the water supply was the cause of the fever. He tteaught it was the duty of the Board to at once stop the supply in question if they possibly could. On the motion of Mr. " Wallington it waa decided that Mr. Farrington ehould take two samples of-tire water for analysist and if the analyst con- demned the water he was empowed to take the necessary steps to have the pipes stooped. • THE INSPECTOR AND SIR RICHARD BROOKE'S AGENT. The following letter was read :—Lialton, near Runcorn, , , January 9th, 1884.—Dear sir, In consequence of some com- plaints being made to the Runcorn Rnral Sanitary Author- ity of the defectiveness of the Halton drainage scheme, we I are requested by Mr. Farrington to meet him and the con- tractor (Mr. Littler), and examine the same. We did so this morning, and found no sewage matter coming through,. but when a few gallons of water had been put in at the in- let to the sewer, it came down in qeite a flush at the out- fall. We are quite satisfied with the drainage, and con- sider it is in conserinence of so few houses being drained in to it, and a certain amount of it percolating through the joints of the newly-laid pipes, which gave the impressiam of the sewage coming through.—We are, yours respectively, Thomas Wright, Hugh Rowe, Overseers of the poor for the township of Halton. To Henry Linaker Esq.—Mr. Farring- ton,, writing on the same subject said that he and Mr. Littler had tested the new main sewer at Halton, and found it as he expected—in first-glass working order. They flushed it in the presence of Messrs, Rowe, Wright, Nickson, and Gamon, and they intimate& that they were perfectly convinced and satisfied that there is no fault to be found withlt.— Inspector FARRINSTON asked theindulgence of the members whilst he made a statement respecting certain proceedings recently taken by the Authority against Mr. Evans, the agent to Sir Richard Brook. He had seen the gentleman in , question, and he thought it was his (the speaker's) duty to I bring the whole matter before the Authority, and he trusted that a stop would be put to the behaviour in which Mr. Evans had been indulging. It might not be in Hit' recol- lection of all the members of the Board that the Halton sewerage scheme was first brought before the Board about he 21s t t August, 1877, when Mr. Holland was the agent. It had been more or less before the Authority since that time. Mr. Evans said the Board had treated him harshly. In justi- fication of the Board and himself, Mr. Farrin gton pointed out that before proceedings were taken he had no less than half-a-dozen special interviews with Mr. Evans, and the iourneys were made at the expense of his own physical force and his own pocket. he contended that Mr. Evens , had been shown every kindness both by himself and the ; Authority. Mr. Evans had also asked him why he did not take action in another case. If Mr. Evans had known any- thing about the Public Health let, and he thoughts gentle- man in his position ought to hav,:, some knowledge of it, he

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 26, 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 26, 1884.

would have known that the two notices were entirely different. One stated that if the order were not complied with the justices would be appealed to, while the other said that if it was not complied with the Authority would do the work. He thought it was unjust and unfair for Mr. Evans to make such a statement. With respect to the main sewer at Halton, which had been recently cut, Mr. Evans had stated that the sewer would not run, but it had been tested and found to be quite satisfactory. He thought it was a great injustice not only to himself but to the Authority, that such a statement should be circulated, because in his opinion it implied incompetency on all the parties connected with it. Mr. Evans' conduc6 reminded him very forcibly of an old adage which, however, he would not use. Then there was the nuisance on Halton Common, which had been before the Authority since 1877. Mr. Evans had said he would not drain the farm ; he would ran the drainage on the ground. He (Mr. Farrington) left it to any practical man to point out hew they could drain a yard on to a garden five feet higher than the level of the yard. (Loud laughter.) Mr. Evans then said, "I will sewer the property as soon as ever you bring the sewer up to it." He replied that he was under no obligation, under the Public Health Act, to bring the sewer up to two houses. Mr. Evans said be did not care for the Public Health Act, and that he (Mr. Farrington) had better not take any more proceedings against him. He (Mr. Farrington) then gave over conversing with Mr. Evans. He could assure the Authority that whilst he had the hon- our to hold the position be did he should endeavour to ful- fil his duty fearlessly—(hear, hear)—and, to say the least. intimidation would have no effect upon him. (Hear, hear.) —The Cmana said it might be satisfactory to know that a letter had been received from the overseers of Helton, which stated they were quite satisfied with the drainage.—Mr. Derbyshire was about to move a resolution with reference to the nuisance, but Mr. Farrington pointed out that he had promised to give Mr. Lockwood a sketch, and that gentle- man would lay it before Sir Richard Brooke.

The minutes of the District Education Committee, which were passed on the motion of Mr. DEACON, stated that during the month of December (3 weeks) there were 31 ap- plications for the payment of school fees, which were re- commended to be paid in 25 cases. There were summoned before the committee 238 persons for contravention of the Education Act, and 44 were prosecuted before the magis- trates. Forty-two were convicted, and two children were sent to an industrial school. SCIOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE. The scbol Management Committe recommended that the resignation of Mrs. E. Jones, assistant mistress in the junior girls' department of the Simm's Cross School, be accepted, and the following teachers be appointed :—Miss S. A. Barton, assistant mistress, senior girls', Simm's Cross ; Miss M. Urquhart, assistant mistress, junior girls', Simm's Cross; Miss E. Williams, junior girls', West Bank; and Miss E. Keenan, senior girls', West Bank. The committee recommended the substitution of a new scale of payments to teachers, and the minutes, after a short conversation, were adopted.-1 Tne Rev. Father FINEGAN, as chairman of the committee, , also submitted a report showing the average amount of grants earned by the Widnes Board Schools. The report showed that in England and Wales the amount earned w. 16s Ip. while in Widnes the amount earned was 17s 11d, or a difference in favour of Widnes of up. The compari- son of grants earned per child in Widnes Board Schools showed an increase of 2i-d in 1883 over 1882. Total grants earned in board schools and the average attendance: Total grant, 1882, £l, 597 9a; 1883, £1,648 75 6d; increase, 3•19. Average attendance. 1882, 1,864 ; 1883 1,906 ; increase, 2 per cent. Results of pupil teachers and candidates: Num- ber examined, 1882, 31; seven passed well and 21 fairly ; marked in one or more subjects, 3; number examined, 1883, 33 ; eleven passed well and 13 fairly; marked in one or more subjects, nine.—Mr. GLOVER said he was surprised to find a decrease in the grant earned by the senior girls' department at Simm's Cress School, at which he should have been dis- posed to think they had one of the most efficient teachers.— ['he Rev. Father FINEGAN replied that he should be sorry to judge Miss Clayton by that report. fie had made in- quiries aud found that some of the children were examined during the dinner hour. He thought the examinations core too serious to be run through when the children were ex- hausted.—The minutes and report were adopted. FINANCE COMMITTEE. The Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £432 16s 2d. There had been paid into bank the sum of £BO2 53 64. These cash receipts, amounting to £BO2 5s 61, are debited in the Cash Book, folio 64. The Finance Committee submitted a state- ment of accounts for the year ending September 29th, 1883: —ln hands of treasurer, £l2B 14s 8d ; petty cash keeper, £ll 75 31; due from Education Department (Government grants), £1,64$ 7s 6d; total, £1,788 9s sd. The outstanding liabilities were :—Orders of the Board not paid by treasurer, £9 63 9d; proportion of Government grant due to teachers, £126 83 74; estimated interest on loans, £350; outstanding accounts, £l6 2s 4d ; audit stamp, £5; total, £506 17s Bd, leaving a balance ef £1,281 us 9d. The estimates of the committee for the ensuing year amounted to £3,578. In moving the adoption of the minutes Mr. Straw referred to the position of West flank School. He observed that in 1881 the school fees amounted to £464 16s 24; in 1882, £477 12s Id; and in 1833 they only amounted to £462 Ss lid. If the committee found that this diminution was owing to the raising of the fees some time ago, he thought they ought to come to the conclusion at once that they were losing by the transaction, because while the Government grant had been increasing, the average attendance was leas. In 1881 there were 714 children in the schools; in 1882, 731; and in 1883, 716. He moved that a precept be served upon the overseers for the sum of £3,500, being the esti- mated amount of the deficiency in the school fund up to the 29th September, 1881 ; also that the precept be signed and sealed, and made payable on or before the 31st day of March, 1884. The minutes were adopted and the motion passed, and the meeting concluded.

....,o.ttiNG MEN'S COMMITTEE. A meeting of the Warrington Working Men's Committee connected with the proposed Manchester Ship Canal was held at the offices of the Chamber of Commerce, Bewsey- street, on Wednesday evening, principally for the purpose of taking action on the question of railway rates. Mr. H. Whitham presided, and there was a fair attendance. The CHAinates regretted there was not a larger meeting, because the subject they had to consider was one of very great importance. They, as working men, were looking for- ward to two points or features from which they expected great help. In the first instance it was the scheme of the Ship Canal, and from that the railway question which was at present being agitated throughout tne country. He ob- served that a large meeting was held at Oldham on the pre- vious evening, at which Mr. Jacob Bright made a statement of considerable interest. Mr. Bright told them in one part of his speech that " the bill, as it is to be passed, we hope, but at any rate as it is presented to Parliament. contains a clause by which the maximum ratet that the canal can charge will not exceed one-half of the present rates." (Hear hear.) He meant by that the transit of manufactured goods, and that was very impoctant. For some time past there had been a Chamber of Oommerce in Warrington, but he would say, although they were meeting in one of its rooms, that there were very few outside that honourable body who knew of its existence—(a laugh)—and bethought it should have been their duty to deal with the question in a better fashion than they had done. There were great reasons for complaining of the attitude of their manufac- turers and tradesmen with regard to the Ship Canal ques- tion, because with very few exceptions he bad not noticed that they had made or contributed any large sum of money towards floating the scheme, and he thought they should have done. (Hear, hear.) He had said there were great reasons for them doing so, one of the most important being, according to the reports they heard and speeches being made in one town and another, that trade was not in such a flourishing condition as they would like it. There WAS no doubt they required some out- let for • the conveyance of their goods, and if the Ship Canal was made a good navigable river they would have by that means an outlet by which they could compete fairly with continental countries, and have a chance of doing a good trade. Australia had crept up very largely of late, India was calculated to take a great deal more of their trade the better it was looked after, and so was Aftrica, but they must keep in sight the fact that while they in England had up to within the last few years the trade of the world in their hands, that state of things was now altered. Russia, Germany, and Austria were now competing with them very considerably in manufactures, and therefore their own manufacturers in England should set themselves to work, and if they did not he supposed it was the duty of working- men to set the example. (Hear, hear.) The opposition which the Ship Canal scheme had met with was more especially from Liverpool and the railway companies. They could understand why railway companies opposed it, as they were afraid it would be so much added to the competition against which they had to fight and struggle, but why Liverpool, of all places, should be antagonistic to the canal he could not tell. There was no doubt that if trade was driven out of the country Liverpool would go with it. (Hear, hear.) Liverpool had not so much to fear from the Ship Canal as she had from what was taking place in other countries. In an article on "The trade of Antwerp" in a Manchester paper, he found it stated." The amazing increase of late years in the shipping trade of the Scheldt has a peculiar interest for us here in Manchester. Since 1830, 49 millions of francs—in round figures £2,ooo,ooo—haye been expended upon the improvement of the docks and quays which Napoleon I. constructed at Antwerp. In addition to this large sum—large, that is for a country which even now con- tains very few more people than the London area of taxation and police—the Belgian Government has within the last three or four years granted a lump sum of two and a quarter million pounds for the reconstruction of these docks. Antwerp has possessed five docks for more than'a generation, but those which are .00w approach- ing completion will be amongst the finest in the world. . . . It is clear that unless something unforeseen hap- pens the first English port to suffer by such competition as tale most be Liverpool." That clearly proved that there were other things besides the Ship Canal which Liverpool had cause to fear. There was Antwerp progressing at such a rate that she was prepared to take a large proportion of the emigrant trade to herself, and, therefore, the best thing Liverpool could do was to help on the Ship Canal and the trade of the country. (Applause.) They would, however, leave the Ship Canal, which he thought was in good hands, as Mr. Adamson' and the promoters with him, were doing all they could to bring it to a successful issue; but there was the railway question, in which they as work- ingmen were interested, and if they could see their way to have an agitation raised in Warrington, and 80 strengthen the hands of the association which was formed in Birming- ham, they would be doing a really go.d work. The freights which were charged were of such an anomalous character, that they required to be strictly looked into. Everybody who transmitted manufactured goods had cause for com- plaint. There was a body called the Railway Commsssioners, but of all the deputations which had waited on that body he had never heard of one receiving a satisfactory answer to their request—they were respectfully received, and that was all. They in England stood in an unfair position with respect to railway charges in comparison with other coun- tries. The Birrnirishdru Post, in an article on the meeting to consider the question of railway rates, which was held in Birmingham, said : "In France the average rates for hardware from Paris to the shipping ports is about 2d per ton per mile, whilst in this conatry it is 3d and 4d per ton per mile. In Holland the cost is just over 2d, in Australia it is under lid, and in Italy it is about the same. In the United States corn is carried from Chicago to New York—a distance of 960 miles —for 163 per ton, or about one-fifth of a penny per ton per mile. It is true that some slight concession has been re- cently made to our drawers of wire, a moribund iedustry, we are afraid, so far as this district is concerned ; but on the other hand, the companies have raised the rates for various kinds of traffic to the continent as much as 3s 4d per ton, and notices have been served upon ironfounders of increases of various rates ranging from 56 to 93 per cent. upon recent charges. Under this dispensation our rail trade has already gone, our iron wire trade is on its last legs, and our manufactures of cut and malleable nails, iron plates, galvanised iron, and iron tubes, are rapidly declining, or shifting their ground to other districts. It is in the interest of railway shareholders quite as much asof our 'iron and hardware producers, that the suicidal policy which is producing such lamentable results should be put a stop to, and if railway directors and managers cannot be brought to see this matter in the right light perhaps an organised appeal to the rail- way proprietary might be more effectual." The Chairman said the extra penny or twopence would affect such towns as Sheffield and Birmingham very considerably, and there- fore it was their duty to do something to get the cost re- duced, and their 'manufacturers placed on a similar level with continental cities. They were labouring in this coun- try under great opposition, and the sooner they commenced such an agitation as should result in the railway companies not only doing the best for them as working people but the best for their shareholders the better it would be. He had a resolution in his hands which, if carried out, would be of advantage, viz., "That Mr. Thomas Morris be requested to convene a public meeting on the railway question, and re- quest the manufacturers of Warrington and district to take part therein." (Applause.) It had been suggested, hos,- ever, that it would be advisable to invite Mr. Morris to e preliminary meeting in that room. Mr. HENRY ROBERTS (secretary) said that was a meoting of the members of the old working men's committee of the Ship Canal scheme, but he wished them to form themselves into a new committee to consider this particular question. What they wanted to know was whether it was possible to compel the railway companies to carry manufactured goods from Warrington to shipping ports or other parts of the country at such rates as to improve the production of their manufactured goods and the interest of the working men concerned in their production. That he look It to be the position of affairs. (Hear, hear.) He could not understand bow that a company could afford to carry passengers under the restrictions which various acts of Parliament had in- sisted upon at the minimum fare of a penny per mile, and yet they could not carry wire at the same rate. (Hear, hear.) Regarding competition with other countries, Mr. Roberts said there was every appearance that they would have enormous competition 'from America because very likely new American ports would be opened before many years were over, and the result would be that they would have to find a market for their surplus production which they could not find at home, and so they in England would conse- quently have to meet that. The question of railway rates was one of considerable interest to the people of Warring- ton. If their staple trades were harrassed by excessive railway rates and it was generally admitted that they were excessive, it behoved them to do something to obtain, if possible, a reduction. He thought that instead of calling a public meeting they should ask Mr. Teomas Morris or someone of the same character to meet the committee and prepare figures, and then convene a public meeting for their ideas to be propagated. (Ap- plause.) •

Mr. RATHBONE thought the suggestion of Mr. Roberts was a good one, and he would second it. He was amazed when reading the report of the meeting which took place in Birrningham or somewhere in the district, at the difference in the charges on manufactured goods by their own railway companies and the rates charged in other countries, it seemed astonishing that America was able to convey a ton of iron a distance of 960 miles for a sum of money about equal to what they had to pay between Warrington and London. Having referrqd to railway compani-,s monopolis- ing the canals of the country, he drew attention to the fact that when the present rates were fiirst levied on manufactured goods trade in this country was exceedingly brisk, and every trade could afford to pay the rates which were then fixed, but it was different now. (Hear, hear.) If the trade of the country was to be driven out through, or partly through, the excessive rates charged by railway companies for the conveyance of manlfactured goods, the railway companies would in the long run suffer as much if not more than the manufacturers themselves would. (Hear, hear.) He did not think it would be wise to assume a very dignified position in the matter,as it would be far better to reason with the railway companies as to the desirability of their reducing the rates rather than command thiem to do so. U the companies were brought to see that

in doin 'so they would be benefitting their own interests as well as e interests of the manufacturers it would be the better rse to pursue. ilit Mr. - NETT then moved a resolution to the effect that the members of that committee, with power to add to their number, should form themselves into a committee for the purpose of considering the rates charged by the various railway companies for the transit of manufactured goods, and the effect of such rates upon trade in this district. The resolution having been seconded by Mr. Enuraunsobt, and carried item con, The CHAIRMAN moved "That Mr. Thomas Morris be re- quested to meet this committee for the purpose of further- discussing this important question."—This was also agreed to, and Mr. Henry Roberts having been formally elected secretary of the new committee, the business of the meeting concluded.

PARR'S BANKING COMPANY, LIMITED. ANNUAL MEETING. The 19th ordinary general meeting of the above com- pany was held at the Bank premises, Winwick-street, War- rington, yesterday. Joseph Charlton Parr, Esq., chairman I of the directors, presided, and the other directors present ! were—Mr. Nathaniel Eckersley, M.P., Mr. Peter Stubs, Mr. Edward Greenall. Mr. Henry Woodcock, Mr. John I Pearson, Mr. Alfred Hewlett, Sir A.B. Walker, Mr. George McCorquodale, Mr. John Thompson, Mr. A. Turner, Mr. H. Warren Meade-King, Mr. Christopher Atkinson and Mr. I Cecil F. Parr. The following is a list of shareholders present :—Messrs. H. Milling, Dr. Mackie, George Mason (Liverpool), J. N. Padgett (Northwich), Charles Griffiths, ; Charles Reynolds, Dr. Molyneux, H. B. Parr, J. R. Buekton, ; Wm. Davies (Liverpool), James Handley, Wm. S. Barrett ' (Liverpool), John Lythgoe, Thomas Litton, R. Dobaon, Wm. Sharp, C. Broadbent, J. R. Pickmere, James Jolley, D. Garnett, John White, W. Robinson, W. Silcock, jun., T. Fairhurst, E. Davies, G. Blackhurst, A. M. McGregor. The report of the directors, which was taken as read, was as follows:—" The directors, in submitting to the share- holders the annual balance sheet, certified by the auditor, have to report that the position and prospects of the busi- ness continue to be in every way satisfactory. Including £12,196 1.23 11d, brought from previous account, the net balance of profits, after providing amply for all bad and doubtful debts, and rebating the current bills at five per cent., is £115,379 Os 9d. The distribution of this sum, re- commended by the directors, is as follows :—lnterim half- yearly dividend. at 15 per cent, per annum, declared 17th July. £38,935 10s; dividend to be now paid at the rate of 15 per cent, per annum, free of income tax (£42,000), bonus of las per share, free of income tax (£14,000)—£30,000 ; to reserve fund, £5,310; balance to next account, £15.133 103 9d; total, £115,379 Os 9d. Lieutenant-Colonel J. F. Greenall, having ceased to hold his director's qualification, has retired from the board, and Mr. Thomas Philip Parr has been elected in his place. The directors who retire at this time by rotation are Mr. Thomas Philip Parr, Mr. George McCorquodale, Mr. Edward Greenall, the Right Honourable Lord Delamere, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., Sir Thomas G. Frost, and Mr. John Thompson, all of whom are eligible and are recommended for re-election." The CHAIRMAN, in moving the adoption of the report, congratulated the shareholders upon the very satisfactory figures which they were able to place before them. He must express his regret at the retirement of Colonel Greenall, who had been connected with the bank for a long series of years, and the directors felt sorry that circumstances should have arisen to cause his absence from their board. Mr. Thomas Phillip Parr had been elected a director in his place, and as he retired that day by rotation Mr. Parr would come before them for re-election, if such was-their pleasure. The retirement of Colonel Greenall caused a vacancy in • the office of deputy-chairman, and he was very glad to say that Mr. : ....kereley, M.P., had been chosen, and had accepted that position. (Hear' hear.) The year that had passed by had been very much like its immediate predeces- sors, that was not very good nor very bad. Some of the trades had shown a little revival, whilst others were ex- tremely dull, and they would agree with him that there was ample room for improvement. Agriculture showed signs of improvement, the prospects being brighter, and the farmers were more hopeful. The Liverpool business in connection with the bank, Ile was glad to say, had fully borne out the expectation that was formed of it, although a period of one year was too short to speak with very great confidence. The position and prospects of the bank generally, as the report stated, were most satisfac- tory. The bad and doubtful debts were unimportant and called for no special remark, the number of accounts had very materialiy increased, which, of course, to a considerable extent was due to the accession of accounts from Liverpool, but also to the large area covered by the bank's operations. The number of shareholders had increased from 541 to 889, showing an addition of 348, the paid-up capital had increased by £67,000, and the money lodged by £10,000,000. The chair- man, having referred to various items in the balance sheet which showed an addition an the preceding year, said that coming to the distribution of the annual profits the directors were happy to recommend the usual substantial dividend of 15 per cent., and a bonus of 10s, per share, making in all 14 per cent. The directors proposed to carry £5,310 to re- serve fund, bringing the fund to the satisfactory and hand- some figure af £295,000, sad they would carry forward the balance of £15,133 to the next account.

At the annual match of the above Society, held 00 land in the occupation of Mr Thomas Hall at Daresburla there was a good attendance. The land was not in a fa' vourable state for good ploughing, being exceedingly heavy' and stiff. The judges were Mr J Southern, of Croft; Mt T button, of Heatley ; and Mr T Billington, of Duttoo• In the evening about 60 persons sat down to a rood old English dinner, spread in the Sessions House, and provided by Mr Philips, of the Ring O'Bells. Mr Mainwaring Pre- sided at the meeting which was afterwards held, Mr John Weir, of Lower Walton, acting as vice-chairman. After the usual loyal and patriotic toasts bad been duly honoured, ' the Secretary (Mr J G Hamilton) read the Ile; of successful competitors as follows : Class + (for men) : 1, £4, F Weir, owner; 2, £3, T Parsons, ploughman to Sir Gilbert Greenall ; 3. £2, T Hewit, plougt° man to Mrs Hewit ; 4, £1 10s, J Webb, ploughman to A Broady; 5, £1 ss, S Bayley, ploughman to Sir Gilbert Greenall ; 6, £l, Alfred Hall, ploughman to Thomas Hall, senior; 7,15 s, T Weir, ploughman to J Weir; 8,10 s, Wm Hall, ploughman to Thomas Hall. Class 2 (for youtlp): £3, Joseph Astbrook, ploughman to Joseph Ellam ; '2, £2, Frank Weir, ploughman to W Weir; 3, £l, P Broadrurst, ploughman to W Beswick. For the best turn-out: 1, £l,j, T Parsons ; 2,15 s, S Bayley; 3, 100, F Weir; 4,7 s 6d, A Weir; 5, a whip, J Webb.—Mr T 8 BURGESS, treasurer to -the Society, replied to the toast "The Patron of the Societ!", Sir Gilbert Greertall," and said that he believed Sir Gilbert was always willing to do anything in his power for the good of the farms on his estate. (Heir. hear.) Referrtng to the Agricultural Holdings Act af 1883, he sad he he" lieved that Sir Gilbert's tenants would rather stick to the old conditions under which they held their tenements thao avail themselves of anything which the Act contained, for they knew that they would gain by it.—Mr. J. SotTruartS, in replying to "The Judges," said they were all very prone to desire a good word to be spoken in their favour at anY time, but still he could not congratulate them upon having done as good work as ho had seen. But the land had been very unfavourable, and he hoped that in future years they.' would have a better field, one with a more even surface! Mr. DUTTON and Mt. BILLINGTON also replied.-Other toasts followed, and the rest of the evening was spent in an enjor able manner, songs being given at intervals.
