div.head: ENPORT UPON WORKS IN THH TOWNSHIP OF CLIFTON.
div.p: ENPORT UPON WORKS IN THH TOWNSHIP OF CLIFTON.

"According to instructions given at the last meeting, I have visited the mill or works situate upon the bank of the River Weaver Canal, in the township of Clifton. and late in the occupation of Mr. Robert Cameron, and I find that the works are now in the hands of a company of which Mr. William Henry King, of 41, Russel-street, Liverpool, is the acting manager. The business at present carried on upon the premises is what may be termed calcining "solidifiel blood" for manuring purposes, and will not, in my opinion, come under the category of offensive trades, as there is not the slightest offensiveness arising from the operation. The blood is brought to the premises in a pre- pared state, in bags, and is simply laid in thin layers upon a large stove or drying-flat, whereby it is rendered friable by the application of fire, which causes evaporation to take place, but the fumes given off are in no way odious or ob- noxious.—Jasots FARRINGTON." _ .
After the reading and consideration of the foregoing re- port the Inspector was directed to write to the manager, ask- ing for the date of the commencement of the business and the nature thereof.
PRESENTATION TO M. AND MRS. S. K. MUSPRATT, AT WIDNES. -

On Monday afternoon the workmen of Mess-s. James Muspratt and Sons, chemical manufacturers, Widnes, as- sembled in the ash store-room of the works for the purpose of celebrating in a suitable way the marriage of Mr. S. K. Muspratt. The building had been appropriately decorated, and tasteful mottoes, such as " Long life and prosperity to Mr. and Mn. S. K. Muspratt," " May they be happy," "Welcome home," "May our trade flourish," were displayed in conspicuous positions. At one end of the room had been erected a platform, and upon this were seated Mr. and Mrs. S. K. Muspratt, Mr. and Mrs. J. L. Muspratt, Miss Muspratt (Flint), Mr. J. H. Lewis (manager), Mr. D. Forster, Dr. Eschellania (chemist), Mr. J. Hadley, and Mr. J. Williams.— Mr. LEWIS commenced the proceedings by presenting to Mr. S. K. Muspratt, a handsome silver tray, bearing the following inscription :—" Presented to Mr. and Mrs. S. K. Muspratt, on the occasion of their marriage by tke employee of James Muspratt and Sons, Widnes, November 27th, 1883." In making the presentation, Mr. Lewis said the men were glad to have that opportunity of welcoming Mr. Muspratt home, and to have an opportunity of expressing their great grati- hcation of his marriage, and the fervent hope that the mar- riage might be a happy one. At the same time they wished him to accept the tray, which they offered to him as a token of the esteem and respect they cherished towards him- self and his wife. Mr. MusEEATT, who was warmly re- ceived, said they had taken him by surprise, and with con- siderable emotion he thanked them on behalf of himself and his wife for the handsome silver tray. Words could not express how they would value the present, because he be- lieved it was the outcome of that mutual friendship and respect, which he had always maintained ought in public and in private to exist between masters and men. (Cheers.) They found that individually they could not do without each other. He should always have at heart the prosperity ' and welfare of the Widnes works. (Cheers.)—Mr. LBWIS then presented Mrs. S. K. Muspratt with a beautiful gold necklet, having a pendant set with four large amethysta, accompanied by a few suitable sentences ex- pressive of good feeling and hearty wishes for her future welfare. He called upon the men to give the lady three cheers, which were given with much enthusiasm. Mr. S. K. INICTSPIIATT appropriately responded on behalf of his wife, who he remarked wished every prosperity to the works and workmen. (Cheers ) Mr. J. L. MusPnarr then delivered a short address, in 'which he observed that their family would be much grati- fied whets they heard how his brother had been received, and the presents they had given him and his wife, not only because it was due to him as a man, but for the way in which he had laboured in the Widnes works which had been established so long. They were nearly the oldest works in Widnes. It was only on Christmas Day that his grandfather, who is over 90 yeais of age, was inquiring most particularly into the details of their Widnes works. This showed how even the first of their alkali manufacturers was still deeply Interested in that chemical masufacture, which was the staple production of this part of the kingdom. He should have been almost disheartened if he had not been asked to witness that presentation to his brother. He felt very much the honour they conferred upon him some years ago when he was married, and he could only say that such exhibitions 'of kindly feeling increased the interest which the family had in Widnes, which was the birthplace of some ef the ' laluspratts.—ln response too a call from Mr. J. Mcllroy, three cheers were given for the welfare of the happy couple; and Mr. S. K. MIISPRATT again thanked the men for the enthusiastic reception they had given him and his wife. Ha also personally thanked Mr. Lewis for the kind remarks he 1 bad made in presenting that handsome tray and chain, ! which had been chosen with a taste that he did not think could be surpassed. He WAS sure that if one thing would bring happiness and prosperity it would be their kind-hearted gift.—Three hearty cheers haying been given for the firm, the proceedings terminated.—We may state that the necklet was obtained from Mr. Wm. Nicolls, of Lord-street, Liver- pool; and the tray froin'Mr. T. J. Paris, of the earns city. The united value of the articles amounted to nearly 100 guineas.

div.head: MYSTERIOUS DEATH OF A WOMAN
div.p: MYSTERIOUS DEATH OF A WOMAN
AT WIDNES.

At the Angel Holel, Widnes, on Tuesday afternoon, Mr. Brighouse, coroner, held an adjourned inquest touching the death of Martha Ellen Birkenhead, of 17, Beamont-street, Widnes. Mr. H. Sherratt was the foreman of the jury—Dr. McDonnell stated that he had made a post mortem examina- tion of the deceased, and he described the state of the body. He was satisfied that inflammation of the brain had been set up by some external violence, which had terminated in snppuration and abscess causing death. The brain primarily was not in A healthy condition. It was in such a condition that external injuries would soon cause death. All the symptoms described might arise without external injuries. The injuries were sticli as would be caused by a fall down- stairs.—Jane McKeevan said she lived at 19, Beamont- street, which was next door to the house where the deceased lived. About half-past twelve on Sunday morning, the 13th Inst., she was sitting by the the in the kitchen, when she heard an awful noise iu the next house as though a person was falling downstairs. She listened, but did not hear any tries. The deceased had only lived in the house a fortnight, land she had never heard, her quarrel with her husband.— John Birkenhead said thwdeceased, who was 36 years of age, was his wife. They had been married 15 years. On Saturday, the 12th inst., he went to bed about 10 o'clock, leaving his wife downstairs. She was in drink, and there was a gill of beer in the house. Witness had only had three glasses of beer, and he was sober. He did not awake until about five o'clock on the following morning, when his wite came to bed. He judged the hour by the darkness. When his wife came to bed ehe did not say anything. She had i come to bed early n the mornint on other occasions. Wit- , ness rose at about eight o'clock on the Si.nday morning, leaving his wife in bed'. Deceased rose about nine o'clock and about 11 o'clock she complained uf her head aching: She went to bed hout thee o'clock in the afternoon. On Monday she only got up foe an hour, and then went to bed again. He sent for e doctor on Wednesday, and Dr. Mc- Donnell's assistant came. She was at that time insensible, and the doctor applied remedies, but his wife died on Thurs- day. In cross-examination, witness stated he did not know that his wife had fallen dostairs or been injured in any way. She was drunk when she came to bed. She was ad- dicted to drink, and he had often seen her drunk.— The Coroner said it was clear from the evidence of the doctor that the deceased came to her death by inflammation of the brain, set up by ex- ternal injuries. They could not say with cer- tainty how they were caused, hut presuming the Pay worst —that her husband pushed her downstairs, there was no proof of it, and it was only supposition, and they could not come to a conclusion. On the other hand, there was direct evidence to show that the woman living next door heard a fall as of someone falling downstairs. Now it appeared the woman had only lived in the houso a fortnight, and it was quite likely that going upstairs in a drunken state she had fallen deism. The husband, after working hard all the week and having bad an extra glass or two, most likely would be in such a round slumber that a Tall downstairs would not disturb him. No doubt the woman had fallen ,down and lay at the bottom in a drunken slumber until she , came to her senses, and then went to bed.-1 be jury re- turned a yerdict that "The deceased died from inflamma- tion of the brain set up by external injuries, as would injuries west from the medical evidence, but how the said were caused there was no evidence to show."

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The ordinary fortnightly meeting cf this Board was held in the Boardroom, Whiston Workhouse,-on Thursday fore- noon, Mr. W. Tyrer presiding. There were also present Messrs. W. Newsome, John Fidler, James Agnew, J. T. Hall, T. Dobell, W. Birchall, John Lowe, T. Saddler, W. Gerrard, S. Marsh, W. G. Ashton, John Leatherbarrow, James Buckley, Joseph Jackson, Edward Syder, John Grifßth, John Kenwright, Henry Hahne, T. P. F. Hill, W. Swift, J. Matthews, T. Eatock, W. Gilbody, B. Longton ; the Heys. J. Barnacle and T. Chambers; Mr. H. S. Hartley (clerk).

div.head: MASTER'S REPORT.
div.p: MASTER'S REPORT.

The WORM:MUSH —lll—ri-ST--;1; —r-,;;;;a that there were at present 08 inmates ia the Workhouse, 485 in the preceding week, and 588 in the corresponding week of last year. There were 51 vagrants relieved during the week, and there were 288 patients in the Workhouse.

div.head: ORGANIST AND HER DUTIES.
div.p: THE ORGANIST AND HER DUTIES.

A letter was read by the Clerk from Miss Charlotte A. Saunders, Prescot, organist at the Workhouse Chapel, in which she resigned her post, at the same time saying she must express her surprise that obtaining assistance in the discharge of her duty should be considered a matter of com- plaint. She had never failed to be present at two services each Sunday, and the chaplains had never made any complaint. The CHAIRMAN said he understood the organist had been present at the Catholic services, and had got an assistant to 'attend the Protestant services. He had, however, been under the impression at last meeting that the organist had not attended any service for six months.—Several Guardians also said that they had been under the same impression as the Chairman.—lt war, however, agreed that another organist should be advertised for, at the same salary as hitherto.

div.head: TILE FISH DINNERS.
div.p: TILE FISH DINNERS.

_ ..... The CLERK said that the Loci' Government Board had requested that at the expiratiOn of three months after the commencement of a fish diepry at the Workhouse, they should be furnished with a report as to its effect on the health of the inmates He (the clerk) had written to the medical officer (Mr. Hall) on the subject, and he replied that he thought the fish dinners had been a great boon to the inmates generally.—The WORKHOUSE MASTER also re- ported that the dinners had given general satisfaction.

div.head: COMTLIMENTING TR-E SALVATION ARMY.
div.p: COMTLIMENTING TR-E SALVATION ARMY.

The CLERK said he had re-e-eirTecr .:CO-roni:iTii;alion from a gentleman named Jones, who livee at Southport, which showed that he was desirous of adopting the girl Anders, who was so cruelly treated at St. Helens some time ago.-.-A GUARDIAN: Does he keep a lodging-house 7—The CLERIC coeld not say what he was. He was inclined to think he was a retired cap in, but whether of the navy or Salvation Army he could rt say. (Laughter.)—Mr. FIDLER For God's Bike keep her out of that. (Laughter.)—The CLERK also mentioned that a man named Runcorn had left his wife chargeable to the Union. He had heard that the man had become connected with the Salvation Army, but on writing to their headquarters he was informed that such a MCI was not known there. He suggestel that in order to find his whereabouts they offer a reward of £3. They had already offered £1 but that had not had effect, but if they offered £3 it might tempt 80R18 of the "brethren " to tura upon him. (Laughter.)—The Clerk's suggestion was adopted.

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF TREASURER.
div.p: APPOINTMENT OF TREASURER.

Two applica-tiM;-ijii7l.i;e To-os-OlTreal-s-M•ar to the Board were read, one being from Mr. G. Cochrane, newly-appointed manager to Parr's Bank at Prescot ; and the other by Mr.. C. C. White, of the Manchester and Salford Bank, St lielens.—Mr.NEWSollo moved, and Mr. LIILTIIERBARROW seconded that Mr. White be appointed.—Mr. DOBELL moved, and Mr. KENWRIORT seconded that Mr. Cochrane be appointed.—On being put to the vote, Mr. White was elected by 10 votes to 11 which were recorded for Mr. Coehrane.—Mr. White was therefore appointed, the security being fixed at £lO,OOO.

div.head: TENDERS.
div.p: TENDERS.
Several tenders for alterations at the Workhouse were considered, and that of Mr. R. H. Davies, Boundary-road, St. Helens, of £260 was accepted.

div.head: INCREASED ASSESSMENT OF THE RAILWAYS.
div.p: THE INCREASED ASSESSMENT OF THE RAILWAYS.

_ Mr HALL moved a vote of thanks to the Clerk, the Board's solicitor (sir. Tyrer), and Mr. Leatherbarrow, the chairman of the Finance Committee, for the able manner in which they had sustained the new and increased assessment of railways, in face of the appeal of which the London and North-Western Railway Company bad given notice, but had now withdrawn from.—Mr. NEWSOME seconded this vote of thanks, and in doing so said that the increased assessment of railways would relieve the rest of the ratepayers of the Union of lid in the £.—The vote was cordially given and responded to, Mr. LEACHERBAREOW mentioning that the increase in the assessment of the railways amounted to £80,098 ss, viz.: London and North- Western, £1T,293 51; other railways, £l2,Bos.—This con- cluded the business.

TIM TRAMWAY ACClDhNf.—lnumpson, the driver of the tram engine which ran away on the Wigan and remberton tramway and caused the accident which resulted in the death of Mr. T. W. Barker, district couqy coroner, was charged on remand at the Wigin County Police Court on Saturday with having caused the death of Mr... Barker. No evidence was offered, the coroner's inquiry not having con- cluded, and Thompson was further remanded until the 3let inst.

The third annual ball of the Rainhill Conservative As- sociation was held in the R tinhill Boys' School on FridAy evening. Much labour and skill,bad been expended in the decorations of the room. The attendance was very good, about 90 persons being present. The dinning was kept up with great zest until the small hours of morning, to the strains of the excellent quadrille band of the County Asy- lum. Mr. G. Collins acted as M.C.

• MOTHER AND DAUGHTER.—Margaret MeQuirts, a young woman, was on Tuesday charged at the Prescot Police Court with having assaal.ed her mother, Bose Bohan, at Rainbill.—lt appeared that the prisoner was married but still lived in the same loAlse with ner mother. They seem to have lived in a very unhappy manner together, and on Friday night, the 18th inst., according to the complainant, the assault complained of was committed.—Superintendent Barker said the prisoner was a perfect nuisance at Rainbill, and when out of gaol she woald not keep *away from her mother, who:n she ill-used. She bad been before convicted of aseaulting the complainaut.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for six weeks.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
THE TRANS VAAL.

• The Central News learns that the *Ay of Lord Derby to the Transvaal delegates will be delivered to-day. The pro- position of the delegates respecting the neutralisation of the trade route has been declined. and their proposed boundary line has been rejected on the ground that it is destitute of water and otherwise impracticable. One of the alternative propositions made by the Boer representatives has, however, teen practically entertained, and it is now hoped that a settlement upon these points will be speedily arrived at. Oa completion of the negotiations respecting the boundary the delegates still press for a solution of the suzerainty and debt questions, but it is well understood that these will be adjourned with little difficulty. The delegates will not visit Holland until after the whole of the business which brought them to Eng- land is finally settled.
The Marquis of Hertford died last night at half-past seven.

The ship Allegiance, of Liverpool, was towed into Cardiff yesterday. During Tuesday night's gale one of the men was washed overboard and drowned, and several seamen were injured. At V,Velsbpool, yesterday, Evan Evans, late assistant overseer for Llanfair, was committed for trial on a charge of embezzling and falsifying his accounts to the extent of about £5BO.

A Darenr.m.ro RATE COLLECTOR.—At Durham- Assizes, yesterday, Joseph Moore, a defaulting rate collector, was sentenced by Mr. Justice Field to eighteen months' hard labour for embezzling rates amounting to £l,OOO. A painful double drowning case was investigated by Coroner's jury, at Little Eaton, near Derby, yesterday evening. Two boys, aged respectively seven and twelve years, were playing beside a flooded brook, when one fell in. He called to his companion, who made an effort to save him, but both were drowned.

TERRIBLE COLLIERY EXPLOSION IN AMERICA: FIFTY- SEVEN MINERS KILLED.—From Intelligence received at New York regarding the explosion in the colliery at Crested Butte, it appears that fifty-seven persons were imprisoned in the mine, none of whom have yet been. discovered. It is believed that they were all killed instantly. A Cnurtm BLOWN DOWN.—lntelligence has reached Dublin that the recently built Roman Catholic church of Manorhamil ton has been destroyed by the gale. The roof collapsed and fell in with a crash, carrying with it the nave and the side walls, and crushing the beautiful pillars of Aberdeen granite. The altars and seats were destroyed, and what was a handsome place of worship has been transformed into a desolate ruin.

STRANGE CONDUCT OF MR. PARNELL.—Dctring the past three days several telegrams of an urgent character were despatched to Mr. Parnell by the Cork secretaries of the National League, urging him to state whether or not he in- tends addressing his constituents in Cork on Monday next, the theatre having been engaged for that purpose. To none of these communications has Mr. Parnell replied. Nothing more definite regarding his visit can be learned than that early in the week he telegraphed he would prefer waiting until the writ is issued._

GALLANT LIFEBOAT RESCUE—EarIy on Thursday morn- ing, daring the height of the gale, the vessel Edith. of Padstow, was reported in distress at Hasborough. The local lifeboat went to her assistance and found all the men on beard except one had been drowned. Communication was effected with the vessel, but while the surviving sea- man was being hauled into the boat he was killed by being crushed between it and the ship. On the way back the lifeboat was capsized mad the crew thrown into the water, but all were rescued.

FUNERAL OF Eau, GaosvErrou.—The remains or Earl Grosvenor, which had been removed from Saighton Towers on Thursday evening to Eccleston Church', were at noon consigned to their last resting place in the pretty little churchyard adjacent, side by side with the gravis of the late Duchess of Westminster and Lady Richard Grosvenor. Ile arrangements for the ceremony were of the simplest possible description. The Duke of Westminster is a patron of the Funeral Reform Association, and resolved to carry out the ceremony in accordance with the programme of that society.
